Thus P, A, O, B occur in that order, and AB is a diameter. Draw the joins required below. All radii of the circle are equal. For any other secant ray from P, call its first intersection the convex, or near, endpoint and its second intersection the concave, or far, endpoint. On either side of PO, the nearer ray means the one making the smaller angle with PO. [3.1, P1, P2, D1.17, D1.15]

**Step 2.** Let X be any point of the circumference not on PO. In triangle POX, the triangle inequality gives
PX < PO + OX = PO + OB = PB.
It also gives
PO < PX + OX.
But PO = PA + AO and AO = OX; removing the equal radii therefore gives PA < PX. Moreover, PA < PB because PA is a proper part of PB. Consequently PB is uniquely greatest and PA uniquely least among the segments from P to the circumference. [1.20, D1.15, CN3, CN5]

**Step 3.** Consider two nonaxial secant rays on the same side of PO, with PC nearer to PO than PD, and let C and D be their far endpoints. Since PC lies inside angle OPD, it meets OD at a point K between O and D. The point K is inside the circle, so the far endpoint C lies beyond K on the ray from P. Hence OC lies between OB and OD, and angle POC contains angle POD as a proper part. Thus angle POC is greater than angle POD. In triangles POC and POD, PO is common and OC = OD. Apply I.24 directly: its equal-side hypotheses are already supplied by the common side and the radii, and the greater included angle gives PC > PD. This proves the required ordering of the concave endpoints on either side of PO. [D1.15, CN5, 1.24]

**Step 4.** Let E and F be the near endpoints of those same rays, respectively. The ray PE lies inside angle OPF and meets OF at a point L between O and F. Since L is inside the circle and E is the first intersection with the circumference, E lies between P and L. Thus E is strictly inside triangle POF. Use I.21 here, since its nested-triangle configuration occurs directly: the two segments PE and EO, drawn from the ends of side PO to the interior point E, satisfy
PE + EO < PF + FO.
Since EO = FO, cancellation gives PE < PF. Therefore, among the convex endpoints on either side, the nearer ray to PA gives the smaller segment. [D1.15, 1.21, CN3, CN5]

**Step 5.** Let X be any nonaxial point of the circumference. At O, on the opposite side of the line PO, construct a ray OY such that angle POY equals angle POX, and let Y be its intersection with the circumference. The triangles POX and POY have PO common, OX = OY, and their included angles equal. Hence PX = PY, and angle OPX equals angle OPY. Thus every nonaxial segment has an equal mate on the other side of PA, equally inclined to it. Applying this construction to both intersections of a secant places their mates on the same opposite ray with their respective distances from P unchanged; the near endpoint therefore remains near, and the far endpoint remains far. Consequently, if two rays being compared lie on opposite sides of PA, replace one by its equal mate and apply Step 3 or Step 4 on a single side. The required strict orderings therefore hold without restriction to one side. [1.23, D1.15, 1.4, CN5]

**Step 6.** For uniqueness, use I.7, the direct same-side criterion. If distinct circumference points X and Z on the same side of PO satisfied PX = PZ, then also OX = OZ, since both are radii. On the fixed base PO there would therefore be two distinct vertices on the same side with both corresponding sides equal, contrary to I.7. Thus an equal length can occur at most once on each side. Step 5 supplies exactly one equal mate on the opposite side for every nonaxial segment, while Step 2 excludes any mate for either axial extreme. Hence no three segments from P to the circle are equal: each nonaxial length occurs exactly twice, once on each side of the least segment PA. Together with Steps 2–5, this proves all the assertions. ## Proposition 3.10
**Statement:** A circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.

**Step 1.** Suppose, for a contradiction, that two circles cut one another at three distinct points A, B, C. Let their centres be O and P. Since the circles cut one another, O ≠ P. Their radii give OA = OB = OC and PA = PB = PC. [D1.15, D1.16, 3.5]

**Step 2.** Join O to P and each centre to A, B, C, and produce OP in both directions. We use I.7 directly: the equal radii supply precisely its two pairs of equal sides on the common base OP. We therefore seek two common points strictly on the same side of this line. [P1, P2, 1.7]

**Step 3.** The points A, B, C are not collinear. Otherwise one would lie between the other two; but the segment joining those other two points lies within either circle, so its intermediate point cannot also lie on the circumference. [3.2]

**Step 4.** None of A, B, C lies on the line OP. For suppose one of them, X, did. By Step 3, another, Y, lies off OP. Also X differs from both centres, since each centre lies within its own circle. Of the three distinct collinear points O, P, X, one lies between the other two; consequently one of the lengths OP, OX, PX equals the sum of the other two. But OX = OY and PX = PY, since X and Y belong to both circumferences. Thus one side of the nondegenerate triangle OPY equals the sum of its other two sides, contrary to I.20. [D1.15, D1.16, 1.20]

**Step 5.** Since A, B, C all lie off OP, two of them must lie on the same side of it; call them A and B. On the same base OP and the same side of it, the segments OA, PA meet at A, while OB, PB meet at the distinct point B, with OA = OB and PA = PB. This is impossible by I.7. The supposition is therefore false: **a circle does not cut a circle at more points than two.** [1.7]

**Statement:** If two circles touch one another internally, and their centres be taken, the straight line joining their centres, if it be also produced, will fall on the point of contact of the circles.

Since the contact is external, the circles have no overlapping interiors: they meet without cutting one another (D3.3 and the external-contact hypothesis). Thus the order along AB is A, D, E, B, allowing D and E to coincide; the opposite order of D and E would give a segment inside both circles. Consequently,
AD + EB ≤ AB,

This contradicts Step 3. Therefore the straight line joining the centres A and B passes through the point of contact C, as required.

## Proposition 3.13
**Statement:** A circle does not touch a circle at more points than one, whether it touch it internally or externally.

**Step 1.** Suppose, for contradiction, that two circles touch at two distinct points A and B. Let their centres be O and P. Since touching circles do not have the same centre, O and P are distinct. [D1.15, D1.16, 3.6]

**Step 2.** Take the direct line-of-centres route: draw OP and produce it as necessary. If the contact is internal, apply 3.11 at A and again at B; both points lie on the produced line of centres. If the contact is external, apply 3.12 at each point, with the same result. Thus A, B, O, and P lie on one straight line in either case. [P1, P2, 3.11, 3.12]

**Step 3.** The radii of each circle are equal, so OA = OB and PA = PB. Each centre must lie strictly between A and B: it cannot coincide with a circumference point, since it lies within its circle; and if it lay outside the segment AB, one of its two equal radii would be a proper part of the other, contrary to the whole being greater than the part. [D1.15, CN5]

**Step 4.** Since the centres are distinct and both lie between A and B, interchange their names if necessary so that their order is A, O, P, B. Then AP > AO and OB > PB. Together with AO = OB, these give AP > AO = OB > PB, contradicting PA = PB. Therefore two circles cannot touch at two distinct points. A circle consequently does not touch another circle at more than one point, whether internally or externally. [CN5, D1.15]

## Proposition 3.14
**Statement:** In a circle equal straight lines are equally distant from the centre, and those which are equally distant from the centre are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let AB and CD be chords of a circle with centre O, and first suppose that neither chord passes through O. Bisect AB at M and CD at N, and join OM, ON, OA, and OC [1.10, P1]. We choose the midpoint construction because the straight lines through O which bisect the chords are immediately perpendicular to them by III.3 [3.3]. Thus OM and ON are precisely the perpendiculars whose equality means that the chords are equally distant from the centre [D3.4].

**Step 2.** The radii OA and OC are equal [D1.15]. Applying I.47 to the right-angled triangles OMA and ONC gives
OA² = OM² + AM²,
OC² = ON² + CN² [1.47].
Consequently,
OM² + AM² = ON² + CN² [CN1].
Here squares denote the areas of the squares on the indicated segments. We use I.47 because this single equality proves both implications by subtraction.

**Step 3.** Suppose AB = CD. Since M and N are midpoints, AM = CN: otherwise doubling the greater half would give a greater chord [CN2, CN5]. Subtracting their equal squares from the equality in Step 2 gives OM² = ON², and hence OM = ON [CN3]. Therefore AB and CD are equally distant from O [D3.4].

**Step 4.** Conversely, suppose AB and CD are equally distant from O. Then OM = ON [D3.4]. Subtracting their equal squares from the equality in Step 2 gives AM² = CN², and hence AM = CN [CN3]. Since MB = AM and ND = CN, adding equal halves gives AB = CD [CN2].

**Step 5.** It remains to include chords through the centre, whose distance from it is zero. Such a chord has length twice a radius [D1.15, CN2]. Any chord XY not through O is shorter: joining OX and OY gives a triangle, and XY < OX + OY, which is twice a radius [P1, 1.20, D1.15]. Thus, if two equal chords include one through O, both must pass through O and have the same zero distance. Conversely, if two equally distant chords include one through O, both have zero distance and therefore both pass through O; each is twice a radius, so they are equal [D1.15, CN1, CN2]. Together with Steps 3 and 4, this proves that equal straight lines in a circle are equally distant from the centre, and those equally distant from the centre are equal to one another.

## Proposition 3.15
**Statement:** Of straight lines in a circle the diameter is greatest, and of the rest the nearer to the centre is always greater than the more remote.

**Step 1.** Let O be the centre of the circle, AB any diameter, and CD any chord not passing through O. Join OC and OD. Since AB passes through O, AB = AO + OB. [D1.17, P1]

**Step 2.** All radii are equal, so AO + OB = OC + OD. In triangle COD, OC + OD > CD. Therefore AB > CD. Thus every diameter is greater than every chord not through the centre; moreover, all diameters are equal, each consisting of two radii. [D1.15, CN2, 1.20]

**Step 3.** Now let CD and EF be chords not through O, with CD nearer to O than EF. Bisect CD at H and EF at K, and join OH, OK, and OE. The midpoint-to-perpendicular direction of 3.3 gives OH perpendicular to CD and OK perpendicular to EF. Consequently OH < OK, by the definition of greater distance from the centre. Also CH = HD and EK = KF. [1.10, P1, 3.3, D3.5]

**Step 4.** Write S(XY) for the square on a segment XY. The direct route is to compare the right triangles OHC and OKE, since their perpendicular legs are precisely those defining the distances. By the theorem on the square of the hypotenuse,
S(CH) + S(OH) = S(OC),
S(EK) + S(OK) = S(OE).
Since OC and OE are radii, these two sums are equal. [1.47, D1.15]

**Step 5.** Since OH < OK, the square on OK is greater than the square on OH: by 2.4, the square on a greater segment consists of the square on a part equal to the smaller segment together with additional positive areas. Remove an area equal to S(OH) from each of the equal sums in Step 4. On one side there remains S(CH); on the other there remains S(EK) together with the positive excess of S(OK) over S(OH). Hence S(CH) > S(EK). [2.4, CN3, CN5]

**Step 6.** Therefore CH > EK. Indeed, equality of the segments would give equal squares, while CH < EK would, by 2.4 and the whole–part principle, give S(CH) < S(EK). Since CD consists of two parts each equal to CH, and EF of two parts each equal to EK, it follows that CD > EF. Together with Step 2, this proves that the diameter is greatest, and that of the remaining chords the nearer to the centre is always greater than the more remote. [2.4, CN5, CN2, 3.3]

## Proposition 3.16
**Statement:** The straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of a circle from its extremity will fall outside the circle, and into the space between the straight line and the circumference another straight line cannot be interposed; further the angle of the semicircle is greater, and the remaining angle less, than any acute rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a diameter of the circle, O its centre, and let the straight line through B perpendicular to AB have ray BT on the side of a chosen semicircle. Thus ∠OBT is right. The angle of this semicircle at B is the curvilinear angle between BA and its circumference; the remaining angle is between that circumference and BT. [D1.17, D1.18, D1.10, D3.7]

**Step 2.** Suppose the perpendicular met the circumference again at C, and join OC. Since OB = OC, the angles OBC and BCO are equal. The equal radii make the isosceles-triangle theorem the immediate route here. But ∠OBC is right, so both these angles would be right, contrary to the theorem that any two angles of a triangle are together less than two right angles. Thus the perpendicular has no second point on the circumference. Nor can it enter the circle: if it did, its continuation would meet the circumference again. This applies to both rays of the perpendicular, which therefore lies outside the circle except at B. [P1, P2, D1.15, D1.10, 1.5, 1.17]

**Step 3.** Consider any ray r from B strictly between BO and BT. Draw OF perpendicular to the straight line containing r. Its foot F lies on r: if F lay on the opposite ray, the angle OBF would be greater than a right angle, which, together with the right angle at F, would contradict the two-angle bound for a triangle. In the right-angled triangle OBF, ∠BOF is less than a right angle. Therefore the side OB opposite the right angle is greater than OF. Consequently F is inside the circle. Indeed, if F were on or outside it, OF would meet the circumference at G on or before F, giving OF ≥ OG = OB, a contradiction. [1.12, D1.10, D1.12, 1.17, 1.19, D1.15, CN5]

**Step 4.** Continue r through the interior point F until it meets the circumference at C. The chord BC lies within the circle. Hence every ray strictly between BO and BT has an initial portion inside the chosen semicircle. Any straight line interposed at B between BT and the circumference would have to follow such a ray while remaining outside the circle, which is impossible. No straight line can therefore be interposed in that space. [P2, 3.2; Step 3]

**Step 5.** Let α be any acute rectilineal angle. At B construct ∠OBR equal to α, toward BT. Because α is less than a right angle, BR lies strictly between BO and BT. By Step 4, its initial portion lies inside the semicircle. Thus ∠OBR is a proper part of the curvilinear angle between BA and the circumference. The angle of the semicircle is therefore greater than α, and hence greater than every acute rectilineal angle. [1.23, D1.12, D3.7, CN5; Step 4]

**Step 6.** Again let α be any acute rectilineal angle, and construct ∠TBS equal to α, toward BO. The ray BS also lies strictly between BT and BO and initially lies inside the semicircle. The circumference therefore lies, near B, between BT and BS, so the remaining curvilinear angle between BT and the circumference is a proper part of ∠TBS. It is consequently less than α, and hence less than every acute rectilineal angle. Together with Steps 2 and 4, this proves all the assertions. [1.23, D1.12, CN5; Step 4]

## Proposition 3.17
**Statement:** From a given point to draw a straight line touching a given circle.

**Step 1.** Let Γ be the given circle and A the given point, outside Γ or on its circumference. These are the admissible cases: a line through an interior point cuts the circle and therefore cannot touch it. Find the centre O of Γ. [D3.2, 3.1]

**Step 2.** First suppose A is outside Γ. Join OA, and let B be its intersection with Γ between O and A. Describe the auxiliary circle Ω with centre O and radius OA. [P1, P3]

**Step 3.** At B draw a perpendicular to OA, and produce it to meet Ω at D, choosing either side of OA. Join OD, let E be its intersection with Γ between O and D, and join AE. [1.11, P2, P1]

**Step 4.** Compare triangles OBD and OEA. We have OB = OE, since both are radii of Γ, and OD = OA, since both are radii of Ω. Moreover, ∠BOD = ∠EOA: OB and OA lie along the same ray, as do OE and OD, so these angles coincide. Thus side–angle–side is the direct choice, since the two pairs of sides and their included angles are already equal. By I.4, ∠OBD = ∠OEA. But ∠OBD is right by construction; therefore AE is perpendicular to OE. [D1.15, CN4, 1.4, 1.11]

**Step 5.** Produce EO through O to the opposite circumference of Γ, obtaining a diameter with extremity E. The line AE is perpendicular to this diameter at E. By III.16 it falls outside Γ apart from E. It therefore meets Γ without cutting it, even when produced, and so touches Γ at E. Thus AE is the required straight line from the exterior point A. [P2, D1.17, 3.16, D3.2]

**Step 6.** If instead A lies on Γ, join OA and produce it through O to form a diameter with extremity A. At A draw a straight line perpendicular to that diameter. By III.16 this line falls outside Γ apart from A, and hence touches Γ at A. Therefore, in either admissible case, a straight line touching the given circle has been drawn from the given point. [P1, P2, D1.17, 1.11, 3.16, D3.2]

## Proposition 3.18
**Statement:** If a straight line touch a circle, and a straight line be joined from the centre to the point of contact, the straight line so joined will be perpendicular to the tangent.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line ℓ touch the circle at A, let O be its centre, and let OA be joined. The centre O lies inside the circle. Since a tangent, even when produced, does not cut the circle, ℓ contains no interior point of the circle; in particular, O is not on ℓ. [D1.15, D1.16, D3.2]

**Step 2.** Use the perpendicular-foot route. Suppose that OA is not perpendicular to ℓ. From O draw OB perpendicular to ℓ, with B on ℓ. Then B differs from A, and ∠OBA is a right angle. [1.12, D1.10]

**Step 3.** In triangle OAB, the angles OBA and OAB together are less than two right angles. Since ∠OBA is right, ∠OAB is less than ∠OBA. Here the two-angle bound is the natural first result needed; a full triangle angle-sum formula is unnecessary. The greater angle is subtended by the greater side, so OA > OB. [1.17, 1.19]

**Step 4.** But B, being on the tangent, is not inside the circle. Since O is inside, the segment OB meets the circumference at a point E, either before reaching B or at B itself. If E is between O and B, OB > OE because the whole is greater than its part; if E = B, OB = OE. Thus OB ≥ OE. [D3.2, D1.15, D1.16, CN5]

**Step 5.** As OA and OE both join the centre to the circumference, OA = OE. Consequently OB ≥ OA, contradicting OA > OB from Step 3. The supposition is therefore false: OA is perpendicular to the tangent ℓ. Hence the straight line joined from the centre to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent. [D1.15, D1.16, D1.10]

## Proposition 3.19
**Statement:** If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact a straight line be drawn at right angles to the tangent, the centre of the circle will be on the straight line so drawn.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line t touch the circle at A, and let ℓ be the straight line drawn through A at right angles to t. Let O be the centre of the circle, and join AO. [P1]

**Step 2.** Apply III.18 directly: it concerns precisely the given tangent and the radius to its point of contact. Thus AO is perpendicular to t, and the angles it makes with t are right angles. [3.18, D1.10]

**Step 3.** Suppose that O does not lie on ℓ. Choose a ray AX of ℓ on the same side of t as O, producing ℓ through A if necessary, and choose a ray AT along t. Since AX and AO are distinct rays in the same half-plane bounded by t, one of the angles TAX and TAO is a proper part of the other. Therefore these angles are unequal, since the whole is greater than the part. [P2, CN5]

**Step 4.** But angle TAX is right by hypothesis, and angle TAO is right by Step 2. All right angles are equal, contradicting Step 3. Therefore O lies on ℓ: the centre is on the straight line drawn at right angles to the tangent from the point of contact. [P4]

## Proposition 3.20
**Statement:** In a circle the angle at the centre is double of the angle at the circumference, when the angles have the same circumference as base.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be distinct points on a circle with centre O. Let Γ be the arc AB not containing C, and let Θ be the angle at O standing on Γ. Thus Θ is measured through that same arc, including a reflex central angle if required. We must prove Θ = 2∠ACB. Join OA, OB, and CO, and produce CO through O to meet the circle again at D. This diameter gives the direct route: first compare angles having D as one endpoint, then add or subtract them. [D3.9, P1, P2]

**Step 2.** For either endpoint X = A or X = B, provided X ≠ D, consider triangle COX. Its radii OC and OX are equal, so ∠OCX = ∠CXO. Since CD has the same direction from C as CO, ∠OCX = ∠XCD. Use the exterior-angle clause of 1.32 directly, since OD is already the produced side CO: ∠XOD = ∠OCX + ∠CXO = 2∠XCD. Consequently,
∠AOD = 2∠ACD and ∠BOD = 2∠BCD,
whenever the respective endpoint differs from D. [D1.15, 1.5, 1.32, CN2]

**Step 3.** If D coincides with A, the central angle on Γ is ∠BOD and ∠ACB = ∠BCD. Step 2, with X = B, therefore gives Θ = 2∠ACB. If D coincides with B, the same conclusion follows from Step 2 with X = A. This disposes of the cases in which CD is a side of the circumference angle. [D3.9; Step 2]

**Step 4.** Suppose D lies strictly on Γ. Then CD lies inside ∠ACB, and the central angle on Γ is the sum of the central angles on AD and DB. Hence
∠ACB = ∠ACD + ∠DCB,
Θ = ∠AOD + ∠DOB.
Adding the equalities from Step 2 gives
Θ = 2∠ACD + 2∠DCB = 2∠ACB.
This addition also covers the case in which Θ is reflex. [D3.9, CN2; Step 2]

**Step 5.** Finally, suppose D lies outside Γ and is distinct from A and B. Then A and B lie on the same side of the diameter CD. Interchanging their names if necessary, let CA be the ray nearer CD. The angle at C and the central angle on Γ are now the corresponding differences:
∠ACB = ∠BCD − ∠ACD,
Θ = ∠BOD − ∠AOD.
Subtracting the equalities from Step 2 therefore gives
Θ = 2∠BCD − 2∠ACD = 2∠ACB.
The three positions of D exhaust the possibilities. Thus, in a circle, the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference standing on the same circumference. [D3.9, CN3; Step 2]

## Proposition 3.21
**Statement:** In a circle the angles in the same segment are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the base of a segment of a circle, and let P and Q be any two points on its circumference, distinct from A and B. Join PA, PB, QA, and QB. The angles APB and AQB are angles in this same segment. Both have as their circumference-base the same arc AB opposite the segment containing P and Q. [D3.6, D3.8, P1]

**Step 2.** Find the centre O of the circle and join OA and OB. Let Θ denote the angle at the centre corresponding to that common arc AB. We compare the two given angles directly through Θ, choosing the central angle with their common arc as base. [3.1, P1]

**Step 3.** The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference when they have the same circumference as base. Applying this first to APB and then to AQB gives Θ = 2∠APB and Θ = 2∠AQB. Thus each given angle is half of the same central angle Θ. [3.20]

**Step 4.** Consequently ∠APB = ∠AQB, since both equal the same half of Θ. As P and Q were arbitrary, the angles in the same segment of a circle are equal to one another. [CN1]

## Proposition 3.22
**Statement:** The opposite angles of quadrilaterals in circles are equal to two right angles.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, with its vertices in that order. Join AC and BD. These diagonals divide the interior angles at their endpoints. [P1]

**Step 2.** Choose the same-segment route, since the diagonals directly supply angles to compare with those of a triangle. The angles BAC and BDC stand on BC in the same segment, and the angles BCA and BDA stand on BA in the same segment. Hence
∠BAC = ∠BDC and ∠BCA = ∠BDA.
Adding these equalities gives
∠BAC + ∠BCA = ∠BDC + ∠BDA = ∠CDA. [3.21, CN2]

**Step 3.** In triangle ABC,
∠ABC + ∠BAC + ∠BCA = two right angles.
Using Step 2, it follows that
∠ABC + ∠CDA = two right angles. [1.32, CN2, CN1]

**Step 4.** Likewise, the angles ABD and ACD stand on AD in the same segment, and the angles ADB and ACB stand on AB in the same segment. Thus
∠ABD = ∠ACD and ∠ADB = ∠ACB.
Adding gives
∠ABD + ∠ADB = ∠ACD + ∠ACB = ∠BCD. [3.21, CN2]

**Step 5.** In triangle ABD,
∠BAD + ∠ABD + ∠ADB = two right angles.
Using Step 4, it follows that
∠BAD + ∠BCD = two right angles.
Therefore each pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle is together equal to two right angles. [1.32, CN2, CN1]

## Proposition 3.23
**Statement:** On the same straight line there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles on the same side.

**Step 1.** Suppose that two similar but unequal circular segments are constructed on the same straight line AB and on the same side of it. Each is bounded by AB and a circular arc. Their circles are distinct and already meet at A and B, so their arcs cannot meet again; consequently one segment lies within the other. Call the outer segment ACB and the inner segment ADB. [D3.6, 3.10]

**Step 2.** Take D on the arc of the inner segment, distinct from A and B. Draw AD and produce it to meet the outer arc at C, so that A, D, C occur in that order. Join DB and CB. [P1, P2]

**Step 3.** The angles ADB and ACB are angles in the two respective segments. Since the segments are similar, these angles are equal:
∠ADB = ∠ACB. [D3.8, D3.11]

**Step 4.** Apply the exterior-angle theorem directly, since the collinearity just constructed makes ∠ADB an exterior angle of triangle BDC. It is therefore greater than the opposite interior angle BCD. But the rays CA and CD coincide, so ∠BCD = ∠ACB. Thus ∠ADB > ∠ACB, contradicting Step 3. Hence on the same straight line there cannot be constructed two similar and unequal segments of circles on the same side. [1.16]

## Proposition 3.24
**Statement:** Similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let S and T be similar segments of circles on equal straight lines AB and DE. By the definition of similar segments, the angles admitted by S and T are equal. [D3.11]

**Step 2.** Apply S to the position of T, placing A on D and AB along DE, with the two segments on the same side of DE. Since AB equals DE, B falls on E. Denote the placed segment by S′. This application preserves the figure and its angles: corresponding figures and angles coincide under superposition and therefore are equal. Thus S′ equals S and remains similar to T. [CN4, D3.11]

**Step 3.** Use III.23 directly, since the application has put the segments on the same straight line and on the same side. That proposition forbids two similar and unequal segments in this position; hence S′ and T are equal. Since S also equals S′, S and T are equal. Therefore similar segments of circles on equal straight lines are equal to one another. [3.23, CN1]

## Proposition 3.25
**Statement:** Given a segment of a circle, to describe the complete circle of which it is a segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the straight boundary of the given segment, and choose a third point C on its curved boundary. Denote by Γ the circle of which it is a segment; this names the existing circle without assuming that it has been drawn. If S is on the straight line AB, the equal radii SA and SB force S to be the midpoint M: S cannot be beyond either endpoint, since then one radius would be a proper part of the other. Thus S lies on ℓ in this case also. Applying the same reasoning to AC and its midpoint N shows that S lies on m. [D1.15, D1.16, P1, 3.3, CN5]

**Step 6.** With centre O and distance OA describe a circle. Since O is the centre of Γ and A lies on Γ, this is precisely the complete circle whose segment was given. Therefore the required circle has been described. [P3, D1.15, D1.16]

## Proposition 3.26
**Statement:** In equal circles equal angles stand on equal circumferences, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.

**Step 1.** Let two equal circles have centres O and P, and let α and β be the circumferences cut off between endpoints A, B and C, D respectively. Choose X and Y on the complementary circumferences; if the given angles are at the circumferences, use their vertices as X and Y. Join the chords, radii, and sides of the angles AXB and CYD. These inscribed angles stand on α and β respectively. [P1; D3.8; D3.9]

**Step 2.** By III.20, the central angles standing on α and β are respectively double ∠AXB and ∠CYD. Consequently, whether the given equal angles are central or inscribed, both corresponding pairs are equal. Indeed, equal magnitudes have equal doubles, and equal doubles have equal halves: an inequality between the halves would persist upon doubling. [3.20; CN2; CN5]

**Step 3.** Since the circles are equal, OA = PC and OB = PD. The ordinary included angles between these pairs of radii are also equal. For minor intercepted circumferences they are the central angles already compared; for major intercepted circumferences they are the remainders after subtracting those equal central angles from a full turn. Thus, by I.4, AB = CD. If the endpoints are diametrically opposite, the triangle argument is unnecessary: AB and CD are equal diameters directly. [D3.1; CN3; 1.4]

**Step 4.** Consider the segments bounded by AB and the circumference AXB, and by CD and the circumference CYD. Since ∠AXB = ∠CYD, these segments are similar. Their bases AB and CD are equal, so III.24 makes the segments equal, and hence their corresponding curved boundaries AXB and CYD are equal. This is the direct equal-base segment route: III.24 applies precisely to the similarity and equal bases just established. [D3.6; D3.11; 3.24]

**Step 5.** The whole circumferences of the given equal circles are equal. Subtract from them the equal complementary circumferences AXB and CYD. The remaining circumferences α and β are therefore equal. Thus, in equal circles, equal angles stand on equal circumferences, whether the angles are at the centres or at the circumferences. [D3.1; CN3]

## Proposition 3.27
**Statement:** In equal circles angles standing on equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.

**Step 1.** Let two equal circles have equal circumferences (arcs) AB and CD. Choose any point X on the remaining circumference of the first circle and any point Y on the remaining circumference of the second. Join XA, XB, YC, and YD, so that ∠AXB and ∠CYD stand on the given arcs. [P1] We prove equality at the circumferences first, using the immediately preceding proposition III.26; III.20 will then give equality at the centres by doubling.

**Step 2.** Suppose ∠AXB and ∠CYD are unequal. Interchanging the circles if necessary, let ∠AXB be the smaller. At Y, on YC and toward YD, construct ∠CYE equal to ∠AXB, and produce its second side to meet the circle again at E. Since the constructed angle is smaller than ∠CYD, its second side lies strictly inside that angle; hence E lies strictly within the specified arc CD, and arc CE is a proper part of arc CD. [1.23, P2]

**Step 3.** The equal angles ∠AXB and ∠CYE stand in equal circles, so the arcs AB and CE on which they stand are equal. [3.26] But arc AB equals arc CD by hypothesis; therefore arc CE equals arc CD. [CN1] This is impossible, because arc CE is a proper part of arc CD, and the whole is greater than the part. [CN5] Thus ∠AXB = ∠CYD. Since X and Y were arbitrary points on the remaining circumferences, the required equality holds for angles at the circumferences.

**Step 4.** Find the centres O and P of the two circles, and join OA, OB, PC, and PD. [3.1, P1] The angle at O standing on arc AB is double ∠AXB, and the angle at P standing on arc CD is double ∠CYD. [3.20] Since ∠AXB = ∠CYD, adding each angle to itself gives equal doubles. [CN2] Consequently the corresponding angles at the centres are also equal. Therefore, in equal circles, angles standing on equal circumferences are equal to one another, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.

## Proposition 3.28
**Statement:** In equal circles equal straight lines cut off equal circumferences, the greater equal to the greater and the less to the less.

**Step 1.** Let Γ and Γ′ be equal circles, and let AB and DE be equal straight lines joining points on their respective circumferences. The circles have equal radii. Consequently, when their centres are superposed, their complete circumferences coincide and are equal. [D3.1, D1.15, CN4]

**Step 2.** First dispose of the diameter case. If AB is a diameter, then DE equals a diameter of Γ′, since the circles are equal. Therefore DE must itself be a diameter: otherwise it would be shorter than a diameter. The same argument applies with the circles interchanged. Each diameter bisects its circle, and superposing the equal circles with these diameters aligned makes their corresponding semicircumferences coincide. Thus the cut-off circumferences are equal in this case. Henceforth suppose neither chord is a diameter. [D3.1, 3.15, D1.17, CN4]

**Step 3.** Find the centres O and P of Γ and Γ′, and join OA, OB, PD, and PE. Since these are radii of equal circles,
OA = PD and OB = PE.
Also AB = DE by hypothesis. [3.1, P1, D1.15, D3.1]

**Step 4.** The triangles OAB and PDE therefore have their three sides respectively equal. Hence their angles contained by the radii are equal:
∠AOB = ∠DPE.
This central-angle route is direct because the given chord equality and the equality of radii supply exactly the side equalities required by I.8. [1.8]

**Step 5.** The ordinary, non-reflex central angles ∠AOB and ∠DPE stand on the respective lesser circumferences cut off by AB and DE. Equal angles in equal circles stand on equal circumferences; therefore these lesser circumferences are equal. [3.26]

**Step 6.** Subtract these equal lesser circumferences from the equal complete circumferences established in Step 1. The remaining circumferences—the respective greater ones—are equal. Thus equal straight lines in equal circles cut off equal circumferences, the greater equal to the greater and the less to the less. [CN3]

## Proposition 3.29
**Statement:** In equal circles equal circumferences are subtended by equal straight lines.

**Step 1.** Let two equal circles have equal arcs AB and CD, subtended by the straight lines AB and CD. If these arcs are semicircles, their chords are diameters, and therefore AB = CD by the definition of equal circles. Thus it remains to consider the non-semicircular case. [D1.18, D3.1]

**Step 2.** Find the centres O and P of the respective circles, and join OA, OB, PC, and PD, as well as the chords AB and CD. [3.1, P1]

**Step 3.** Radii of a circle are equal, and equal circles have equal radii. Consequently OA = PC and OB = PD. [D1.15, D3.1]

**Step 4.** Since the arcs AB and CD are equal, the angles they subtend at the centres are equal; hence the included angles ∠AOB and ∠CPD are equal. We use the centre-angle form of III.27 because it directly supplies the included angles for the two pairs of equal radii. [3.27]

**Step 5.** The triangles AOB and CPD therefore have two sides respectively equal and their included angles equal. By I.4 their bases are equal: AB = CD. Thus, in equal circles, equal circumferences are subtended by equal straight lines. [1.4]

## Proposition 3.30
**Statement:** To bisect a given circumference.

**Step 1.** Let the given circumference be an arc with endpoints A and B. Join AB, and bisect it at D, so that AD = DB. [P1, 1.10]

**Step 2.** At D draw a perpendicular to AB, and produce it on the side containing the given arc until it meets that arc at C. Join AC and BC. The angles ADC and BDC are right angles and therefore equal. [1.11, P2, P1, P4]

**Step 3.** In triangles ADC and BDC, AD = DB, DC is common, and the included angles ADC and BDC are equal. Hence the corresponding remaining angles DAC and DBC are equal. Since D lies between A and B, these are respectively the angles BAC and ABC. Thus ∠BAC = ∠ABC. [1.4]

**Step 4.** Use the equal-angle route, since the preceding congruence supplies exactly the angles needed. The given circle is equal to itself, and equal angles at its circumference stand on equal circumferences. Now ∠BAC stands on the subarc BC not containing A, while ∠ABC stands on the subarc AC not containing B. These are precisely the two parts into which C divides the given arc. Therefore arc AC equals arc CB, and the given circumference has been bisected at C. [D3.1, 3.26]

## Proposition 3.31
**Statement:** In a circle the angle in the semicircle is right, that in a greater segment less than a right angle, and that in a less segment greater than a right angle; and further the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle, and the angle of the less segment less than a right angle.

**Step 1.** Let O be the centre of a circle, BC a diameter, and A any point on one of its semicircumferences, distinct from B and C. Join AB, AC, and AO, and produce BA through A to F. Thus O lies between B and C. [D1.17, D1.18, P1, P2]

**Step 2.** Use the equal radii and the isosceles triangles supplied directly by this construction. Since OA = OB, ∠OAB = ∠ABO = ∠ABC. Since OA = OC, ∠OAC = ∠ACO = ∠ACB. Adding, and observing that AO divides ∠BAC, gives
∠BAC = ∠ABC + ∠ACB.
[D1.15, 1.5, CN2]

**Step 3.** By the exterior-angle theorem in triangle ABC,
∠FAC = ∠ABC + ∠ACB.
Consequently ∠BAC = ∠FAC. These are adjacent angles made by AC standing on the straight line BAF, so each is right. Since A was arbitrary, every angle in a semicircle is right. Write R for a right angle; all right angles are equal. [1.32, CN1, D1.10, D3.8, P4]

**Step 4.** Consider the two segments with base AC, and choose D arbitrarily on the arc AC not containing B. The segment ABC is greater than a semicircle: it contains the entire semicircle on BC opposite A, together with an additional part. The complementary segment ADC is a proper part of the semicircle on BC containing A, and is therefore less than a semicircle. This configuration covers any non-diametral chord: name its endpoints A and C and take B diametrically opposite C. [D1.17, D1.18, D3.6, 3.2, CN5]

**Step 5.** Reusing the triangle-angle sum in 1.32, the angles of triangle ABC total two right angles. Subtracting the right angle BAC gives
∠ABC + ∠ACB = R.
Hence ∠ABC < R. This is an angle in the greater segment ABC, and every other angle in that segment equals it. Thus every angle in a segment greater than a semicircle is less than a right angle. [1.32, CN3, CN5, D3.8, 3.21]

**Step 6.** The quadrilateral ABCD is inscribed in the circle, so its opposite angles satisfy
∠ABC + ∠ADC = 2R.
Since ∠ABC < R, its supplement ∠ADC is greater than R. Because D was arbitrary on the lesser arc, every angle in a segment less than a semicircle is greater than a right angle. [3.22, CN3, CN5, D3.8]

**Step 7.** Finally distinguish the angle *of* a segment—the angle between its base and its circumference—from an angle *in* it. At A, on the greater-segment side of AC, the chord AB lies strictly inside the circle and between AC and the bounding circumference. Hence the angle of the greater segment ABC strictly contains ∠BAC, which is right, and is therefore greater than a right angle. On the lesser-segment side of AC, the bounding arc AD lies between AC and the outward continuation AF of BA. Consequently the angle of the lesser segment ADC is a proper part of ∠FAC, which is right, and is therefore less than a right angle. Either endpoint of the base could have been designated A, so the comparisons hold at either endpoint. [D3.7, 3.2, CN5]

Therefore the angle in a semicircle is right; the angle in a greater segment is less than a right angle; the angle in a lesser segment is greater than a right angle; and the angles of the greater and lesser segments are respectively greater and less than a right angle.

## Proposition 3.32
**Statement:** If a straight line touch a circle, and from the point of contact there be drawn across, in the circle, a straight line cutting the circle, the angles which it makes with the tangent will be equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line TAU touch the circle at A, with AT and AU opposite rays, and let AB be the straight line drawn from A to another point B of the circle. Find the centre O, join AO, and produce it through O to meet the circle again at C. Then AC is a diameter. We choose this diameter route because the radius–tangent theorem applies directly: AC is perpendicular to TAU. Thus ∠TAC and ∠CAU are right angles. Write R for a right angle. [3.1, P1, P2, D1.17, 3.18, P4]

**Step 2.** If B coincides with C, both angles made by AB with the tangent are right angles. The two segments cut off by AB are semicircles, and every angle in either semicircle is right. Therefore the required equalities hold in this case. Henceforth suppose B differs from C. [3.31, P4]

**Step 3.** Name the tangent rays so that T is on the same side of AC as B. Then AB lies inside ∠TAC, and T and C are on opposite sides of AB. Join BC. Since AC is a diameter, ∠ABC is right. The angles of triangle ABC therefore give
∠BAC + ∠BCA = R.
But the right angle TAC also gives
∠TAB + ∠BAC = R.
Subtracting the common angle BAC, we obtain
∠TAB = ∠BCA. [P1, 3.31, 1.32, P4, CN3]

**Step 4.** Let X be any point, other than A and B, on the circumference of the segment with base AB that contains C, and join AX and BX. Angles in this same segment are equal, so ∠AXB = ∠ACB; for X = C the equality is immediate. Consequently ∠TAB = ∠AXB. Since this segment lies on the opposite side of AB from T, it is the alternate segment for ∠TAB. [P1, 3.21, CN1, D3.8]

**Step 5.** Let Y be any point, other than A and B, on the circumference of the other segment, and join AY and BY. The quadrilateral AYBC is inscribed in the circle, so its opposite angles satisfy
∠AYB + ∠ACB = 2R.
Because AT and AU are opposite rays,
∠TAB + ∠BAU = 2R.
By Step 3, ∠TAB = ∠ACB. Subtracting these equal angles from the equal sums gives
∠BAU = ∠AYB.
This second segment lies opposite U across AB, so it is the alternate segment for ∠BAU. Thus each angle made by the chord with the tangent equals the angles in its alternate segment, as required. [P1, 3.22, 1.13, P4, CN3, D3.8]

## Proposition 3.33
**Statement:** On a given straight line to describe a segment of a circle admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line and θ the given rectilineal angle. At A construct a ray AT such that ∠BAT = θ, and bisect AB at M. [1.23, 1.10]

**Step 2.** Draw the straight line ℓ through A perpendicular to AT, and the straight line m through M perpendicular to AB. If θ is right, take O = M; then AO is perpendicular to AT. If θ is not right, choose the ray of ℓ making an acute angle α with AB: when θ is acute, this ray lies on the side of AB opposite T and α is the difference between a right angle and θ; when θ is obtuse, it lies on T’s side and α is the difference between θ and a right angle. These angle relations follow from the perpendicular construction and the supplementary-angle relation. [1.11, D1.10, 1.13]

**Step 3.** In the non-right case, consider ℓ and m cut by the transversal AM, on the side containing the chosen ray of ℓ. Their interior angles are α and a right angle, and hence together are less than two right angles. Therefore ℓ and m, produced if necessary, meet on that side; call their intersection O. Thus in every case O is constructed and OA is perpendicular to AT. [P2, P5]

**Step 4.** We have OA = OB. Indeed, when O = M this follows from the bisection of AB. Otherwise join OB. In triangles AMO and BMO, AM = BM, MO is common, and ∠AMO and ∠BMO are equal right angles. Therefore their bases OA and OB are equal. [P1, P4, 1.4]

**Step 5.** Describe the circle with centre O and radius OA. Since OB = OA, it passes through both A and B. The line OA, produced through the circle, is a diameter line; AT is perpendicular to it at A. Consequently the straight line containing AT falls outside the circle except at A and therefore touches the circle there. [P3, D1.15, P2, D1.17, 3.16, D3.2]

**Step 6.** Take the segment bounded by AB and the arc lying on the side of AB opposite T. Let C be any point of this arc other than A and B, and join CA and CB. The tangent–chord theorem is the direct choice here, because the construction has supplied a tangent making the prescribed angle with the chord. It gives
∠ACB = ∠BAT = θ.
By definition, ∠ACB is an angle in the chosen segment. Thus the segment admits an angle equal to the given rectilineal angle, including when that angle is right. The required segment has therefore been described on AB. [D3.6, P1, 3.32, CN1, D3.8]

## Proposition 3.34
**Statement:** From a given circle to cut off a segment admitting an angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let the given circle be Γ and the given rectilineal angle be α. Choose a point A on Γ and draw a tangent AT at A. We use the tangent–chord route because it transfers the prescribed angle directly to a segment of the given circle. [3.17]

**Step 2.** At A, on the side of the tangent containing the circle, construct an angle TAB equal to α, letting its other side meet Γ again at B. Thus AB is a chord and ∠TAB = α. [1.23]

**Step 3.** Take the segment S bounded by AB and the arc AB lying on the opposite side of AB from T; this is the alternate segment corresponding to ∠TAB. Let P be any point of that arc other than A and B, and join PA and PB. Then ∠APB is an angle in S. [D3.6, P1, D3.8]

**Step 4.** Since AT touches Γ and AB is drawn from the point of contact across the circle, the angle between AT and AB equals the angle in the alternate segment: ∠APB = ∠TAB. But ∠TAB = α, so ∠APB = α. Since P was arbitrary, S admits an angle equal to the given angle. Thus the chord AB cuts off the required segment from the given circle. [3.32, CN1]

## Proposition 3.35
**Statement:** If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.

**Step 1.** Let the chords AB and CD intersect inside the circle at E. Write R(u,v) for the rectangle contained by the straight lines u,v, and S(u) for the square on u. We use the midpoint-and-square route: II.5 applies directly to the internal division of each chord, while III.3 supplies the required right angles. [D2.1, D1.22, 2.5, 3.3]

**Step 2.** Find the centre O, and join O to A, B, C, D, and, if distinct from O, to E. The radii OA, OB, OC, OD are equal. If E=O, the four segments EA, EB, EC, ED are therefore equal; each of the two rectangles in question is the square on this same length, so they are equal. Henceforth suppose E≠O. [3.1, P1, D1.15, D2.1, D1.22, CN4, CN1]

**Step 3.** Apply the following argument to each chord in turn, writing its endpoints as X,Y. Bisect XY at H. We shall establish
R(XE,EY)+S(OE)=S(OX).
First suppose that XY passes through O. Since OX=OY, its midpoint H is O. The chord is thus bisected at O and divided unequally at E. By II.5,
R(XE,EY)+S(OE)=S(OX),
as required. [1.10, D1.15, 2.5]

**Step 4.** Now suppose that XY does not pass through O. Join OH. Since the line through O bisects XY, it is perpendicular to XY. If H=E, then XE=EY, and the rectangle R(XE,EY) is S(EX). The right-angled triangle OEX therefore gives
R(XE,EY)+S(OE)=S(EX)+S(OE)=S(OX).
This establishes the required equality in this case. [P1, 3.3, D2.1, D1.22, CN4, 1.47]

**Step 5.** It remains, for a chord not through O, to consider H≠E. The triangles OHX and OHE are right-angled at H, so
S(OX)=S(OH)+S(HX),
S(OE)=S(OH)+S(HE).
Since XY is bisected at H and divided unequally at E, II.5 gives
R(XE,EY)+S(HE)=S(HX).
Adding S(OH) to both sides and substituting the two right-triangle equalities yields
R(XE,EY)+S(OE)=S(OX).
Thus the required equality holds for either chord in every case. [3.3, 1.47, 2.5, CN2, CN1]

**Step 6.** Applying Steps 3–5 first to AB and then to CD gives
R(AE,EB)+S(OE)=S(OA),
R(CE,ED)+S(OE)=S(OC).
Since OA=OC, their squares are equal. Consequently,
R(AE,EB)+S(OE)=R(CE,ED)+S(OE). [D1.15, CN4, CN1]

**Step 7.** Subtract the common square S(OE). The remainders are equal:
R(AE,EB)=R(CE,ED).
Therefore the rectangle contained by the segments of one chord is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other. [CN3]

## Proposition 3.36
**Statement:** If a point be taken outside a circle and from it there fall on the circle two straight lines, and if one of them cut the circle and the other touch it, the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference will be equal to the square on the tangent.

**Step 1.** Let P be the external point, let the secant meet the circle first at A and then at B, and let PT touch the circle at T. Find the centre O, and join OP, OA, OB, and OT. The radii satisfy OA = OB = OT. Write XY² for the square on XY and XY·ZW for the rectangle contained by XY and ZW. We must prove PA·PB = PT². [3.1, P1, D1.15]

**Step 2.** The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent PT. Hence the triangle OTP is right-angled at T, and
OP² = OT² + PT².

## Proposition 3.37
**Statement:** If a point be taken outside a circle and from the point there fall on the circle two straight lines, if one of them cut the circle, and the other fall on it, and if further the rectangle contained by the whole of the straight line which cuts the circle and the straight line intercepted on it outside between the point and the convex circumference be equal to the square on the straight line which falls on the circle, the straight line which falls on it will touch the circle.

**Step 1.** Let P be outside the circle, let the secant meet it first at A and then at B, and let C be the point where the other straight line meets the circle. Thus, by hypothesis, the rectangle contained by PB and PA equals the square on PC. Draw a tangent PT to the circle, touching it at T [3.17]. We choose this direct route because the known tangent allows the given rectangle to be evaluated by 3.36.

**Step 2.** The rectangle contained by PB and PA equals the square on PT [3.36]. Consequently the squares on PC and PT are equal [CN1], and hence PC = PT. Indeed, if their sides were unequal, fitting the squares together at a corner along corresponding sides would make the smaller square a proper part of the larger, contradicting their equality [D1.22, CN5].

**Step 3.** Find the centre O and join OP, OC, and OT [3.1, P1]. The radii OC and OT are equal [D1.15]. Since PT touches the circle at T, OT is perpendicular to PT; thus angle OTP is right [3.18].

**Step 4.** The lengths OC, CP, and PO equal respectively OT, TP, and PO. Since the latter are the sides of the nondegenerate right triangle OTP, they satisfy the strict triangle inequalities [1.20]; therefore O, C, and P are not collinear. Compare triangles OCP and OTP by side–side–side, the natural choice because all three corresponding side equalities are now known. Their sides OC and CP equal OT and TP, and their base OP is common. Hence angle OCP equals angle OTP [1.8], and is therefore right.

**Step 5.** Extend CO through O to form the diameter having C as an extremity [P2]. The straight line PC is at right angles to this diameter at C [D1.10]. Therefore it falls outside the circle [3.16]. Since it meets the circle at C but does not cut it when produced, it touches the circle [D3.2]. Thus the straight line which falls on the circle is a tangent, as required.

**Statement:** Into a given circle to fit a straight line equal to a given straight line which is not greater than the diameter of the circle.

**Step 1.** Let Γ be the given circle and let ℓ be the given straight line, not greater than its diameter. Find the centre O of Γ, and draw through O a straight line terminating at A and B on the circumference. Thus AB is a diameter. [3.1, P1, P2, D1.17]

**Step 4.** Describe a circle with centre A and radius AE. It meets Γ: A is inside this auxiliary circle, whereas B is outside it because AB is greater than AE, so the circumference of Γ passes from inside to outside it. Let C be a point where the two circumferences meet, and join AC. [P3, P1]

**Step 5.** Since E and C lie on the circle with centre A, AC equals AE. But AE equals ℓ; therefore AC equals ℓ. Moreover, A and C both lie on Γ, so AC is fitted into Γ. Thus a straight line equal to the given straight line has been fitted into the given circle, as required. [D1.15, CN1, D4.7]

## Proposition 4.2
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe a triangle equiangular with a given triangle.

**Step 1.** Let the given circle be κ and the given triangle be DEF. Choose a point A on κ and draw the tangent at A, producing it in both directions to points X and Y, with A between them. We choose the tangent–chord route because it directly converts constructed angles at A into angles of an inscribed triangle. [3.17, P2]

**Step 2.** The angles DEF and DFE together are less than two right angles, since the three angles of triangle DEF equal two right angles. [1.32, CN5] On the side of XY containing the circle, construct a ray AC such that ∠XAC = ∠DEF. Since ∠XAC and ∠CAY together equal two right angles, ∠DFE is less than ∠CAY. Therefore construct a ray AB within ∠CAY such that ∠YAB = ∠DFE. Produce the rays to meet the circle again at C and B, respectively. Their order on this side of the tangent is AY, AB, AC, AX, so B and C are distinct. [1.23, 1.13, P2]

**Step 3.** Join B to C. Thus ABC is a triangle whose vertices lie on κ. [P1]

**Step 4.** Apply the tangent–chord theorem to AC and the tangent ray AX. The point B lies in the alternate segment, so ∠ABC = ∠XAC. Apply the same theorem to AB and the tangent ray AY. The point C lies in the alternate segment, so ∠ACB = ∠YAB. Consequently, by the constructed equalities, ∠ABC = ∠DEF and ∠ACB = ∠DFE. [3.32, CN1]

**Step 5.** The angles of each of triangles ABC and DEF sum to two right angles. The sums ∠ABC + ∠ACB and ∠DEF + ∠DFE are equal. Subtracting these equal sums from the equal totals gives ∠BAC = ∠EDF. Thus ABC is equiangular with DEF. [1.32, CN2, CN3]

**Step 6.** Since A, B, and C all lie on the circumference of κ, triangle ABC is inscribed in κ. It is therefore the required inscribed triangle equiangular with the given triangle DEF. [D4.3]

## Proposition 4.3
**Statement:** About a given circle to circumscribe a triangle equiangular with a given triangle.

**Step 1.** Let the given triangle be DEF, with angles α, β, γ at D, E, F respectively, and let R denote a right angle. We take the direct route: copy exterior angles at the centre of the circle, then draw perpendicular tangents. Produce a side at D and a side at F. The resulting exterior angles are 2R−α and 2R−γ. Also α+β+γ=2R, so each of α, β, γ, and each of these exterior angles, lies strictly between zero and 2R. [P2, P4, 1.13, 1.32, CN3]

**Step 2.** Find the centre O of the given circle, choose A on its circumference, and join OA. On opposite sides of OA construct angles AOB=2R−α and AOC=2R−γ, taking B and C where the constructed rays meet the circumference. Since the angles about O total 4R, the remaining sector BOC, not containing OA, equals
4R−(2R−α)−(2R−γ)=α+γ=2R−β.
Thus the successive central sectors AOB, BOC, COA have angles 2R−α, 2R−β, 2R−γ; each is less than 2R. [3.1, P1, 1.23, 1.13, P4, 1.32, CN2, CN3]

**Step 3.** Produce the radii to diameters and draw lines t_A, t_B, t_C through A, B, C perpendicular to OA, OB, OC respectively. Each perpendicular falls outside the circle and therefore touches it at its designated point. This perpendicular construction is the natural choice because the contact points have already been fixed. [P2, 1.11, 3.16, D3.2]

**Step 4.** Join AB, BC, CA. We verify that the tangent lines form a triangle whose sides contain the contact points. In triangle OAB, the radii OA and OB are equal, so its base angles are equal; call each u. If θ=∠AOB, then 2u+θ=2R, whence u<R. On the side of AB opposite O, the tangents at A and B consequently make angles R−u with AB. Their sum is 2R−2u=θ<2R; therefore the tangents meet on that side. Call their intersection X. Apply the same reasoning to BC and CA, obtaining Y=t_B∩t_C and Z=t_C∩t_A.

These meetings use the tangent rays directed into the respective central sectors. Since the three sectors are consecutive and each is less than 2R, the meetings belonging to the two sectors adjacent to any radius lie on opposite rays of its tangent. Consequently A lies between Z and X, B between X and Y, and C between Y and Z. Thus X, Y, Z form a triangle with the three contact points on its sides. [P1, D1.15, 1.5, 1.32, CN3, P5]

**Step 5.** In triangle AXB, the angles at A and B have sum θ=2R−α, as established above. Its angle at X therefore equals α. The same argument in triangles BYC and CZA gives angles β at Y and γ at Z. Because A, B, C lie between the corresponding vertices, these are precisely the interior angles of triangle XYZ. Hence XYZ is equiangular with DEF. [1.32, CN3]

**Step 6.** The sides XZ, XY, YZ touch the given circle at A, B, C respectively. Therefore triangle XYZ is circumscribed about the circle and, by Step 5, is equiangular with the given triangle DEF. The required construction is complete. [D4.4]

## Proposition 4.4
**Statement:** In a given triangle to inscribe a circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given triangle. Use the route of two internal angle bisectors: bisect ∠ABC and ∠BCA. Their halves together are less than two right angles, since the original two angles are already less than two right angles. Hence the bisector rays meet, by the parallel postulate, at a point I on the same side of BC as A. Since both rays lie inside their respective vertex angles, I is inside triangle ABC. [1.9, 1.17, P5]

**Step 2.** From I draw perpendiculars IE, IF, IG to the straight lines AB, BC, CA, respectively. The feet E and F lie on the rays BA and BC, and the feet F and G lie on the rays CB and CA. Indeed, each bisector makes an acute angle with either bounding ray; a foot on the opposite ray would therefore give a right triangle with an obtuse angle at the vertex, contradicting the fact that two angles of a triangle are less than two right angles. For now, the feet need not be assumed to lie on the finite sides. [1.12, 1.13, 1.17]

**Step 3.** Compare triangles BIE and BIF. Their angles at B are equal because BI bisects ∠ABC; their angles at E and F are right and therefore equal; and BI is common. Apply 1.26, the direct fit to these two equal angles and the common side. It follows that IE = IF. [1.9, P4, 1.26]

**Step 4.** Similarly, triangles CIF and CIG have equal angles at C, equal right angles at F and G, and the common side CI. Thus IF = IG. Consequently IE = IF = IG. [1.9, P4, 1.26, CN1]

**Step 5.** Describe the circle with centre I and distance IE. Since IE, IF, and IG are equal, this circle passes through E, F, and G. [P3, D1.15]

**Step 6.** The lines AB, BC, and CA are perpendicular at E, F, and G to the respective radii. Each radius lies along a diameter, so 3.16 applies directly: a perpendicular at the extremity of a diameter falls outside the circle. Thus each of these three lines meets the circle at its indicated point without cutting it, and therefore touches it. This is the direct tangency criterion supplied by the constructed perpendiculars. [3.16, D3.2]

**Step 7.** The circle lies on the same side of each tangent line as its centre I. Since I is inside ABC, these are precisely the three inward half-planes whose intersection is the triangle. Hence the circle lies within ABC; in particular, E, F, and G lie on the finite sides AB, BC, and CA. Its circumference therefore touches every side of the triangle, so the circle is inscribed in ABC, as required. [3.16, D4.5]

## Proposition 4.5
**Statement:** About a given triangle to circumscribe a circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given triangle. We take the direct route of constructing the perpendicular bisectors of two sides. Bisect AB at D and AC at E, so that AD = DB and AE = EC. [1.10]

**Step 2.** Through D draw a straight line p perpendicular to AB, and through E draw a straight line q perpendicular to AC. Produce these lines in both directions as necessary. [1.11, P2, D1.10]

**Step 3.** The lines p and q must meet. For suppose they do not; they are then parallel. If AC were parallel to p, it would also be parallel to q, since straight lines parallel to the same straight line are parallel to one another. But AC meets q at E. Thus AC is not parallel to p and, when produced if necessary, meets p at a point F. Since AC is perpendicular to q and p is parallel to q, the equality of angles made by a transversal of parallel lines shows that AC is perpendicular to p at F. Now F is distinct from A and D, and triangle ADF has right angles at both D and F. This contradicts the fact that any two angles of a triangle are together less than two right angles. Therefore p and q meet; call an intersection O. [D1.23, 1.30, P2, 1.29, D1.10, 1.17]

**Step 4.** Join OA, OB, and OC. If O = D, then OA = OB immediately from AD = DB. Otherwise, in triangles ODA and ODB, OD is common, AD = DB, and the included angles ODA and ODB are right angles and hence equal. Consequently OA = OB by side–angle–side. This is the natural comparison: the midpoint equalities and the common perpendicular already give the two sides and their included angle. [P1, 1.10, D1.10, P4, 1.4]

**Step 5.** Likewise, if O = E, then OA = OC from AE = EC. Otherwise, triangles OEA and OEC have OE common, AE = EC, and equal included right angles at E. Side–angle–side therefore gives OA = OC. [1.10, D1.10, P4, 1.4]

**Step 6.** Describe the circle with centre O and distance OA. Since OB = OA and OC = OA, its circumference passes through A, B, and C. It is therefore circumscribed about triangle ABC, as required. [P3, D1.15, D4.6]

## Proposition 4.6
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe a square.

Applying 1.4 to triangle AOB and each of triangles BOC, COD, and DOA gives AB = BC, AB = CD, and AB = DA. Hence ABCD is equilateral. [P1, D1.15, D1.16, 1.4, CN1]

**Step 5.** The quadrilateral ABCD is both equilateral and right-angled, so it is a square. Its four vertices lie on the circumference of the given circle, so it is inscribed in that circle. Therefore a square has been inscribed in the given circle, as required. [D1.22, D4.3]

## Proposition 4.7
**Statement:** About a given circle to circumscribe a square.

**Step 1.** Let the given circle have centre O, found by 3.1. Choose A on its circumference, join AO, and produce it through O to meet the circle again at C. Through O draw the perpendicular to AC, meeting the circle at B and D, with A, B, C, D in cyclic order. Thus AC and BD are perpendicular diameters. [3.1, P1, P2, 1.11]

**Step 2.** At A and C draw straight lines a and c perpendicular to AC; at B and D draw straight lines b and d perpendicular to BD. Each such line meets the circle at its designated endpoint and otherwise falls outside it, so each touches the circle there. We use the perpendicular-at-a-diameter-endpoint route directly, since 3.16 is the first applicable tangency result for these already chosen points. [1.11, 3.16, D3.2]

**Step 3.** Since all right angles are equal, 1.28 gives a ∥ BD and c ∥ BD, and likewise b ∥ AC and d ∥ AC. Hence a ∥ c and b ∥ d. No line of the first pair can be parallel to a line of the second pair: otherwise transitivity of parallelism would make AC parallel to BD, although they meet at O. Consequently adjacent tangents intersect. Set E = a ∩ b, F = b ∩ c, G = c ∩ d, and H = d ∩ a. These form a parallelogram EFGH. The opposite tangent pairs lie on opposite sides of O, so A, B, C, D lie respectively on the side segments HE, EF, FG, GH. [P4, 1.28, 1.30, D1.23]

**Step 4.** The lines a and c are perpendicular to AC, while b and d are parallel to AC. Applying 1.29 to these parallels shows that the angles at E, F, G, and H are all right angles. Thus EFGH is right-angled. [1.29]

**Step 5.** The radii OA, OB, OC, and OD are equal. Adding OA = OB to OC = OD gives OA + OC = OB + OD; therefore AC = BD. [D1.15, CN2]

**Step 6.** The quadrilateral AEFC is a parallelogram: AE ∥ FC because a ∥ c, and EF ∥ AC because b ∥ AC. Its opposite sides therefore give EF = AC. Similarly, BFGD is a parallelogram because BF ∥ GD and FG ∥ BD, so FG = BD. Since AC = BD, it follows that EF = FG. Finally, opposite sides of the parallelogram EFGH are equal, so EF = GH and FG = HE. Hence all four sides of EFGH are equal. [1.34, CN1]

**Step 7.** The quadrilateral EFGH is both equilateral and right-angled, and therefore is a square. Its four sides touch the given circle at A, B, C, and D respectively; hence it is circumscribed about that circle. Thus a square has been circumscribed about the given circle, as required. [D1.22, D4.4]

## Proposition 4.13
**Statement:** In a given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, to inscribe a circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon, with vertices in order, and let α denote half its common interior angle. **Step 2.** In triangles ABO and CBO, AB = CB, BO is common, and ∠ABO = ∠CBO. Hence, by 1.4, ∠BAO = ∠BCO = α. Since O is on the interior side of AB, AO lies within ∠BAE. Subtracting ∠BAO from that whole angle gives ∠OAE = α; thus AO bisects the angle at A (CN3).

**Step 3.** In triangles BCO and DCO, BC = DC, CO is common, and ∠BCO = ∠DCO. Hence ∠CDO = ∠CBO = α (1.4). Since O is on the interior side of CD, DO lies within ∠CDE, and subtraction gives ∠ODE = α (CN3). Thus DO bisects the angle at D. The original bisectors place O on the interior sides of AB, BC, and CD; the bisections just established place it on the interior sides of AE and DE also. Therefore O is inside the pentagon.

**Step 4.** In triangles BAO and EAO, BA = EA, AO is common, and ∠BAO = ∠EAO. Consequently ∠AEO = ∠ABO = α (1.4). Subtracting this from the whole angle AED gives ∠OED = α (CN3). Hence EO also bisects its vertex angle. Thus the lines from O to all five vertices bisect their respective interior angles.

**Step 5.** Draw OP, OQ, OR, OS, and OT perpendicular respectively to the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, and EA, producing those lines as necessary for the construction (P2, 1.12). Each foot lies strictly on its corresponding side segment. Indeed, both endpoint angles in each triangle formed by O and a side equal α and are acute. A foot beyond an endpoint would make the angle at that endpoint an exterior angle of a right triangle, hence greater than a right angle by 1.16. A foot at an endpoint would make that endpoint angle right. Both are impossible.

**Step 6.** Consider triangles OBP and OBQ. Their angles at P and Q are equal right angles (P4), their angles at B are equal because BO bisects ∠ABC, and OB is common. Apply 1.26, the natural criterion here because two equal angles and the common side opposite the right angles are already known. It gives OP = OQ. Applying the same proposition to triangles OCQ and OCR, ODR and ODS, and OES and OET gives OQ = OR, OR = OS, and OS = OT. Therefore OP = OQ = OR = OS = OT (CN1).

**Step 8.** The diameter through each of these points is collinear with its radius from O (P2, D1.17). Each corresponding side of the pentagon is therefore perpendicular to a diameter at its extremity and, by 3.16, falls outside the circle apart from that point. Thus each side touches the circle (D3.2). Its circumference consequently touches all five sides of ABCDE, so it is inscribed in the given pentagon (D4.5), as required.

**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular hexagon.

## Proposition 4.16
**Statement:** In a given circle to inscribe a fifteen-angled figure which shall be both equilateral and equiangular.

**Step 1.** Let the given circle be Γ. Use the triangle–pentagon route, obtaining the triangle directly from the earlier triangle-inscription construction. Construct an equilateral triangle by 1.1; its angles are equal by 1.5. Inscribe in Γ a triangle equiangular with it by 4.2, and call one vertex A. Thus the inscribed triangle has three equal angles. [1.1, 1.5, 4.2]

**Step 2.** Inscribe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon in Γ, taking A as one of its vertices. Choose a direction around Γ; let B be the next triangle vertex and C the next pentagon vertex. The triangle’s equal angles stand on equal circumferences, so its three successive arcs are equal. The pentagon’s equal sides likewise cut off five equal successive arcs. Consequently, if L denotes the whole circumference, arc AB is L/3 and arc AC is L/5, measured in the chosen direction, and C lies between A and B. Here fractions denote equal parts of the same circumference. [4.11, 3.26, 3.28]

**Step 3.** Subtracting arc AC from arc AB gives
arc CB = L/3 − L/5 = 2L/15.
Bisect arc CB at D. Then each of arcs CD and DB is L/15. Join C to D. Thus CD is a constructed chord subtending exactly one fifteenth of the circumference. [CN2, CN3, 3.30, P1]

**Step 4.** Since CD is a chord, it is not greater than the diameter. Therefore, starting with C and D, fit chords equal to CD successively into Γ, always proceeding in the chosen direction and taking the minor arc at each fitting. This is the direct chord-fitting construction of 4.1. Equal chords cut off equal minor arcs, so every successive arc equals arc CD, namely L/15. Fifteen such arcs make the whole circumference; fewer than fifteen do not. Hence the fifteenth chord returns to C, and the preceding endpoints are fourteen distinct further vertices. These fifteen equal chords therefore form an equilateral fifteen-sided figure. [3.15, 4.1, 3.28, CN2]

**Step 5.** At each vertex of this figure, the interior angle stands on the arc between its two neighboring vertices which does not contain that vertex. This arc consists of thirteen of the fifteen equal elementary arcs: it is the whole circumference with the two adjacent elementary arcs removed. Such intercepted arcs are equal at every vertex, by addition and subtraction of equals. Angles standing at the circumference on equal circumferences are equal; therefore all fifteen interior angles are equal. [CN2, CN3, 3.27]

**Step 6.** Every vertex lies on Γ, so the figure is inscribed in the given circle. By Steps 4 and 5 it is both equilateral and equiangular. Thus the required fifteen-angled figure has been constructed. [D4.3]

## Proposition 5.1
**Statement:** If a magnitude be the same multiple of a magnitude that a part subtracted is of a part subtracted, the remainder will also be the same multiple of the remainder that the whole is of the whole.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the whole magnitudes, and let C and D be the respective parts subtracted. Suppose A is the same multiple of B that C is of D. By the definition of a multiple, A consists of some number n of parts each equal to B, while C consists of the same number n of parts each equal to D. We use these equal constituent parts directly, without invoking a theorem about ratios. [D5.2]

**Step 2.** In each of the n parts of A equal to B, take away a part equal to D; this is possible since D is a part of B. Each remainder is equal to the remainder B − D, because equal magnitudes have been subtracted from equal magnitudes. Thus there are n remaining parts, each equal to B − D. [CN3]

**Step 3.** The parts taken away together equal C: both consist of n parts each equal to D, and repeated addition of equals gives equal wholes. Consequently, subtracting their total from A leaves a magnitude equal to A − C. But what remains after these removals is precisely the collection of the n remaining parts from Step 2. Hence A − C consists of n parts each equal to B − D. [CN2, CN3]

**Step 4.** Therefore B − D measures A − C exactly n times. By the definition of a multiple, A − C is the same multiple of B − D that A is of B, as required. [D5.2]

## Proposition 5.2
**Statement:** If a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and a fifth also be the same multiple of the second that a sixth is of the fourth, the sum of the first and fifth will also be the same multiple of the second that the sum of the third and sixth is of the fourth.

**Step 1.** Denote the first through sixth magnitudes by A, B, C, D, E, F, respectively. Choose the direct route of counting measuring parts, since the hypotheses concern multiples rather than general ratios. By the definition of a multiple, A consists of some number m of parts each equal to B, while C consists of the same number m of parts each equal to D. Likewise, E consists of some number n of parts each equal to B, and F consists of the same number n of parts each equal to D. The numbers m and n need not be equal. [D5.2]

**Step 2.** Add the expressions for A and E as sums of their measuring parts. Since equals added to equals give equal wholes, A + E equals the sum of the m parts equal to B followed by the n parts equal to B: altogether m + n such parts. In precisely the same way, C + F equals the sum of m + n parts each equal to D. [CN2]

**Step 3.** Thus B measures A + E exactly as many times as D measures C + F. By the definition of a multiple, the sum of the first and fifth is therefore the same multiple of the second as the sum of the third and sixth is of the fourth, as required. [D5.2]

## Proposition 5.3
**Statement:** If a first magnitude be the same multiple of a second that a third is of a fourth, and if equimultiples be taken of the first and third, then also ex aequali the magnitudes taken will be equimultiples respectively, the one of the second and the other of the fourth.

By the meaning of multiple, E consists of some number n of copies of A, and F consists of the same number n of copies of C. Thus it suffices to show that these two sums are equimultiples of B and D. **Step 2.** We use successive addition, since Proposition 5.2 directly preserves the required relation. The first pair of summands, A and C, are equimultiples of B and D by hypothesis. Whenever the sums of the first k copies are equimultiples of B and D, adding one further A to the first sum and one further C to the second gives sums that are again equimultiples of B and D: this is precisely Proposition 5.2, applied to the two partial sums and the additional pair A, C. [5.2]

**Step 3.** Continuing through all n pairs of summands, the resulting sums E and F are therefore equimultiples of B and D respectively. Hence, ex aequali, the magnitudes taken are the same multiple of the second and fourth magnitudes, as required. [5.2, D5.2]

## Proposition 5.4
**Statement:** If a first magnitude have to a second the same ratio as a third to a fourth, any equimultiples whatever of the first and third will also have the same ratio to any equimultiples whatever of the second and fourth respectively, taken in corresponding order.

**Step 2.** Take any equimultiples K and M of E and G, and any equimultiples L and N of F and H, respectively. Since E and G are equimultiples of A and C, Proposition 5.3 shows that K and M are equimultiples of A and C. Likewise, L and N are equimultiples of B and D. [5.3]

**Step 4.** The equimultiples K, M and L, N were arbitrary. Therefore E has to F the same ratio as G has to H. Since E, G and F, H were themselves any equimultiples of the original magnitudes in corresponding order, the proposition follows. [D5.5]

**Statement:** If two magnitudes be equimultiples of two magnitudes, and any magnitudes subtracted from them be equimultiples of the same, the remainders also are either equal to the same or equimultiples of them.

**Step 1.** Let X and Y be equimultiples of A and B respectively, and let U and V, subtracted from X and Y, also be equimultiples of A and B respectively. Write R and S for the remainders. We use repeated measurement directly, since it is the defining property of a multiple: X consists of m copies of A and Y of m copies of B, while U consists of n copies of A and V of n copies of B. [D5.2]

**Step 2.** Since U and V are parts removed with remainders left, each is less than its respective whole. Thus n is less than m: n copies cannot exhaust or exceed the m copies constituting the whole. Removing the first n copies from each of the two lists therefore leaves the same positive number k of copies in each. [D5.2, CN5]

**Step 3.** The first n copies of A together equal U. Subtracting these from the m-copy representation of X leaves an aggregate equal to R, by subtraction of equals from equals. Hence R equals the remaining k copies of A. In precisely the same way, S equals the remaining k copies of B. [D5.2, CN3]

**Step 4.** If k is one, R equals A and S equals B. If k is greater than one, A measures R exactly k times and B measures S exactly k times; consequently R and S are equimultiples of A and B. Thus the remainders are either equal to the original magnitudes respectively or equimultiples of them, as required. [D5.2]

## Proposition 5.7
**Statement:** Equal magnitudes have to the same the same ratio, as also has the same to equal magnitudes.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be equal magnitudes, and let C be a magnitude with which their ratios are considered. We use the definition of equal ratios directly for both assertions, checking arbitrary equimultiples rather than invoking a theorem about ratios. [D5.5]

**Step 3.** Compare mA and mB with nC. Since mA = mB, they alike exceed nC, alike equal nC, or alike fall short of nC; in particular, equality of either with nC entails equality of the other with nC. As m and n were arbitrary, the definition of equal ratios gives A:C = B:C. Thus equal magnitudes have to the same magnitude the same ratio. [CN1, D5.5]

**Step 4.** Now compare mC with nA and nB. Since nA = nB, mC alike exceeds both, equals both, or falls short of both; again, equality with either entails equality with the other. Since m and n were arbitrary, the same definition gives C:A = C:B. Thus the same magnitude also has the same ratio to equal magnitudes, completing both assertions. [CN1, D5.5]
