## Proposition 8.23
**Statement:** If four numbers be in continued proportion, and the first be cube, the fourth will also be cube.

**Step 1.** Let the four numbers be A, B, C, D, with A:B = B:C = C:D. Since A is a cube, write A = a³. Throughout, powers denote repeated multiplication. [D7.15, D7.19]

**Step 2.** Choose the least terms p, q of the common ratio, so that A:B = B:C = C:D = p:q. Such least terms are obtained by VII.33 and are prime to one another by VII.22. A least term may be the unit; those cases are treated explicitly below. We choose this route because the cubes of the least terms will provide a cube divisor of A, allowing a direct passage to its side. [7.33, 7.22]

**Step 3.** By the equality of cross-products of proportional numbers,
pB = qA,  pC = qB,  pD = qC.
Successive substitution therefore gives
p³D = q³A.
Equivalently, A:D = p³:q³. [7.19; D7.15]

**Step 4.** If p and q both exceed the unit, their cubes are prime to one another by VII.27. Hence p³ and q³ are the least numbers in their ratio by VII.21. Since A:D = p³:q³, VII.20 shows that p³ measures A. If p is the unit, the same divisibility is immediate; if q is the unit, it follows directly from p³D = A. Thus in every case p³ measures A = a³. [7.27, 7.21, 7.20]

**Step 5.** Since the cube p³ measures the cube a³, its side p measures the side a by VIII.15. When p is the unit this is immediate as well. Consequently a = pk for some whole multiplier k, possibly the unit. This is the direct application of cube divisibility appropriate to the divisor established in Step 4. [8.15; D7.15]

**Step 6.** Substitute a = pk and A = a³ into the identity from Step 3:
p³D = q³(pk)³ = p³(qk)³.
Cancelling the positive factor p³ gives D = (qk)³. Thus D is contained by three equal numbers and is a cube. Therefore, if four numbers are in continued proportion and the first is a cube, the fourth is also a cube. [D7.15, D7.19]

## Proposition 8.24
**Statement:** If two numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and the first be square, the second will also be square.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be numbers such that A:B=C:D, where C and D are square numbers, and suppose A is square. Choose the square-number mean-proportional route, since it applies directly to the given comparison numbers. By 8.11, there is a number E such that C:E=E:D.

**Step 2.** Since one mean proportional falls between C and D, and A:B=C:D, proposition 8.8 gives one mean proportional F between A and B. Thus A:F=F:B, so A, F, B are in continued proportion. [8.8]

**Step 3.** Three numbers are therefore in continued proportion, and their first, A, is square. By 8.22, their third, B, is also square. Hence the second of the two given numbers is square, as required.

## Proposition 8.26
**Statement:** Similar plane numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be similar plane numbers, and let a and c be corresponding sides. Use the duplicate-ratio conclusion of VIII.18 directly, since it describes the required ratio: A:B is the duplicate of a:c. [8.18]

**Step 2.** Form S = a·a and T = c·c. These are square numbers, with sides a and c respectively. [D7.18]

**Step 3.** The ratio S:T is the duplicate of the ratio of their sides, a:c. [8.11]

**Step 4.** Thus A:B and S:T are both the same duplicate ratio of a:c. Ratios which are the same with the same ratio are the same with one another; hence A:B = S:T. Since S and T are square numbers, similar plane numbers have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number. [5.11]

## Proposition 8.27
**Statement:** Similar solid numbers have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be similar solid numbers, and let a and b be corresponding sides. Choose the direct triplicate-ratio route: by VIII.19, A has to B the triplicate ratio of that which a has to b. [8.19]

**Step 2.** Form C = a·a·a and D = b·b·b. These are cube numbers with sides a and b, respectively. [D7.19] For these cubes, use the earlier, cube-specific proposition VIII.12: C has to D the triplicate ratio of that which a has to b. [8.12]

**Step 3.** Thus A:B and C:D are both the same triplicate ratio of a:b. Ratios which are the same with the same ratio are the same with one another, so A:B = C:D. [5.11] Since C and D are cube numbers, similar solid numbers have to one another the ratio which a cube number has to a cube number.

## Proposition 9.1
**Statement:** If two similar plane numbers by multiplying one another make some number, the product will be square.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be similar plane numbers, and let P be the number produced by multiplying A by B. Choose the mean-proportional route because it directly supplies a number whose square can be identified with P. By 8.18, there is a number M such that A:M = M:B. [8.18]

**Step 2.** Apply 7.19 to the four proportional numbers A, M, M, B. The product of the first and fourth equals the product of the second and third; hence P = A·B = M·M. [7.19]

**Step 3.** A number produced by multiplying equal numbers is a square number. Since P = M·M, P is square. Thus the product of two similar plane numbers is square, as required. [D7.18]

## Proposition 9.2
**Statement:** If two numbers by multiplying one another make a square number, they are similar plane numbers.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be numbers whose product is square. By the definition of a square number, there is a number C such that AB = CC. [D7.18]

**Step 2.** Apply the converse direction of VII.19 to the four numbers A, C, C, B. Since the product of the first and fourth equals the product of the second and third, A:C = C:B. Thus C is a mean proportional between A and B. [7.19]

**Step 3.** Use the mean-proportional criterion, since Step 2 supplies exactly its hypothesis: numbers between which one mean proportional falls are similar plane numbers. Therefore A and B are similar plane numbers, as required. [8.20]

## Proposition 9.3
**Statement:** If a cube number by multiplying itself make some number, the product will be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A be a cube number, and let B = A·A. By the definition of a cube, there is a number c such that, putting d = c·c, we have A = d·c. By commutativity of multiplication, also A = c·d. [D7.19, 7.16]

**Step 2.** Since c multiplying c and d produces d and A respectively, the products have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied. Hence c:d = d:A. [7.17]

**Step 3.** Form E = d·d and F = d·A. Applying the same multiplication theorem gives:
- A:E = c:d, since d multiplying c and d produces A and E;
- E:F = d:A, since d multiplying d and A produces E and F;
- F:B = d:A, since A multiplying d and A produces F and B.
The first and third assertions use commutativity to identify the products. [7.17, 7.16]

**Step 4.** Combining Steps 2 and 3, we obtain A:E = E:F = F:B. Thus A, E, F, B are four numbers in continued proportion. [CN1]

**Step 5.** Apply VIII.23, the direct choice because the constructed four numbers are in continued proportion and their first number A is already cube. Their fourth number B is therefore cube. Since B = A·A, a cube number multiplying itself produces a cube number, as required. [8.23]

## Proposition 9.4
**Statement:** If a cube number by multiplying a cube number make some number, the product will be cube.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be cube numbers, and let A by multiplying B produce C. Take the direct route of comparing C with the self-product of A: let A by multiplying itself produce D. Then D is a cube by IX.3. [9.3]

**Step 2.** Since A by multiplying A and B produces D and C respectively, the products have the same ratio as the numbers multiplied. Hence D:C = A:B. [7.17]

**Step 3.** Thus D and C have to one another the ratio of the cube A to the cube B. VIII.25 applies directly to this ratio: since D is a cube, C is also a cube. Therefore a cube number multiplied by a cube number produces a cube. [8.25]

## Proposition 9.7
**Statement:** If a composite number by multiplying any number make some number, the product will be solid.

**Step 1.** Let the composite number A, by multiplying any number B, produce C. We take the direct route through the definition of composite: choose a number D measuring A as a proper part, and let E be the number of times D measures A. Since D is less than A, E is a number, not merely a unit. By the definition of multiplication, E multiplied by D produces A. [D7.13, D7.3, D7.15]

**Step 2.** Thus C is produced by multiplying the three numbers E, D, and B in succession: first E multiplied by D makes A, and then A multiplied by B makes C. In symbols, C = (ED)B. [D7.15]

**Step 3.** A number produced by three numbers multiplying one another is, by definition, solid. Therefore C is a solid number, with sides E, D, and B. Hence a composite number multiplying any number produces a solid number. [D7.17]

## Proposition 9.8
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the third from the unit will be square, as will also those which successively leave out one; the fourth will be cube, as will also all those which leave out two; and the seventh will be at once cube and square, as will also those which leave out five.

**Step 1.** Let the given continued proportion be u, a₁, a₂, …, aₙ, where u is the unit, counted as the first term. We use the arithmetic ex-aequali theorem, since comparing equal-length portions of this progression directly supplies the required factors. For any positive integer r with 2r ≤ n, compare the portions u, a₁, …, aᵣ and aᵣ, aᵣ₊₁, …, a₂ᵣ. Their corresponding successive ratios are equal, so
u : aᵣ = aᵣ : a₂ᵣ.
If 3r ≤ n, comparison with the portion a₂ᵣ, a₂ᵣ₊₁, …, a₃ᵣ likewise gives
u : aᵣ = a₂ᵣ : a₃ᵣ.
For r = 1 these equalities belong to the given continued proportion itself. [7.14]

**Step 2.** From u : aᵣ = aᵣ : a₂ᵣ, the unit measures aᵣ the same number of times that aᵣ measures a₂ᵣ. Thus a₂ᵣ consists of as many copies of aᵣ as there are units in aᵣ: it is aᵣ multiplied by itself, and hence a square. This holds for every r with 2r ≤ n. These terms occupy positions 3, 5, 7, …, counting the unit first; therefore the third term and all those thereafter obtained by leaving out one term are square. [D7.2, D7.20, D7.15, D7.18]

**Step 3.** Whenever 3r ≤ n, the second equality in Step 1 shows that a₂ᵣ measures a₃ᵣ as many times as the unit measures aᵣ. Therefore aᵣ multiplying a₂ᵣ produces a₃ᵣ. By Step 2, a₂ᵣ is aᵣ multiplied by itself; consequently a₃ᵣ is contained by three equal numbers, each equal to aᵣ, and is a cube. These terms occupy positions 4, 7, 10, …; therefore the fourth term and all those thereafter obtained by leaving out two terms are cube. [D7.2, D7.20, D7.15, D7.19]

**Step 4.** For every positive integer k with 6k ≤ n, Step 2 applied with r = 3k makes a₆ₖ a square with side a₃ₖ, while Step 3 applied with r = 2k makes that same a₆ₖ a cube with side a₂ₖ. Thus these terms are simultaneously square and cube. They occupy positions 7, 13, 19, …: the seventh term and all those thereafter obtained by leaving out five terms. All three assertions follow. [Steps 2–3; D7.18, D7.19]

## Proposition 9.9
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be square, all the rest will also be square.

**Step 1.** Write the given continued proportion as \(1,a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\), where \(a_1\) is square. Separate the terms after the unit into alternate positions, using IX.8 first because it applies directly to this progression: the third, fifth, seventh, and subsequent alternate terms, counting the unit as first, are square. Thus every existing term \(a_2,a_4,a_6,\ldots\) is square. [9.8]

**Step 2.** For the remaining positions, use VIII.22: in three numbers in continued proportion, if the first is square, the third is square. Since \(a_1\) is square, applying this to \(a_1,a_2,a_3\) shows that \(a_3\) is square; applying it next to \(a_3,a_4,a_5\) shows that \(a_5\) is square. Repeating for as long as the finite progression continues proves that every existing term \(a_1,a_3,a_5,\ldots\) is square. Together with Step 1, this covers every number after the unit. Therefore all the rest are square. [8.22]

## Proposition 9.10
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be not square, neither will any other be square except the third from the unit and all those which leave out one.

**Step 1.** Write the given progression as 1, a₁, a₂, …, aₙ, where a₁ is not square. By IX.8, a₂, a₄, a₆, …, whenever present, are square. These are precisely the third term from the unit and the terms obtained thereafter by leaving out one. [9.8]

**Step 2.** Since 1 : a₁ = aⱼ : aⱼ₊₁, each succeeding number is the same multiple of its predecessor. Thus, for j ≥ 1, every reversed triple aⱼ₊₂, aⱼ₊₁, aⱼ is also in continued proportion: its successive ratios express that same multiple. [D7.20]

**Step 3.** We use VIII.22 on these reversed triples, since it directly transfers squareness by two places. Suppose that some a₂ᵣ₊₁ with r ≥ 1 were square. Applying VIII.22 to a₂ᵣ₊₁, a₂ᵣ, a₂ᵣ₋₁ shows that a₂ᵣ₋₁ is square. Repeating the same application backwards through the progression shows successively that a₂ᵣ₋₃, …, a₁ are square. This contradicts the hypothesis that a₁ is not square. Hence none of a₁, a₃, a₅, … is square. [8.22]

**Step 4.** Therefore, among the numbers following the unit, only the third term from the unit and those which successively leave out one are square, and all those terms are indeed square. This proves the proposition. [9.8, 8.22]

## Proposition 9.11
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, the less measures the greater according to some one of the numbers which have place among the proportional numbers.

**Step 1.** Let the given continued proportion be a₀, a₁, …, aₙ, where a₀ is the unit. The unit is a part of a₁; hence, since a₀:a₁ = aₖ:aₖ₊₁, each aₖ is likewise a part of aₖ₊₁. Thus the terms increase. Take any less term aᵢ and greater term aⱼ, so that i < j. If i = 0, the unit measures aⱼ according to aⱼ itself, which is one of the given terms. It remains to consider i > 0. [D7.2, D7.3, D7.20]

**Step 2.** Put d = j − i. The direct route is to compare two equally long portions of the progression by ex aequali. Consider

a₀, a₁, …, a_d
and
aᵢ, aᵢ₊₁, …, aⱼ.

Corresponding successive terms have the same ratio, by the given continued proportion. Therefore, ex aequali,

a₀:a_d = aᵢ:aⱼ. [7.14]

**Step 3.** The unit a₀ measures a_d as many times as there are units in a_d. By the proportion just obtained, aᵢ is the same part of aⱼ that the unit is of a_d. Consequently aᵢ measures aⱼ according to a_d. Since 1 ≤ d ≤ n, this measuring number a_d has a place among the given proportional numbers. Thus every less term measures every greater term according to one of those numbers, as required. [D7.2, D7.3, D7.20]

## Proposition 9.12
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same.

**Step 1.** Let the given progression be 1, a₁, a₂, …, aₙ, where 1 denotes the unit and a₁ is the number next to it. For every i ≥ 2, continued proportion gives 1 : a₁ = aᵢ₋₁ : aᵢ. Thus aᵢ₋₁ is the same part of aᵢ that the unit is of a₁. Since a number is composed of units, aᵢ consists of as many copies of aᵢ₋₁ as there are units in a₁. By the definition of multiplication, therefore, aᵢ = a₁ · aᵢ₋₁. [D7.2, D7.20, D7.15]

**Step 2.** Let p be any prime number measuring aₙ. Among a₁, …, aₙ, choose the first term aⱼ measured by p; such a term exists because p measures the last. We apply the prime-divisor-of-a-product theorem directly, since Step 1 expresses each term after a₁ as a product of earlier terms. If j > 1, then aⱼ = a₁ · aⱼ₋₁, so p measures either a₁ or aⱼ₋₁. Both occur before aⱼ, contradicting its choice as the first term measured by p. Hence j = 1, and p measures a₁. [7.30]

**Step 3.** The prime p in Step 2 was arbitrary. Consequently, every prime number measuring the last term also measures the number next to the unit. Thus, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit is measured by those same prime numbers, as required.

## Proposition 9.13
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, and the number after the unit be prime, the greatest will not be measured by any except those which have a place among the proportional numbers.

**Step 1.** Write the given progression as
\(a_0=1,a_1=p,a_2,\ldots,a_n=N\), where \(p\) is prime. Since \(1:p=a_i:a_{i+1}\), each term after the unit is obtained by multiplying its predecessor by \(p\). Thus \(a_i=p^i\), where \(p^0=1\). A number contains more than one unit, so \(p>1\), and these successive products strictly increase. [D7.20, D7.15, D7.2, CN5]

**Step 2.** Use IX.12 directly, since it transfers prime measures of the last term to the term next to the unit. If a prime \(q\) measures \(N\), IX.12 says that \(q\) measures \(p\). Since \(p\) is prime and \(q\) is not the unit, \(q=p\). Consequently, every prime measure of \(N\) is \(p\). [9.12, D7.11]

**Step 3.** Let \(b>1\) be any measure of \(N\). If \(b\) is prime, Step 2 gives \(b=p\). Otherwise \(b\) is composite, and VII.31 supplies a prime \(q\) measuring \(b\). Because \(N\) consists of repetitions of \(b\), and \(b\) of repetitions of \(q\), \(q\) also measures \(N\). Step 2 again gives \(q=p\). Hence every nonunit measure of \(N\) is measured by \(p\). [D7.11, D7.13, 7.31, D7.15]

**Step 4.** Now let \(d\) be any measure of \(N\). If \(d=1\), it already occurs in the progression. Otherwise Step 3 permits division by \(p\), giving \(d=p d_1\). The quotient \(d_1\) also measures \(N\): it measures \(d\), by commutativity of multiplication, and grouping the repetitions shows that it measures \(N\). Moreover, \(d_1<d\). Whenever the quotient is not the unit, repeat this operation. Every quotient still measures \(N\), and each contains strictly fewer units than its predecessor. Therefore the process must reach the unit after finitely many divisions, say \(r\). Reversing these divisions gives \(d=p^r\). [D7.15, 7.16, CN5, D7.2]

**Step 5.** Since \(d\) measures \(N\), we have \(d\leq N=p^n\). If \(r>n\), the successive multiplications by \(p>1\) would give \(p^r>p^n\), contrary to that inequality. Thus \(r\leq n\), and \(d=p^r=a_r\), a term of the given progression. Therefore the greatest number is measured by no number except those having a place among the proportional numbers. [D7.15, CN5; Steps 1 and 4]

## Proposition 9.14
**Statement:** If a number be the least that is measured by prime numbers, it will not be measured by any other prime number except those originally measuring it.

**Step 1.** Let N be the least number measured by the given prime numbers p₁, …, pᵣ. Suppose that another prime q, distinct from every pᵢ, measures N. No pᵢ can measure q, since a prime has no number other than itself as a divisor. Consequently q cannot equal N, for every pᵢ measures N. [D7.11]

**Step 2.** Since q measures N and q ≠ N, write N = qM, where M counts the copies of q making up N. Because q < N, M is a number rather than the unit. [D7.3, D7.15] Also q, being a number, contains more than one unit; thus qM contains more than one copy of M, and M < N. [D7.2, D7.15, CN5]

**Step 3.** Apply VII.30 directly to the product qM: this is the natural route because each given prime pᵢ measures that product. It follows that pᵢ measures q or M. The former is excluded by Step 1, so every pᵢ measures M. [7.30, D7.11] Thus M is a number smaller than N measured by all the given primes, contrary to the defining leastness of N. Therefore N is measured by no prime other than those originally measuring it, as required.

## Proposition 9.15
**Statement:** If three numbers in continued proportion be the least of those which have the same ratio with them, any two whatever added together will be prime to the remaining number.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the three numbers, with A:B = B:C, and suppose they are the least numbers having these ratios. By VIII.3, A and C are prime to one another. By VII.19 applied to A:B = B:C, AC = B². We use the coprimality of the extremes directly, without constructing a representation of the progression. [8.3, 7.19]

**Step 2.** To prove two numbers prime to one another, it suffices to exclude a prime common measure. Indeed, if they are not prime to one another, they have a common measure d greater than the unit. If d is prime, take p = d; otherwise d is composite, and VII.31 supplies a prime p measuring d and therefore both numbers. We use VII.31 only in the composite case, since the prime case needs no further theorem. Here and below, the elementary rules about measures follow by writing measured numbers as multiples: a measure of a number measures its products; a measure of two numbers measures their positive difference; and measurement is transitive. [D7.12, D7.11, D7.13, 7.31, D7.5]

**Step 3.** Suppose A+B and C are not prime to one another. By Step 2, some prime p measures both. Since p measures C, it measures AC, and hence B² by Step 1. By VII.30 applied to B·B, p measures B. Since it also measures A+B, it measures (A+B)−B = A. Thus p measures both A and C, contrary to Step 1. Therefore A+B is prime to C. [7.30, D7.5, D7.12; Steps 1–2]

**Step 4.** Suppose B+C and A are not prime to one another, and take a prime common measure p as in Step 2. Since p measures A, it measures AC = B². By VII.30, it measures B. Subtracting B from B+C shows that p also measures C. This again contradicts the coprimality of A and C. Therefore B+C is prime to A. [7.30, D7.5, D7.12; Steps 1–2]

**Step 5.** Suppose A+C and B are not prime to one another, and take a prime common measure p. Since p measures B, it measures B² = AC. By VII.30, p measures A or C. If it measures A, then it also measures (A+C)−A = C; if it measures C, then it also measures (A+C)−C = A. Either way, p measures both extremes, a contradiction. Therefore A+C is prime to B. Together with Steps 3–4, this proves that any two of the three numbers added together are prime to the remaining number. [7.30, D7.5, D7.12; Steps 1–2]

## Proposition 9.16
**Statement:** If two numbers be prime to one another, the second will not be to any other number as the first is to the second.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be numbers prime to one another. Thus an unit alone is their common measure [D7.12]. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is a number C such that A:B = B:C.

**Step 2.** Choose the least-ratio route, since it applies directly to the given coprimality: A and B are the least numbers among those having the same ratio with them [7.21].

**Step 3.** The least numbers having a given ratio measure the corresponding numbers of any pair having that ratio. Applying this to A:B = B:C, we obtain that A measures B and B measures C [7.20].

**Step 4.** Since A also measures itself, A is a common measure of A and B. But A, being a number—a multitude of units—is not an unit [D7.2]. This contradicts their being prime to one another [D7.12]. Therefore no number C satisfies A:B = B:C: the second number cannot be to any other number as the first is to the second.

## Proposition 9.17
**Statement:** If there be as many numbers as we please in continued proportion, and the extremes of them be prime to one another, the last will not be to any other number as the first to the second.

**Step 1.** Let a₁, a₂, …, aₙ be numbers in continued proportion, with a₁ and aₙ prime to one another. Suppose, contrary to the assertion, that there is a number b such that aₙ:b = a₁:a₂. The sequence therefore remains in continued proportion when b is appended. Apply ex aequali to the two chains a₁, …, aₙ and a₂, …, aₙ, b. Their corresponding consecutive ratios are equal, so a₁:aₙ = a₂:b. This shifted-chain route brings the given coprime extremes directly into a single ratio. [7.14]

**Step 2.** Since a₁ and aₙ are prime to one another, they are the least numbers having their ratio. We use this given pair directly, without constructing another least pair. Since a₁:aₙ = a₂:b, these least numbers measure the corresponding numbers a₂ and b the same number of times. In particular, a₁ measures a₂. [7.21, 7.20]

**Step 3.** Let a₂ consist of k repetitions of a₁. Every successive ratio aᵢ:aᵢ₊₁ equals a₁:a₂. By the definition of proportional numbers, each aᵢ₊₁ therefore consists of the same k repetitions of aᵢ. Starting from a₁ and proceeding along the sequence, every term is consequently a whole multiple of a₁. In particular, a₁ measures aₙ. [D7.20]

**Step 4.** Thus a₁ measures both itself and aₙ. But a₁ is a number, a multitude of units, and not the unit; it is therefore a common measure other than the unit. This contradicts the hypothesis that a₁ and aₙ are prime to one another, whose only common measure is the unit. Hence no number b can satisfy aₙ:b = a₁:a₂: the last is not to any other number as the first is to the second. [D7.2, D7.12]

## Proposition 9.18
**Statement:** Given two numbers, to investigate whether it is possible to find a third proportional to them.

**Step 1.** Let the given numbers, in their given order, be A and B. A third proportional must be a number C such that A:B = B:C. Choose the product criterion, since it translates this requirement immediately into an equality involving the given numbers: by VII.19, such a C exists exactly when A·C = B·B for some number C. [7.19]

**Step 2.** Form P = B·B. Repeatedly subtract A from P while the remainder is at least A, keeping count of the subtractions. This process terminates, since each subtraction removes units from a fixed finite multitude of units. Answer yes precisely when P is exhausted and the count is a number C; answer no when a positive remainder remains or exhaustion requires only one subtraction. The latter count is merely a unit, not a number in Euclid’s sense. Thus the test is finite and uses only multiplication and subtraction. [D7.15, D7.2]

**Step 3.** If the answer is yes, P consists of C copies of A. Hence C·A = P by the definition of multiplication, and A·C = P by commutativity. Since P = B·B, VII.19 gives A:B = B:C. The count C therefore supplies the required third proportional. [D7.15, 7.16, 7.19]

**Step 4.** If the answer is no, suppose nevertheless that a number X is third proportional, so that A:B = B:X. Then VII.19 gives A·X = B·B = P. By commutativity and the definition of multiplication, P therefore consists of exactly X copies of A. Consequently, successive subtraction of A must exhaust P after a numerical count X of subtractions, contrary to the outcome of the test. No third proportional then exists. Thus the investigation is complete: a third proportional exists exactly when B·B is an exact multiple of A with a number, rather than merely a unit, as multiplier. [7.19, 7.16, D7.15, D7.2]

## Proposition 9.19
**Statement:** Given three numbers, to investigate when it is possible to find a fourth proportional to them.

**Step 1.** Let the three given numbers, in their assigned order, be A, B, C. Form the product P = BC. We use VII.19 directly, because it converts the required proportion A:B = C:D into the product equality AD = P. This gives a direct test without first reducing a ratio to least terms. [D7.15, 7.19]

**Step 2.** Suppose a fourth proportional number D exists. By VII.19, AD = BC = P. By commutativity of multiplication and its definition, P therefore consists of as many copies of A as there are units in D. Consequently A measures P. Moreover, since D is a number—a multitude of units, not merely a unit—P is greater than A. Thus P must be a proper multiple of A. [7.19, 7.16, D7.15, D7.2, D7.5]

**Step 3.** Conversely, suppose A measures P and P is greater than A. Let D contain as many units as the number of times A measures P. Since that count exceeds one, D is a number. By the definition of multiplication, DA = P; hence AD = P by commutativity. Therefore AD = BC, and the converse part of VII.19 gives A:B = C:D. Thus D is the required fourth proportional. [D7.5, D7.2, D7.15, 7.16, 7.19]

**Step 4.** The investigation is therefore this: multiply B by C and test whether A measures the resulting product with a quotient that is a number. If it does, that quotient is the fourth proportional; otherwise no fourth proportional number exists. Equivalently, a fourth proportional exists exactly when BC is a proper multiple of A, and then D = BC/A. The qualification excludes BC = A, which yields only a unit rather than a number in Euclid’s terminology. This completes the investigation. [7.19, D7.2]

## Proposition 9.20
**Statement:** Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.

**Step 1.** Let p₁, …, pᵣ be any assigned finite multitude of distinct prime numbers. Obtain a number M measured by every pᵢ by starting with p₁ and applying VII.34 successively to the current common multiple and the next prime. Each former measure still measures the new multiple, since copies of the former multiple can be regrouped into copies of that measure. We choose the two-number construction because it applies successively to any finite list; leastness itself is not needed. [7.34, D7.3, D7.5]

**Step 2.** Add a unit u to M, and call the resulting number N. Since each pᵢ measures M, each is at most M; and N is greater than M. If N is prime, it is therefore a prime different from every assigned prime. This settles that case. [D7.1, D7.2, D7.3, D7.5, CN5, D7.11]

**Step 3.** Otherwise N is composite. By VII.31, some prime number q measures N. Thus the composite case leads directly to a prime measure, without requiring any further factorization. [D7.11, D7.13, 7.31]

**Step 4.** Suppose q were one of the assigned primes. Then q would measure both M and N. Subtracting from N the whole copies of q which constitute M leaves N − M = u; hence u would also consist of one or more whole copies of q. But q, being a number, is a multitude of units and is greater than a single unit. It therefore cannot measure u. Consequently q is different from every assigned prime. [D7.3, D7.5, CN3, D7.1, D7.2, CN5]

**Step 5.** In either case there is a prime outside the assigned multitude. Adjoining it gives a greater multitude of prime numbers. Since the assigned multitude was arbitrary, prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers. [D7.2, CN5]

## Proposition 9.21
**Statement:** If as many even numbers as we please be added together, the whole is even.

**Step 1.** Let any finite collection of even numbers be given. We use the direct route through the definition of evenness: divide each given number into two equal parts, calling one its first part and the other its second part. Such a division exists for each number because it is even. [D7.6]

**Step 2.** Add together all the first parts, and separately add together all the second parts. Each first part equals its corresponding second part; therefore the two resulting sums are equal, by repeated application of the principle that equals added to equals give equal wholes. [CN2]

**Step 3.** These two sums together constitute the whole of the given numbers, since they contain both parts of every given number. Thus the whole is divided into two equal parts and is therefore even. Hence, if as many even numbers as we please are added together, the whole is even. [D7.6]

## Proposition 9.22
**Statement:** If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be even, the whole will be even.

**Step 1.** Let the given odd numbers be \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\), where their multitude \(m\) is even. Choose the direct unit-removal route: subtract one unit from each odd number, leaving even numbers \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\). Thus \(a_i=e_i+1\) for each \(i\). This uses the even-plus-unit characterization of oddness. [D7.7]

**Step 2.** The sum \(E=e_1+\cdots+e_m\) is even, since a sum of any multitude of even numbers is even. This immediately preceding proposition is the natural result to apply after removing the units. [9.21]

**Step 3.** The removed units are exactly \(m\) in multitude. Since a number is a multitude composed of units, their sum is \(m\), which is even by hypothesis. [D7.2]

**Step 4.** Adding the equalities from Step 1 gives
\[
a_1+\cdots+a_m=E+m.
\]
Both \(E\) and \(m\) are even, so their sum is even. Therefore the whole of the given odd numbers is even, as required. [CN2, 9.21]

## Proposition 9.23
**Statement:** If as many odd numbers as we please be added together, and their multitude be odd, the whole will also be odd.

**Step 1.** If there is only one summand, the conclusion is immediate from the hypothesis. Otherwise, set aside one odd summand, calling it A. Since the original multitude is odd, removing one leaves an even multitude (D7.7). We choose this separation because it brings the remaining summands directly under IX.22.

**Step 2.** Let B be the sum of the remaining summands. They are odd numbers, and their multitude is even; therefore B is even (9.22).

**Step 3.** Since A is odd, it differs by a unit from an even number E (D7.7). Both B and E are even, so B + E is even (9.21).

**Step 4.** The whole sum is B + A. It differs by a unit from B + E, which is even. Therefore the whole sum is odd (D7.7). Thus, whenever an odd multitude of odd numbers is added together, the whole is odd.

## Proposition 9.24
**Statement:** If from an even number an even number be subtracted, the remainder will be even.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given even number and B the even number subtracted, with B<A. We take the direct route through the definition of even: divide A into equal parts A₁, A₂, and B into equal parts B₁, B₂. Thus A=A₁+A₂, B=B₁+B₂, A₁=A₂, and B₁=B₂. [D7.6]

**Step 2.** Since B<A, each half of B is smaller than each half of A. Subtract B₁ from A₁ and B₂ from A₂. The remainders R₁ and R₂ are equal, because equals have been subtracted from equals. [CN3]

**Step 3.** The two parts removed together constitute B; therefore the two remainders together constitute A−B. By Step 2 these remainders are equal, so A−B is divisible into two equal parts and is therefore even. Thus, if an even number is subtracted from an even number, the remainder is even. [D7.6]

## Proposition 9.25
**Statement:** If from an even number an odd number be subtracted, the remainder will be odd.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given even number, B the odd number subtracted, and C the remainder; thus A consists of B and C. By the definitions, A is divisible into two equal parts, whereas B is not. [D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 2.** Use the preceding subtraction proposition, 9.24, since subtracting C from A leaves B. If C were even, then subtracting the even number C from the even number A would leave an even number. Thus B would be even. [9.24]

**Step 3.** This contradicts B being odd: an even number is divisible into two equal parts, while an odd number is not. Therefore C is not even, and hence is odd. Thus, if an odd number is subtracted from an even number, the remainder is odd. [D7.6, D7.7]

## Proposition 9.30
**Statement:** If an odd number measure an even number, it will also measure the half of it.

**Step 1.** Let the odd number A measure the even number B. Then B consists of q copies of A; that is, q multiplying A produces B. The multiplier q is not the unit, since otherwise B=A, whereas an even number cannot be odd. [D7.5, D7.15, D7.6, D7.7]

**Step 2.** Take the direct parity route, applying 9.29 to the multiplier and the given odd measure. If q were odd, then q multiplying the odd number A would produce an odd number. But its product B is even, a contradiction. Therefore q is not odd and so is divisible into two equal parts: q is even. [9.29, D7.7, D7.6]

**Step 3.** Divide the q copies of A constituting B into two groups, each containing half as many copies. The sums of these groups are equal, since each is formed by adding the same number of copies of A. Call either sum C. Thus B consists of the two equal parts C and C, so C is half of B. Moreover, A measures C, since C consists of whole copies of A; if a group contains just one copy, C=A and A measures it once. Hence A measures the half of B, as required. [D7.6, D7.15, CN2, D7.5]

## Proposition 9.31
**Statement:** If an odd number be prime to any number, it will also be prime to the double of it.

**Step 1.** Let A be an odd number prime to B, and let C=B+B be the double of B. Thus C is even, with half B [D7.6], and A and B have no common measure other than the unit [D7.12]. We use the half-measure theorem [9.30], since it applies directly to C and its half B.

## Proposition 9.32
**Statement:** Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.

**Step 1.** Let a₀ be the dyad, and let a₁, a₂, …, aᵣ be obtained by successively doubling it, where r ≥ 1. Thus a₀ is the starting value and a₁, …, aᵣ are the numbers obtained by doubling. The dyad is even, since it divides into two units; each subsequent number is even, since it divides into two equal copies of its predecessor. [D7.6]

**Step 2.** Put N = aᵣ. Its half aᵣ₋₁ is even by Step 1, and this half measures N twice. Therefore an even number measures N according to the even number two, so N is even-times even. [D7.8]

**Step 3.** We use direct repeated halving, since it follows the given doubling chain. Suppose an odd number q measures N. By IX.30, q also measures its half aᵣ₋₁. Repeating the same argument down the chain, q measures a₀, the dyad. Applying IX.30 once more, q measures the unit. But a number is a multitude of units, and no positive number of repetitions of such a multitude can produce a single unit. This is impossible. Hence no odd number measures N. [9.30, D7.2, D7.15]

**Step 4.** If N were even-times odd, an even number e would measure it according to an odd number o; thus o copies of e would produce N. By commutativity of multiplication, e copies of o would also produce N, so the odd number o would measure N, contrary to Step 3. Therefore N is not even-times odd. Since it is even-times even by Step 2, it is even-times even only. As N was any number obtained by continually doubling the initial dyad, the proposition follows. [D7.9, D7.15, 7.16, D7.8]

## Proposition 9.33
**Statement:** If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.

**Step 1.** Let N be a number whose half H is odd. Thus N is twice H. By commutativity of multiplication, N is also the dyad taken H times. Since the dyad is even and H is odd, N is measured by an even number according to an odd number: it is even-times odd. [D7.6, D7.15, 7.16, D7.9]

Because K is even, divide these copies into two groups containing equally many copies. The groups have equal sums, so the sum of each is the half H of N. [D7.8, D7.15, D7.6]

**Step 3.** Each such group consists entirely of even numbers E. Its sum is therefore even by 9.21; if the group contains just one copy, its sum is E itself and is already even. Hence H is even, contrary to its being odd. Thus N cannot be even-times even. Since it is even-times odd by Step 1, it is even-times odd only. [9.21, D7.7, D7.8, D7.9]

## Proposition 9.34
**Statement:** If a number neither be one of those which are continually doubled from a dyad, nor have its half odd, it is both even-times even and even-times odd.

## Proposition 9.35
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please be in continued proportion, and there be subtracted from the second and the last numbers equal to the first, then, as the excess of the second is to the first, so will the excess of the last be to all those before it.

**Step 1.** Let the given numbers in continued proportion be a₁, a₂, …, aₙ, and denote the stated excesses by d = a₂ − a₁ and e = aₙ − a₁. Put
S = a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ₋₁,
T = a₂ + a₃ + ⋯ + aₙ.
Since aₙ = a₁ + e, adding the common intermediate terms gives T = S + e. Thus T − S = e. When n = 2, this is the original equality itself. [CN2]

**Step 2.** We use the numerical sum-of-proportions theorem first, since these two shifted sums differ by precisely the last excess. Continued proportion gives
a₁ : a₂ = a₂ : a₃ = ⋯ = aₙ₋₁ : aₙ.
Therefore, by VII.12,
a₁ : a₂ = S : T.
Alternating by VII.13 gives
a₁ : S = a₂ : T. [7.12, 7.13]

**Step 3.** From the wholes a₂ and T subtract a₁ and S respectively. By Step 2, the wholes have the same ratio as the numbers subtracted. Hence VII.11 gives
(a₂ − a₁) : (T − S) = a₂ : T = a₁ : S.
Using Step 1, this is d : e = a₁ : S. [7.11]

**Step 4.** Alternating this last proportion yields d : a₁ = e : S. Consequently,
(a₂ − a₁) : a₁ = (aₙ − a₁) : (a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ₋₁).
Thus the excess of the second is to the first as the excess of the last is to all the numbers before it, as required. [7.13]

## Proposition 9.36
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be set out continuously in double proportion, until the sum of all becomes prime, and if the sum multiplied into the last make some number, the product will be perfect.

**Step 1.** Write the given progression as
\[
1,2,2^2,\ldots,2^n,
\]
where powers denote repeated doubling. Put \(L=2^n\), let \(p=1+2+\cdots+2^n\) be the given prime sum, and let \(N=pL\). Since the unit is not a number, the prime sum requires \(n\geq1\). Also, \(2\) is prime, since its only smaller measure is the unit, and \(p>L\). [D7.2, D7.11, D7.15]

**Step 2.** Doubling the sum gives
\[
2p=2+2^2+\cdots+2^n+2L.
\]
The terms from \(2\) through \(2^n\) sum to \(p-1\); hence \(2p=p-1+2L\). Subtracting equal quantities therefore gives
\[
p=2L-1,\qquad 1+2+\cdots+2^{n-1}=p-L=L-1.
\]
This obtains the needed sum directly by shifting the given doubling progression. [D7.15, CN3]

**Step 3.** Every entry in the following two lists is a proper measure, and therefore a part, of \(N\):
\[
1,2,\ldots,2^n;
\qquad
p,2p,\ldots,2^{n-1}p.
\]
Indeed, the complementary factors are respectively \(p2^{n-j}\), for \(0\leq j\leq n\), and \(2^{n-j}\), for \(0\leq j<n\); these are all greater than the unit. Each list is strictly increasing, and the lists are disjoint because every entry in the first is at most \(L\), whereas every entry in the second is at least \(p>L\). [D7.3, D7.15]

**Step 4.** We show that there are no other parts. The direct route is to use IX.13 for the measures of \(L\), and VII.30 to pass from \(L\) to \(pL\); no general prime-factor decomposition is needed.

Let \(d\) be any proper measure of \(N\) other than the unit. Write \(dq=N=pL\), with \(d,q>1\). Since the prime \(p\) measures \(dq\), VII.30 says that it measures \(d\) or \(q\).

If \(d=pe\), cancellation in \(peq=pL\) gives \(eq=L\). Thus \(e\) is the unit or a measure of \(L\). By IX.13, applied to the progression beginning with the unit whose next term is the prime \(2\), \(e=2^j\) for some \(0\leq j\leq n\). Since \(d<N\), actually \(j<n\), so \(d=p2^j\) belongs to the second list.

If \(q=pe\), the same cancellation gives \(de=L\). IX.13 then gives \(d=2^j\) for some \(0\leq j\leq n\), placing \(d\) in the first list. These product rearrangements and cancellations express multiplication as repeated addition, with factors interchangeable by VII.16. The unit was already listed. Hence Step 3 lists every part exactly once. [7.30, 9.13, 7.16, D7.15, D7.3]

**Step 5.** Consequently, the sum of all the parts of \(N\) is
\[
(1+2+\cdots+2^n)+p(1+2+\cdots+2^{n-1})
=p+p(L-1)=pL=N.
\]
Here multiplication collects the repeated additions, and Step 2 supplies the second sum. Thus \(N\) is equal to the sum of its own parts and is therefore perfect. [D7.15, D7.22]

## Proposition 10.1
**Statement:** Two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there be subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process be repeated continually, there will be left some magnitude which will be less than the lesser magnitude set out.

**Step 1.** Let A be the greater magnitude and B the lesser. We use the finite-multiple route, directly applying the definition of magnitudes having a ratio: choose a positive integer n such that nB > A. [D5.4]

**Step 2.** Perform n of the prescribed subtractions, unless a remainder less than B has already appeared. Write R₀ = A, and let Sᵢ be the magnitude removed at the ith subtraction and Rᵢ the remainder, so Rᵢ₋₁ = Sᵢ + Rᵢ. Since Sᵢ exceeds half of Rᵢ₋₁, Rᵢ is less than that half; consequently Sᵢ > Rᵢ. Also, each remainder is less than its predecessor, being a part of it. [CN3, CN5]

**Step 3.** Suppose that Rₙ is not less than B. Every preceding remainder Rᵢ is at least Rₙ, and hence, for each i from 1 through n,
Sᵢ > Rᵢ ≥ Rₙ ≥ B.
Thus each of the n removed magnitudes contains a part equal to B together with a positive excess. [CN5]

**Step 4.** Reassembling the removed magnitudes and the final remainder gives
A = S₁ + S₂ + ⋯ + Sₙ + Rₙ.
The n parts equal to B together equal nB, and they form a proper part of A because the removed magnitudes also contain positive excesses. Therefore A > nB, contrary to nB > A from Step 1. Hence Rₙ < B, unless such a remainder occurred earlier. Thus after finitely many prescribed subtractions a magnitude less than the original lesser magnitude is left, as required. [CN2, CN5, D5.4]

## Proposition 10.2
**Statement:** If, when the less of two unequal magnitudes is continually subtracted in turn from the greater, that which is left never measures the one before it, the magnitudes will be incommensurable.

**Step 1.** Let A>B be the two magnitudes satisfying the hypothesis. Suppose, for a contradiction, that they are commensurable, and let E be a common measure. Since E measures B, we have E≤B<A. [D10.1.1, D5.2, CN5]

**Step 2.** Write r₀=A and r₁=B. Collect successive subtractions of the same magnitude into one stage, so that
rᵢ=qᵢrᵢ₊₁+rᵢ₊₂,
where qᵢ is a positive whole number and 0<rᵢ₊₂<rᵢ₊₁. Here qᵢrᵢ₊₁ denotes qᵢ copies of rᵢ₊₁. The hypothesis ensures that these stages continue: an exact subtraction would mean that a remainder measures the magnitude before it, contrary to the hypothesis. [Hypothesis; D5.2]

**Step 3.** E measures every remainder. Indeed, it measures r₀ and r₁. Whenever it measures rᵢ and rᵢ₊₁, both are made up of whole copies of E, as is qᵢrᵢ₊₁. Subtracting those copies from rᵢ leaves rᵢ₊₂ made up of whole copies of E. Repeating this argument proves the assertion at every stage. [D5.2, CN2, CN3]

**Step 4.** Every second remainder is less than half the earlier one. For qᵢ≥1 gives
rᵢ≥rᵢ₊₁+rᵢ₊₂,
and rᵢ₊₁>rᵢ₊₂; hence rᵢ>2rᵢ₊₂. Consequently, passing from rᵢ to rᵢ₊₂ removes more than half of rᵢ. [CN5]

**Step 5.** Choose the exhaustion route of X.1, which applies directly to these magnitudes: consider r₀,r₂,r₄,… . By Step 4, each is obtained from its predecessor by subtracting more than half. Since r₀>E, X.1 therefore guarantees that some remainder r₂ₖ is less than E. [10.1]

**Step 6.** But Step 3 shows that E measures the positive magnitude r₂ₖ. Thus r₂ₖ consists of one or more whole copies of E and cannot be less than E, a contradiction. Therefore A and B have no common measure and are incommensurable. [D5.2, CN5, D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.3
**Statement:** Given two commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the given commensurable magnitudes; thus they have a common measure. If they are equal, either is their greatest common measure. Otherwise let A be the greater. If B measures A, then B is their greatest common measure: it measures both, and no magnitude greater than B can measure B. Hence suppose that B does not measure A. [D10.1.1, D5.2, CN5]

**Step 2.** Use successive subtraction directly, since 10.2 concerns magnitudes themselves and supplies the required termination. Continually subtract the lesser magnitude from the greater, proceeding in turn with the lesser and the remainder. Stop as soon as the lesser of the two current magnitudes measures the greater. This must occur: otherwise the remainders would never measure their preceding magnitudes, and A and B would be incommensurable by 10.2, contrary to the hypothesis. Denote the terminal lesser magnitude by D and the other terminal magnitude by C; thus D measures C. [10.2, D10.1.1]

**Step 3.** The magnitude D measures both terminal magnitudes, C and D. Now reverse the finite sequence of subtractions. At any individual subtraction, a pair X, Y was replaced by X − Y, Y. If D measures X − Y and Y, then each consists of whole copies of D, so their sum X also consists of whole copies of D. Thus D measures both members of the preceding pair. Repeating this backwards shows that D measures both A and B. [D5.2, CN2]

**Step 4.** Let E be any common measure of A and B. Follow the same sequence forwards. Whenever X and Y are both measured by E, subtracting Y from X removes whole copies of E and leaves whole copies of E; hence E measures X − Y as well as Y. Consequently E measures both magnitudes at every stage, and in particular measures the terminal magnitude D. [D5.2, CN3]

**Step 5.** Since every common measure E of A and B measures D, none can be greater than D: D is either equal to E or consists of several copies of E and is greater than one such copy. Since D itself measures A and B, it is their greatest common measure. Therefore the required greatest common measure has been found. [D5.2, CN5]

## Proposition 10.4
**Statement:** Given three commensurable magnitudes, to find their greatest common measure.

**Step 1.** Let the three given commensurable magnitudes be A, B, and C. There is therefore a magnitude U measuring all three. We use successive subtraction twice, because this route preserves every common measure throughout the construction. [D10.1.1]

**Step 2.** Perform successive subtraction on A and B, stopping when the smaller current magnitude measures the greater. Since A and B are commensurable, the process must terminate: otherwise they would be incommensurable by 10.2. Call the smaller magnitude at termination D. If A and B are equal, take D = A immediately. [10.2]

At every subtraction, any measure of both current magnitudes also measures their difference: removing an integral number of equal copies of that measure leaves an integral number of such copies. Thus every common measure of A and B measures D. Conversely, D measures both magnitudes of the terminal pair; reconstructing the preceding pairs by addition shows that D measures A and B. [D5.2, CN3, CN2]

**Step 3.** In particular, U measures D, and U also measures C. Hence D and C are commensurable. Perform the same successive-subtraction construction on D and C, again taking their common value immediately if they are equal. By 10.2 this construction terminates; denote its terminal measure by E. As in Step 2, subtraction shows that every common measure of D and C measures E, while reconstruction by addition shows that E measures D and C. [D10.1.1, 10.2, D5.2, CN3, CN2]

**Step 4.** Since E measures D, and D measures A and B, replacing each copy of D in A and B by its equal copies of E shows that E measures A and B. It also measures C by construction. Thus E is a common measure of all three given magnitudes. [D5.2, CN2]

**Step 5.** Let H be any common measure of A, B, and C. By Step 2, H measures D. Consequently H measures both D and C, so by Step 3 it measures E. A magnitude measuring E cannot be greater than E: it is either equal to E or one of several equal parts composing E. Therefore no common measure of A, B, and C is greater than E. Hence the constructed magnitude E is their greatest common measure, as required. [D5.2, CN5]

## Proposition 10.5
**Statement:** Commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be commensurable magnitudes. By definition, some magnitude C measures both: let A consist of a copies of C and B of b copies of C. We take this direct common-measure route because the definition supplies all that is needed; a greatest common measure is unnecessary. [D10.1.1]

**Step 2.** Form a number M consisting of 2a units and a number N consisting of 2b units. These are multitudes of units, hence numbers. Using two units for each copy of C ensures that both are numbers even when a or b is one. [D7.2]

**Step 3.** Take arbitrary positive whole-number multiplicities r and s. Then rA consists of ra copies of C, and sB consists of sb copies of C; correspondingly, rM consists of ra pairs of units, and sN consists of sb pairs of units. If ra and sb are equal, the respective wholes are equal by addition of equals. If one count is greater, the corresponding whole contains a part equal to the other whole together with additional copies, and is therefore greater. Thus rA exceeds, equals, or falls short of sB precisely as rM exceeds, equals, or falls short of sN. [CN2, CN5]

**Step 4.** Since this agreement holds for every choice of r and s, the definition of equal ratios gives A:B = M:N. Therefore commensurable magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. [D5.5]

## Proposition 10.6
**Statement:** If two magnitudes have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes will be commensurable.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be magnitudes such that A:B = m:n, where m and n are numbers. Regard the numerical terms as finite positive counts of units. We shall construct a common measure by performing corresponding subtractions on the magnitudes and their numerical terms. By the definition of equal ratios, taking single multiples shows that A and B have the same comparison—greater, equal, or less—as m and n. [D7.1, D7.2, D5.5]

**Step 2.** At any stage, suppose the current pairs satisfy X:Y = p:q. If p and q are unequal, interchange both pairs if necessary so that p>q; the equimultiple definition preserves equality of ratios under this interchange and gives X>Y. Then
(X−Y):Y = (p−q):q.
Here we use separando, the form of proportionality naturally suited to subtraction. Replace the two pairs by (X−Y, Y) and (p−q, q), and continue whenever the numerical terms are unequal. [D5.5, 5.17]

**Step 3.** Each subtraction leaves two positive unit-counts and strictly decreases their sum. Since the initial sum contains only finitely many units, the process must stop, and it can stop only when the numerical terms are equal. At that stage let the magnitudes be U and V. Their ratio equals the ratio of two equal numerical terms; taking single multiples in the definition of equal ratios gives U=V. [D7.2, D5.5]

**Step 4.** The magnitude U therefore measures both terminal magnitudes once. Now reverse the finite sequence of subtractions. Each reversed step restores a magnitude by adding the two current magnitudes. If these consist respectively of r and s copies of U, their sum consists of r+s copies of U. Thus U measures both magnitudes at every preceding stage, and consequently measures the original A and B. [CN2, D5.2]

**Step 5.** Magnitudes measured by the same measure are commensurable. Since U measures both A and B, the given magnitudes are commensurable, as required. [D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.9
**Statement:** The squares on straight lines commensurable in length have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number; and squares which have to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number will also have their sides commensurable in length. S(A):S(B) = m²:n².
Thus squares on lines commensurable in length have the ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 2.** Conversely, suppose S(A):S(B) = m²:n², where m and n are numbers. Take a straight line U, and let C and D consist respectively of m and n copies of U. Applying the duplicate-ratio argument of Step 1 to C:D = m:n gives

Hence A:B = m:n (5.11), and A and B are commensurable in length by 10.6. This proves the second assertion.

**Step 4.** Suppose A and B are incommensurable in length. If S(A):S(B) were the ratio of a square number to a square number, Steps 2–3 would make A and B commensurable in length. This contradicts their having no common measure (D10.1.1). Therefore their squares do not have the ratio of a square number to a square number.

**Step 5.** Finally, suppose S(A):S(B) is not the ratio of a square number to a square number. If A and B were commensurable in length, Step 1 would give precisely such a ratio, contrary to the supposition. Thus A and B have no common measure and are incommensurable in length (D10.1.1). All four assertions are proved.

## Proposition 10.10
**Statement:** To find two straight lines incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with an assigned straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the assigned straight line, and write S(x) for the square on a straight line x. Describe the square ABCD on AB, and join AC. Put a = AB and b = AC. Since AB = BC and angle ABC is right, the square on AC equals the two squares on AB and BC; hence S(b) = 2S(a). We choose this diagonal construction because its double-square relation leads directly to the square-ratio criterion. [1.46, P1, D1.22, 1.47]

**Step 2.** The ratio 4:8 cannot be the ratio of a square number to a square number. For 4 is square, whereas 8 is not: it lies strictly between 2·2 and 3·3. If 4:8 were a ratio of square numbers, VIII.24 would imply that 8 was square, a contradiction. [D7.18, 8.24]

**Step 3.** Since S(a):S(b) = 4:8, the squares do not have the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore a and b are incommensurable in length by X.9. But S(a) measures both S(a) and S(b), so a and b are commensurable in square. Thus b is incommensurable in length only with the assigned line a. [10.9, D10.1.2]

**Step 4.** Find a mean proportional c between a and b, so that a:c = c:b. Then the square on c equals the rectangle contained by a and b. [6.13, 6.17]

**Step 5.** The square on a and the rectangle contained by a and b have the same height a and respective bases a and b. Consequently, by VI.1 and the equality established in Step 4,
S(a):S(c) = a:b. [6.1]

**Step 6.** Since a and b are incommensurable in length, their ratio is not the ratio of a number to a number. The same is therefore true of S(a):S(c). By X.8 these squares are incommensurable, and hence a and c are incommensurable in square. Here X.7–8 apply directly because the incommensurable ratio a:b is already established. [10.7, 10.8, D10.1.2]

**Step 7.** Moreover, a ratio which is not the ratio of any number to any number cannot be the ratio of a square number to a square number. Thus X.9 also shows that a and c are incommensurable in length. Accordingly, b is incommensurable with the assigned straight line a in length only, while c is incommensurable with it in square also. The two required straight lines have been found. [10.9]

## Proposition 10.11
**Statement:** If four magnitudes be proportional, and the first be commensurable with the second, the third will also be commensurable with the fourth; and, if the first be incommensurable with the second, the third will also be incommensurable with the fourth.

**Step 1.** Let A, B, C, D be four magnitudes with A:B = C:D. We take the numerical-ratio route, since the given proportion allows such ratios to transfer directly between the pairs. Suppose first that A is commensurable with B. By 10.5, there are numbers m, n such that A:B = m:n. [10.5]

**Step 2.** Since C:D and m:n are both equal to A:B, they are equal to one another by 5.11. Thus C:D = m:n, and 10.6 implies that C is commensurable with D. [5.11, 10.6]

**Step 3.** Suppose instead that A is incommensurable with B. By 10.7, A:B is not the ratio of any number to any number. [10.7]

**Step 4.** Neither can C:D be the ratio of a number m to a number n: otherwise A:B = C:D and C:D = m:n would give A:B = m:n by 5.11, contrary to Step 3. Therefore, by 10.8, C is incommensurable with D. Both assertions are proved. [5.11, 10.8]

## Proposition 10.12
**Statement:** Magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another also.

**Step 1.** Let A and B each be commensurable with the same magnitude C. Choose the direct numerical-ratio route, since it applies immediately to both hypotheses. By 10.5, there are numbers m, n, p, q such that A:C = m:n and C:B = p:q. [10.5]

**Step 2.** Form the numbers P = mp, Q = np, and R = nq. Since m and n multiply the same number p, we have P:Q = m:n. Since n multiplies p and q, we have Q:R = p:q. Thus the two numerical ratios have a common middle term. [7.18, 7.17]

**Step 3.** Ratios equal to the same ratio are equal to one another. Hence A:C = P:Q and C:B = Q:R. [5.11]

**Step 4.** Applying equality of ratios ex aequali to the triples A, C, B and P, Q, R gives A:B = P:R. [5.22]

**Step 5.** Therefore A and B have to one another the ratio of a number to a number, and so are commensurable by the direct criterion 10.6. Consequently, magnitudes commensurable with the same magnitude are commensurable with one another. [10.6]

## Proposition 10.13
**Statement:** If two magnitudes be commensurable, and the one of them be incommensurable with any magnitude, the remaining one will also be incommensurable with the same.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be commensurable, and let A be incommensurable with C. Suppose, for a contradiction, that B is commensurable with C. Having a common measure is symmetric, so C is then commensurable with B. [D10.1.1]

**Step 2.** A and C are therefore both commensurable with B. Hence A and C are commensurable with one another. We use the common-magnitude criterion directly, since B is already the shared magnitude. [10.12]

**Step 3.** Thus A and C have a common measure, contrary to their assumed incommensurability. Consequently B and C cannot have a common measure and are incommensurable. Therefore the remaining magnitude is also incommensurable with the same magnitude, as required. [D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.14
**Statement:** If four straight lines be proportional, and the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line commensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by  the square on a straight line commensurable with the third. And, if the square on the first be greater than the square on the second by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the first, the square on the third will also be greater than the square on the fourth by the square on a straight line in-commensurable with the third.

**Step 1.** Let the four straight lines be a, b, c, d, with a:b = c:d. Write A, B, C, D for their respective squares. Let e be the given straight line whose square E equals the excess of A over B, so A = B + E. Since squares are similar and similarly described figures, A:B = C:D. [6.22]

**Step 2.** Alternately, A:C = B:D. Since A > B, it follows that C > D. [5.16, 5.14]

**Step 3.** Place the smaller square D within C with a common corner and corresponding sides aligned. The remainder is a positive rectilineal figure. Construct a square F equal to this remainder, and let f be its side. Thus C = D + F. [2.14]

**Step 4.** We use the remainder theorem directly, because A:C = B:D compares the whole squares in the same ratio as the squares subtracted. It gives (A − B):(C − D) = A:C, or E:F = A:C. Therefore, alternately, A:E = C:F. [5.19, 5.16]

**Step 5.** Applying the converse theorem for similar and similarly described figures to these squares gives a:e = c:f. This returns directly to a proportion between the straight lines themselves. [6.22]

**Step 6.** If a is commensurable with e, then c is commensurable with f; if a is incommensurable with e, then c is incommensurable with f. In either case, the square on c exceeds the square on d by the square on f, as established in Step 3. Thus the excess square has a side commensurable with c in the first case and incommensurable with c in the second, proving both assertions. [10.11]

## Proposition 10.15
**Statement:** If two commensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole will also be commensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be commensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes will also be commensurable.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the two magnitudes, and let W = A + B. We take the direct common-measure route, since the definition of commensurability supplies exactly what is needed. Suppose first that A and B are commensurable. They therefore have a common measure M; write A = mM and B = nM, where m and n count positive whole numbers of copies of M. [D10.1.1, D5.2]

**Step 2.** Adding these equalities gives W = (m + n)M. Thus M measures W as well as A and B. Consequently W is commensurable with each of A and B. [CN2, D10.1.1]

**Step 3.** Conversely, suppose W is commensurable with A. There is then a common measure N, so W = rN and A = sN for positive whole numbers r and s. Since W is the whole and A is a proper part, W > A; hence r > s. [D10.1.1, D5.2, CN5]

**Step 4.** Subtracting A = sN from W = rN gives B = (r − s)N: removing s copies of N from r copies leaves a positive whole number of copies. Therefore N measures both A and B, so A and B are commensurable. If instead W is commensurable with B, the same argument with A and B interchanged proves the same conclusion. Thus the sum of two commensurable magnitudes is commensurable with each, and commensurability of the sum with either summand implies commensurability of the original magnitudes. [CN3, D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.16
**Statement:** If two incommensurable magnitudes be added together, the whole will also be incommensurable with each of them; and, if the whole be incommensurable with one of them, the original magnitudes will also be incommensurable.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be the two magnitudes, and let S = A + B. By Definition D10.1.1, two magnitudes are incommensurable exactly when they have no common measure, that is, when they are not commensurable. We use the immediately preceding Proposition 10.15 by contraposition, since its two assertions supply precisely the required implications. [D10.1.1; 10.15]

**Step 2.** Suppose A and B are incommensurable. If S were commensurable with A, the second assertion of Proposition 10.15 would make A and B commensurable, a contradiction. The same assertion gives the same contradiction if S is assumed commensurable with B. Thus S is incommensurable with each of A and B. [10.15; D10.1.1]

**Step 3.** Conversely, suppose S is incommensurable with one of A and B. If A and B were commensurable, the first assertion of Proposition 10.15 would make S commensurable with each of them, contradicting the hypothesis. Therefore A and B are incommensurable. Both assertions are proved. [10.15; D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.17
**Statement:** If there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are commensurable in length, then the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line commensurable with  the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it will divide it into parts which are commensurable in length.

**Step 1.** Let the greater straight line have length a and the less length b, so that a > b. Let the given application divide the greater into parts of lengths x and y. Since the deficient figure is a square, the applied parallelogram is a rectangle whose sides are the two parts. Thus, writing xy for this rectangle and t² for the square on a length t,

a = x + y,     4xy = b².
[Definitions D1.22, D2.1]

**Step 2.** We use II.5 directly, because the applied rectangle is precisely the rectangle contained by the two parts of the greater line. First, the parts cannot be equal: if x = y, II.4 gives a² = 4xy = b², contrary to a > b. Here II.4 also shows that the square on a greater positive length is greater than the square on a lesser one.

Interchange the names of the parts if necessary so that x > y, and let d = x − y. Bisect the greater line. The distance between its midpoint and its point of division is d/2. Hence II.5 gives

xy + (d/2)² = (a/2)².

By II.4, the square on twice a length is four times the square on that length. Adding four copies of the preceding equality therefore gives

4xy + d² = a²,

and consequently

a² = b² + d².     (1)
[1.10, 2.5, 2.4, CN2]

**Step 3.** Suppose first that the parts x and y are commensurable in length. Use their common measure directly: let u measure them, so that x consists of m copies of u and y of n copies, where m > n. Then a = x + y consists of m + n copies of u, while d = x − y consists of m − n copies. Thus d is commensurable in length with a. By (1), the square on the greater exceeds the square on the less by the square on this commensurable straight line d. This proves the first assertion. [D10.1.1; Step 2]

**Step 4.** Conversely, suppose that

a² = b² + c²,

where c is commensurable in length with a. For the given deficient application, Step 2 again gives a² = b² + d², where d = x − y > 0. Subtracting b² yields c² = d². Therefore c = d: otherwise II.4 would make the square on the greater of these positive lengths strictly greater. Hence a and d have a common measure u. Write a = mu and d = nu, where m > n are positive integers. [CN3, 2.4, D10.1.1]

**Step 5.** Bisect u, and call its half v. Since a = x + y and d = x − y,

2x = a + d = (m + n)u,
2y = a − d = (m − n)u.

Consequently x = (m + n)v and y = (m − n)v. Thus v measures both parts, so they are commensurable in length. This proves the converse and completes both assertions. [1.10, D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.18
**Statement:** If there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into parts which are incommensurable, the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater. And, if the square on the greater be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the greater, and if there be applied to the greater a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into parts which are incommensurable. Let A, BC be two unequal straight lines, of which BC is the greater, and to BC let there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, A, and deficient by a square figure.

**Step 1.** Let D be the point of division of BC, with the applied parallelogram on BD and its square defect on DC. Because the defect is a square, the applied figure is the rectangle contained by BD and DC. Thus, writing squares and rectangles as areas,
4(BD·DC) = A².
We use 10.17 by contraposition, since its two directions concern precisely this same application; first we identify the square of the excess. [D1.22, D2.1, 10.17]

**Step 2.** Bisect BC at E. The point D cannot coincide with E: otherwise the preceding area equality and the formula for the square on a doubled line would give
A² = 4BE² = BC²,
contrary to A < BC. Indeed, II.4 shows that the square on a longer line contains the square on the shorter together with positive additional areas, and therefore is greater. Let X be a straight line twice ED; since D differs from E, X is positive. [1.10, 2.4, CN5]

**Step 3.** Since BC is cut equally at E and unequally at D, II.5 gives
BD·DC + ED² = BE².
Taking four copies of these equal areas gives
4(BD·DC) + 4ED² = 4BE².
By II.4, the square on twice a line is four times the square on that line. Substituting the equality from Step 1, X = 2ED, and BC = 2BE, we obtain
A² + X² = BC².
Thus the square on BC exceeds the square on A by the square on X. [2.5, CN2, 2.4]

**Step 4.** Suppose first that BD and DC are incommensurable in length. If X were commensurable with BC, the converse direction of 10.17, applied to the equality in Step 3 and to the given parallelogram, would make BD and DC commensurable in length. This contradicts the supposition. Therefore X is incommensurable with BC, proving the first assertion. [10.17, D10.1.1]

**Step 5.** Conversely, suppose that
BC² = A² + K²,
where K is incommensurable with BC. If the given application divided BC into commensurable parts BD and DC, the forward direction of 10.17 would supply a straight line L commensurable with BC such that
BC² = A² + L².
Subtracting A² gives K² = L². Consequently K = L: if either line were greater, II.4 and the whole–part principle would make its square greater. Hence K would be commensurable with BC, a contradiction. The parts BD and DC are therefore incommensurable in length. This proves the converse and completes both assertions. [10.17, CN3, 2.4, CN5, D10.1.1]

## Proposition 10.19
**Statement:** The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in length is rational.

**Step 1.** Let a and b be rational straight lines commensurable in length, and let R be the rectangle contained by them. Let S be the square on a, and Q the square on the assigned rational straight line. Since a is rational, it is commensurable in square with the assigned straight line; hence S is commensurable with Q. **Step 2.** Use the direct comparison with the square on the given side a. The rectangle R and the square S have the same height a and bases b and a respectively. Therefore b : a = R : S. [6.1]

**Step 3.** Since b and a are commensurable in length, the proportion in Step 2 implies that R and S are commensurable. Proposition 10.11 is the direct choice here because it transfers commensurability through precisely this proportion. [10.11]

**Step 4.** Both R and Q are commensurable with S, so R is commensurable with Q. An area commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line is rational. Therefore the rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in length is rational. [10.12, D10.1.4]

## Proposition 10.20
**Statement:** If a rational area be applied to a rational straight line, it produces as breadth a straight line rational and commensurable in length with the straight line to which it is applied.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given rational area and a the rational straight line to which it is applied. Let b be the resulting breadth, so that A is the rectangle contained by a and b. Let u be the assigned rational straight line, and write S_x for the square on a straight line x. Since a is rational, S_a is commensurable with S_u; since A is rational, A is likewise commensurable with S_u. [D10.1.2, D10.1.3, D10.1.4]

**Step 2.** Therefore S_a and A are commensurable with one another, since both are commensurable with S_u. [10.12]

**Step 3.** The square S_a and the rectangle A can be regarded as having the same height a and bases a and b respectively. Hence S_a : A = a : b. The direct route is to transfer commensurability across this proportion by X.11, without introducing numerical ratios. Since S_a and A are commensurable, a and b are commensurable in length. [6.1, 10.11]

**Step 4.** Likewise, the rectangle A and the square S_b have the same height b and bases a and b respectively. Thus a : b = A : S_b. Since a and b are commensurable, A and S_b are commensurable. [6.1, 10.11]

**Step 5.** Both S_b and S_u are commensurable with A, so they are commensurable with one another. Thus b is commensurable in square with the assigned rational straight line u, and consequently b is rational. Together with Step 3, this proves that the breadth is rational and commensurable in length with the straight line to which the area is applied. [10.12, D10.1.2, D10.1.3]

## Proposition 10.21
**Statement:** The rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. Let the latter be called medial.

**Step 1.** Let a and b be rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and let R be the rectangle contained by them. Thus a and b are incommensurable in length. Let u be the assigned rational straight line, U the square on u, and Q the square on a. Since a is rational, Q is commensurable with U. [D10.1.2, D10.1.3]

**Step 2.** The square Q and the rectangle R can be taken with the same height a and bases a and b respectively. Therefore, by the theorem on parallelograms of equal height,
Q : R = a : b. [6.1]

**Step 3.** Since a and b are incommensurable in length, the proportion in Step 2 implies that Q and R are incommensurable. The direct proportionality criterion is the natural choice here, since the required proportion is already available and no passage through numerical ratios is needed. [10.11]

**Step 4.** Now U and Q are commensurable, while Q and R are incommensurable. Hence U and R are incommensurable. Therefore R is irrational, being incommensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line. [10.13, D10.1.4]

**Step 5.** Construct a square equal to R, and let m be its side. Such a square exists by the construction of a square equal to a given rectilineal figure. Since R is irrational, the side of a square equal to it is irrational by definition. Thus m is irrational. Let this straight line be called **medial**. Consequently, both the rectangle contained by the given rational straight lines commensurable in square only and the side of its equal square are irrational, as required. [2.14, D10.1.4]

## Proposition 10.22
**Statement:** The square on a medial straight line, if applied to a rational straight line, produces as breadth a straight line rational and incommensurable in length with that to which it is applied.

**Step 4.** Since S(u) is commensurable with S(a), the proportion in Step 3 implies that S(b) is commensurable with S(v). But S(r) is also commensurable with S(v), so S(b) is commensurable with S(r). Therefore b is rational. [10.11, 10.12, D10.1.2, D10.1.3]

**Step 5.** If b were commensurable in length with a, then, since both are rational, R(a,b) would be rational. But R(a,b) = S(m), which is irrational by Step 1. This is impossible, since a rational area is commensurable with S(r), whereas an irrational area is incommensurable with it. Therefore b is incommensurable in length with a.
