## Proposition 12.4
**Statement:** If there be two pyramids of the same height which have triangular bases, and cach of them be divided into two pyramids equal to one another and similar to the whole, and into two equal prisms, then, as the base of the one pyramid is to the base of the other pyramid, so will all the prisms in the one pyramid be to all the prisms, being equal in multitude, in the other pyramid.

**Step 1.** Let the pyramids be SABC and S′A′B′C′, with common height h and base-areas B₀ and B₀′. Use the division of XII.3 in each. Explicitly, let L, M, N be the midpoints of AB, BC, CA, and U, V, W the midpoints of SA, SB, SC. The residual pyramids are ALNU and SUVW; one prism P has opposite triangular faces BLM and VUW, and the other prism is Q. Thus P = Q. Use corresponding primed letters in the other pyramid, where P′ = Q′. [12.3]

**Step 2.** The midpoint parallels give UV ∥ AB and UW ∥ AC, so the plane UVW is parallel to ABC. Construct also a parallel plane through S. These three parallel planes cut SA and an altitude proportionally; since SU = UA, the distance between UVW and ABC is h/2, as is the distance from S to UVW. Consequently P and P′ have equal heights h/2. The corresponding residual pyramids also have equal heights h/2. [6.2, 11.15, 1.31, 11.17]

**Step 3.** Write b = [BLM] and b′ = [B′L′M′]. For the base comparison, use the earlier same-altitude triangle theorem twice, rather than a similarity-area argument. Since BL is half BA, [BLM] is half [BAM]; since BM is half BC, [BAM] is half [BAC]. Thus B₀ = 4b, and similarly B₀′ = 4b′. The same argument gives [ALN] = B₀/4 and [A′L′N′] = B₀′/4. Moreover, [UVW] = b and [U′V′W′] = b′, because these are opposite triangular faces of the respective prisms. Therefore
b : b′ = B₀ : B₀′,
and each pair of corresponding residual pyramids likewise has its bases in the ratio B₀ : B₀′. [6.1, D11.13, 5.15]

**Step 4.** Compare P and P′ directly by completing them to parallelepipeds K and K′. Complete each triangular base to a parallelogram having that triangle as one of its diagonal halves, and retain the prism’s lateral edges. The resulting parallelogram bases have areas 2b and 2b′. The diagonal plane of each completed solid bisects it into two equal triangular prisms; hence K = 2P and K′ = 2P′. Both completed solids retain height h/2. [1.31, 1.34, 11.28]

**Step 5.** The equal-height parallelepipeds are proportional to their bases, so K : K′ = 2b : 2b′. Taking the same multiples does not change a ratio. Therefore
P : P′ = K : K′ = b : b′ = B₀ : B₀′.
This establishes the required comparison without assuming a formula for the magnitude of a pyramid. [11.32, 5.15, 5.11]

**Step 6.** Since Q = P and Q′ = P′, we also have Q : Q′ = B₀ : B₀′. Adding the antecedents and the consequents of these equal ratios gives
(P + Q) : (P′ + Q′) = B₀ : B₀′.
Thus the assertion holds for the two prisms of the first division. [12.3, 5.12]

**Step 7.** If the division is continued, divide corresponding residual pyramids in the same manner. By Steps 2–3, each such pair has equal heights and bases in the original ratio B₀ : B₀′. Hence the argument of Steps 4–6 applies to that pair, and its corresponding prisms have this same ratio. Its residual pyramids again have equal corresponding heights and bases in the same ratio. Repeating this argument proves that, after any finite number of corresponding divisions, every corresponding pair of prisms has ratio B₀ : B₀′. [12.3, 5.15, 5.11]

**Step 8.** Finally, the prisms in the two pyramids are equal in multitude and can be paired as above. Since every antecedent prism has to its corresponding consequent prism the ratio B₀ : B₀′, all the antecedents together have to all the consequents together that same ratio. Therefore, as the base of one pyramid is to the base of the other, so are all the prisms in the one to all the prisms, equal in multitude, in the other. [5.12]

## Proposition 12.5
**Statement:** Pyramids which are of the same height and have triangular bases are to one another as the bases.

**Step 1.** Let P and Q be pyramids of the same height with triangular bases A and B, respectively; letters also denote their magnitudes. We use the direct prism comparison of XII.4 and exhaustion, verifying the desired proportion by the equimultiple definition rather than assuming an auxiliary fourth proportional solid. Apply XII.3 to both pyramids, and repeatedly apply the same subdivision to every remaining pyramid, proceeding to the same depth on both sides. Let X_k and Y_k be the total prisms removed from P and Q after k stages. The collections contain equally many corresponding prisms, so XII.4 gives
A:B = X_k:Y_k
at every stage. The prism totals strictly increase and remain proper parts of their respective pyramids. [12.3, 12.4, CN5, D5.5]

**Step 2.** Write R_k = P − X_k and S_k = Q − Y_k for the total remainders. At each further stage, more than half of every remaining pyramid is removed as prisms. Consequently, more than half of each total remainder is removed. By X.1, R_k and S_k can each be made smaller than any assigned positive solid magnitude. The same holds for any fixed multiples mR_k and nS_k: their successive reductions likewise remove more than half. Thus all subsequent choices of sufficiently advanced stages require only finite exhaustion, not a passage to a limit. [12.3, 10.1]

**Step 3.** Fix arbitrary positive integers m and n, and first suppose mA > nB. Definition V.5 gives mX_1 > nY_1; let d = mX_1 − nY_1, so d is positive. For k > 1, the ratios X_k:Y_k and X_1:Y_1 are the same by V.11. Subtracting the first prism totals from the later totals, V.19 gives
(X_k − X_1):(Y_k − Y_1) = X_k:Y_k = A:B.
Definition V.5 therefore gives
m(X_k − X_1) > n(Y_k − Y_1).

Thus mA > nB implies mP > nQ. [10.1, CN2, CN5]

**Step 5.** Suppose instead that mA = nB. Definition V.5 gives mX_k = nY_k at every stage. If mP > nQ, put e = mP − nQ and choose k with mR_k < e. Then
mX_k = mP − mR_k > mP − e = nQ > nY_k,
contradicting mX_k = nY_k. If nQ > mP, the same argument with the pyramids interchanged, choosing nS_k smaller than nQ − mP, gives the opposite contradiction. Hence mP = nQ. [D5.5, 10.1, CN3, CN5]

**Step 6.** Finally, if mA < nB, apply Steps 3–4 with the pyramids and their corresponding multiples interchanged; this gives mP < nQ. Therefore, for every pair of positive integers m and n, mA and nB have exactly the same comparison—greater, equal, or less—as mP and nQ. By Definition V.5, A:B = P:Q. Thus pyramids of the same height having triangular bases are to one another as their bases. [D5.5]

## Proposition 12.6
**Statement:** Pyramids which are of the same height and have polygonal bases are to one another as the bases.

**Step 1.** Let P and Q be pyramids of the same height, with polygonal bases A and B. Draw diagonals dividing A into triangles A₁,…,Aᵣ and B into triangles B₁,…,Bₛ. Joining these divisions to the respective apices divides the pyramids into triangular-based pyramids P₁,…,Pᵣ and Q₁,…,Qₛ. Thus A = A₁ + ⋯ + Aᵣ, B = B₁ + ⋯ + Bₛ, P = P₁ + ⋯ + Pᵣ, and Q = Q₁ + ⋯ + Qₛ. Each smaller pyramid has its parent's apex and base-plane, so all have the same height. [P1, D11.12]

**Step 2.** Choose the direct route through the immediately preceding triangular-base case. For every i and j, that theorem gives
Pᵢ : Qⱼ = Aᵢ : Bⱼ.
The two triangulations need not contain the same number of triangles. [12.5]

**Step 3.** Fix j. Add the antecedents of these proportions while keeping the respective consequents Qⱼ and Bⱼ fixed. Repeated application of V.24, together with the decompositions in Step 1, gives
P : Qⱼ = A : Bⱼ.
This holds for every j. [5.24]

**Step 4.** Reverse each proportion to obtain
Qⱼ : P = Bⱼ : A.
This reversal follows directly from the definition of equal ratios: interchange the two arbitrary equimultipliers and reverse the corresponding comparisons. Now apply V.24 repeatedly, keeping P and A as the respective fixed consequents. Summing over j gives
Q : P = B : A. [D5.5, 5.24]

**Step 5.** Reverse this last proportion, again by the definition of equal ratios, to obtain
P : Q = A : B.
Therefore pyramids which are of the same height and have polygonal bases are to one another as their bases. [D5.5]

## Proposition 12.7
**Statement:** Any prism which has a triangular base is divided into three pyramids equal to one another which have triangular bases.

**Step 1.** Let the prism have triangular bases ABC and DEF, with corresponding vertices A,D; B,E; and C,F. Its lateral faces ABED, BCEF, and CADF are parallelograms. [D11.13]

**Step 2.** Join AF, BF, and AE, and cut the prism by the planes ABF and AEF. The section ABF cuts off the triangular pyramid F–ABC; the remainder is the pyramid with vertex F and quadrilateral base ABED. The section AEF divides this remainder into the triangular pyramids F–ABE and F–ADE. Thus the three pieces are
T₁ = ABCF, T₂ = ABEF, and T₃ = ADEF.
They fill the prism without overlapping interiors, meeting along the cutting faces ABF and AEF. [P1, D11.12]

**Step 3.** In the parallelogram BCEF, the diagonal BF divides the area into equal triangles BCF and BEF. Regard T₁ and T₂ as pyramids with these respective bases and common vertex A. Their bases lie in the same plane, so their heights are equal. By XII.5 their magnitudes are proportional to their equal bases; hence T₁ = T₂. This is the direct triangular-base route: choosing bases on a lateral face gives a common vertex and equal heights immediately, so no polygonal-base generalization is needed. [1.34, 12.5]

**Step 4.** In the parallelogram ABED, the diagonal AE divides the area into equal triangles ABE and ADE. Regard T₂ and T₃ as pyramids with these respective bases and common vertex F. Again their bases lie in the same plane and their heights are equal. XII.5 therefore gives T₂ = T₃. [1.34, 12.5]

**Step 5.** Since T₁ = T₂ and T₂ = T₃, the three pyramids are equal to one another. Together with the division in Step 2, this proves that any prism with a triangular base is divided into three equal pyramids having triangular bases. [CN1]

## Proposition 12.8
**Statement:** Similar pyramids which have triangular bases are in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.

**Step 1.** Let the similar triangular pyramids be T = ABCD and T′ = A′B′C′D′, with corresponding vertices so labelled. Their corresponding triangular faces are similar; hence their corresponding face angles are equal, and all corresponding edges have one common ratio, say r = AB:A′B′. In particular, AB:A′B′ = AC:A′C′ = AD:A′D′. We use completion to parallelepipeds, for which the triplicate-ratio theorem is already available. [D11.9, D6.1, 11.33]

**Step 2.** Complete a parallelepiped S having AB, AC, AD as its three edges issuing from A. Label its remaining vertices E, F, G, H so that ABEC and DFHG are opposite faces, and AD, BF, CG, EH are parallel and equal. Make the corresponding construction S′ from A′B′, A′C′, A′D′. These completions are obtained by drawing parallels; their opposite face planes are parallel. [1.31, 1.34, 11.15]

**Step 3.** The three parallelogram faces of S meeting at A are respectively similar to those of S′ meeting at A′. Indeed, their adjacent sides are proportional by Step 1, and their included angles are the corresponding angles BAC, BAD, CAD and B′A′C′, B′A′D′, C′A′D′. The remaining angles agree because adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary, and its opposite angles agree; opposite sides also agree. The opposite faces have the same respective shapes. Thus the two solids are bounded by six respectively similar faces and are similar parallelepipeds. [1.29, 1.34, D6.1, D11.9]

**Step 4.** Cut S by the plane through the diagonals BC and FG of its opposite faces ABEC and DFHG. This bisects S, and one half is the triangular prism Π with opposite triangular faces ABC and DFG. Within Π, the triangular sections DBC and DCF partition it into the three tetrahedra ABCD, BCDF, and CDFG. The first of these is T. [11.28]

**Step 5.** The tetrahedra ABCD and BCDF are equal. Regard them as pyramids with common vertex C and bases ABD and BDF: those bases are the equal halves of the parallelogram ABFD, and their heights are the same. Likewise, BCDF and CDFG are equal when regarded as pyramids with common vertex D and bases BCF and CFG, the equal halves of the parallelogram BCGF. In each case the ratio of the pyramids equals the ratio of their equal bases. Here the triangular-base theorem is the first applicable equal-height result; its polygonal extension is unnecessary. Consequently all three tetrahedra are equal to T. [1.34, 12.5]

**Step 6.** Therefore Π is three times T, and S, being twice Π, is six times T. The identical construction and argument give S′ equal to six times T′. Parts have the same ratio as corresponding equal multiples, so T:T′ = S:S′. [5.15]

**Step 7.** Since S and S′ are similar parallelepipeds, S:S′ is the triplicate ratio of AB:A′B′. By Step 6, T:T′ is therefore that same triplicate ratio. Since every pair of corresponding sides of the original pyramids has the ratio AB:A′B′, similar pyramids with triangular bases are in the triplicate ratio of their corresponding sides. [11.33, 5.11]

## Proposition 12.9
**Statement:** In equal pyramids which have triangular bases the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those pyramids in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

**Step 1.** Let the two triangular pyramids be P and Q, with base areas b and c and respective heights h and k. We must prove that P = Q if and only if b:c = k:h. We use completion to prisms and parallelepipeds, since the reciprocal-base-and-height criterion is already established for parallelepipeds in [11.34].

**Step 2.** By drawing parallels, complete each pyramid to a triangular prism, taking the pyramid’s apex as a vertex of the opposite triangular face. Complete each base triangle to a parallelogram, and correspondingly complete each prism to a parallelepiped. These constructions use [1.31]; the opposite base planes are parallel by [11.15]. Thus the completed parallelepipeds, denoted U and V, still have heights h and k. Since a diagonal bisects a parallelogram, their base areas are respectively 2b and 2c [1.34].

**Step 3.** Apply the division of a triangular prism into three equal pyramids, with the original pyramid as the piece having the prism’s entire lower triangular base. Each prism is therefore three times its original pyramid [12.7]. The plane through the corresponding diagonals of the opposite parallelogram faces bisects the completed parallelepiped, making the triangular prism one of its halves [11.28]. Consequently,
U = 6P and V = 6Q,
where these multiples mean sums of equal copies.

**Step 4.** Parts have the same ratio as their corresponding equal multiples. Hence the ratio of the completed bases is
2b:2c = b:c [5.15].

**Step 5.** Suppose first that P = Q. Adding equal copies gives U = V [CN2]. The bases of equal parallelepipeds are reciprocally proportional to their heights, so
2b:2c = k:h [11.34].
Combining this with Step 4 gives b:c = k:h [5.11]. Thus equal triangular pyramids have bases reciprocally proportional to their heights.

**Step 6.** Conversely, suppose b:c = k:h. Step 4 and [5.11] give 2b:2c = k:h. Therefore the completed parallelepipeds are equal: U = V [11.34]. By [5.15],
P:Q = U:V and Q:Q = V:V.
Since U = V, we have U:V = V:V [5.7]. These ratio equalities give P:Q = Q:Q [5.11], and hence P = Q [5.9]. Thus triangular pyramids whose bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights are equal, completing both directions.

## Proposition 12.10
**Statement:** Any cone is a third part of the cylinder which has the same base with it and equal height.

**Step 1.** Let K be the cone, with vertex V, circular base D, and height h; let C be the cylinder with the same base and height. We also use K and C for their magnitudes. For a convex polygon Q in the base plane, write P(Q) for the pyramid with vertex V and base Q, and R(Q) for the prism erected perpendicularly on Q to height h. If Q lies inside D, then P(Q) lies inside K and R(Q) inside C. We take the direct route through these polygonal solids and exhaustion. [D11.18, D11.21]

**Step 2.** For every such polygon Q,
R(Q) = 3P(Q).
Indeed, divide Q into triangles and divide its prism and pyramid accordingly. By XII.7, each triangular prism is three times a pyramid on its triangular base with a vertex in the opposite base. By XII.5, replacing that vertex by V does not change the pyramid’s magnitude, since its base and height remain unchanged. Adding over the triangles gives the asserted identity. XII.5 is the natural comparison here because the individual bases are triangular. [12.7, 12.5, CN2]

**Step 3.** Inscribe a square Q₀ in D. Refine its sides, and subsequently every side of each resulting polygon, as follows. For a side AB, bisect AB at N. If O is the centre of D, extend ON to meet the minor arc AB at M. Since ON is perpendicular to AB, the line through M parallel to AB is tangent to the circle. Erect a rectangle on AB whose opposite side lies on this tangent and whose other sides are parallel to OM. The circular segment between AB and its minor arc lies properly inside this rectangle, while triangle ABM lies inside the segment. Replace AB by AM and MB. Repeating this construction produces nested inscribed polygons Q₀, Q₁, Q₂, … . [4.6, 1.10, 3.3, 1.31, 3.16]

**Step 4.** For each side AB in this construction, triangle ABM is half the enclosing rectangle, because they have the same base and lie between the same parallels. Consequently, by XII.6, the pyramid with vertex V and base ABM is half the pyramid with vertex V and that rectangular base. Here XII.6 directly applies because the comparison includes a rectangular base. By Step 2, the corresponding triangular prism is likewise half the rectangular prism. [1.41, 12.6, CN2]

The curved portion of K over the circular segment is properly contained in the rectangular pyramid. Therefore the triangular pyramid added in the refinement is greater than half that curved portion. Likewise, the curved portion of C over the segment is properly contained in the rectangular prism, so the triangular prism added is greater than half that portion. Adding these inequalities over all sides shows that each refinement removes more than half the total remainder, both in the cone and in the cylinder. [CN2, CN5]

**Step 5.** Put Pₙ = P(Qₙ) and Rₙ = R(Qₙ). Thus Rₙ = 3Pₙ, and the positive remainders satisfy
K − Pₙ₊₁ < ½(K − Pₙ),
C − Rₙ₊₁ < ½(C − Rₙ).
By X.1, each sequence of remainders can be made smaller than any assigned positive solid magnitude. The same holds for 3(K − Pₙ), since tripling preserves the more-than-half removal at every refinement. [10.1, CN2, CN3]

**Step 6.** Suppose C > 3K. By Step 5, choose n such that
C − Rₙ < C − 3K.
Subtracting gives Rₙ > 3K. But Pₙ is contained in K, so Step 2 gives Rₙ = 3Pₙ < 3K, a contradiction. Hence C is not greater than 3K. [CN2, CN3, CN5]

**Step 7.** Suppose C < 3K. By Step 5, choose n such that
3(K − Pₙ) < 3K − C.
Subtracting gives 3Pₙ > C. But Rₙ is contained in C, and Step 2 gives 3Pₙ = Rₙ < C, again a contradiction. Hence C is not less than 3K either. Therefore C = 3K: any cone is a third part of the cylinder having the same base and equal height. [CN2, CN3, CN5]

## Proposition 12.11
**Statement:** Cones and cylinders which are of the same height are to one another as their bases.

**Step 1.** Let C and D be cones of the same height, and let A and B denote their circular bases, regarded as magnitudes. We first prove C:D = A:B. This is the direct route because XII.6 applies to polygonal pyramids inscribed in the cones; afterward XII.10 transfers the result to cylinders. [12.6, 12.10]

**Step 2.** Inscribe a square in each base, then repeatedly bisect every intervening arc and join consecutive division points. Perform corresponding subdivisions in the two circles. At stage k the resulting polygons a_k and b_k are similar. Join their vertices to the respective cone vertices, obtaining inscribed pyramids P_k and Q_k. These pyramids increase with k and have the same height. By XII.6 their ratio is a_k:b_k. By XII.1 and XII.2, both a_k:b_k and A:B equal the ratio of the squares on the two diameters. Consequently, at every stage,
P_k:Q_k = a_k:b_k = A:B.
[4.6, 3.30, D11.12, 12.6, 12.1, 12.2, 5.11]

**Step 3.** Consider a chord XY of one of these polygons, and let M bisect its minor arc. We describe the next subdivision explicitly. If O is the circle's centre, then XM = YM by III.29. The triangles OXM and OYM give equal angles at O by I.8. Writing H for the intersection of OM with XY, I.4 applied to OXH and OYH gives XH = HY; hence OM is perpendicular to XY by III.3. The perpendicular to OM at M is tangent to the circle by III.16. It is therefore parallel to XY. Together with XY and the perpendiculars at X and Y, it bounds a rectangle R containing the circular segment between XY and its minor arc. The triangle XMY has the same base and lies between the same parallels as R, so R is double that triangle. [3.29, 1.8, 1.4, 3.3, 3.16, 1.41]

**Step 4.** Join the rectangle R, the triangle XMY, and the circular segment to the vertex S of the cone. The solid over the circular segment is precisely the corresponding portion left outside the current inscribed pyramid. It is properly contained in the pyramid over R. By XII.6, the pyramid over R is double the pyramid over XMY, since their bases have that ratio and their heights are equal. Thus the triangular pyramid added at this subdivision is greater than half the corresponding remaining portion of the cone.

Adding over all the intervening arcs shows that each subdivision removes more than half the entire remainder. Therefore, by X.1, C−P_k and D−Q_k can each be made smaller than any assigned positive solid magnitude. The same holds for any fixed positive integral multiple of either remainder, because those multiples also decrease by more than half at each subdivision. [D11.18, 12.6, CN5, 10.1]

**Step 5.** Take arbitrary positive integers m and n, and suppose first that mA > nB. Since P_0:Q_0 = A:B, the definition of equal ratios gives mP_0 > nQ_0. Put Δ = mP_0−nQ_0, a positive solid magnitude.

For k>0, the wholes P_k, Q_k and the subtracted parts P_0, Q_0 have the same ratio. Hence, by V.19,
(P_k−P_0):(Q_k−Q_0) = A:B.
The definition of equal ratios therefore gives
m(P_k−P_0) > n(Q_k−Q_0),
and consequently mP_k−nQ_k > Δ. Choose k large enough that n(D−Q_k) < Δ, as Step 4 permits. Then
mC > mP_k > nQ_k+Δ > nD.
Thus mA > nB implies mC > nD. [D5.5, 5.19, 5.11, 10.1, CN5]

**Step 6.** If mA < nB, interchange the two cones and apply the argument of Step 5 with multipliers n and m. It follows that nD > mC, or mC < nD. [D5.5, 5.19, 10.1]

**Step 7.** Suppose instead that mA = nB. Then mP_k = nQ_k at every stage, by the definition of equal ratios. If mC > nD, choose k so that
m(C−P_k) < mC−nD.
This gives mP_k > nD > nQ_k, contradicting mP_k = nQ_k. If mC < nD, choose k so that
n(D−Q_k) < nD−mC.
This gives nQ_k > mC > mP_k, the same contradiction. Thus mC = nD. [D5.5, 10.1, CN5]

**Step 8.** For every pair of positive integers m,n, the multiples mC,nD therefore exceed, equal, or fall short of one another exactly as mA,nB do. By the definition of equal ratios,
C:D = A:B.
Thus cones of the same height are to one another as their bases. [D5.5]

**Step 9.** Now let U and V be cylinders of the same height, with bases A and B. Take cones C and D on those respective bases and with that same height. By XII.10, U = 3C and V = 3D. Equal multiples have the same ratio as their corresponding parts, so
U:V = C:D = A:B.
Hence cylinders also are to one another as their bases. Therefore cones, and likewise cylinders, which are of the same height are to one another as their bases. [12.10, 5.15, 5.11]

## Proposition 12.12
**Statement:** Similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases.

**Step 1.** Let C and D be similar cones, with vertices S and T, base centres O and U, and base diameters d and e. Their axes are proportional to their diameters; their base radii therefore also have the ratio d:e. Write R for the triplicate ratio of d:e. We prove the assertion for cones by exhaustion with triangular pyramids, since their similarity supplies precisely the required ratio, and then pass to cylinders. [D11.18, D11.24, 5.15, D5.10]

**Step 2.** In each base draw two perpendicular diameters, choosing corresponding radii in the two circles. Repeatedly bisect every angle between consecutive radii, and join consecutive endpoints on the circles. This central-angle construction keeps the two inscribed polygons corresponding at every stage. Let P_j and Q_j be the pyramids joining the resulting polygons to S and T respectively. These pyramids increase as j increases. [1.11, 1.9]

Divide each polygon into triangles by joining its vertices to its centre. The resulting triangular pyramids correspond in pairs, of the form SOA_iA_{i+1} and TUB_iB_{i+1}. The corresponding base triangles have equal included central angles and proportional radii. The corresponding meridian triangles SOA_i and TUB_i have equal right angles and proportional axes and radii. Thus their corresponding sides are proportional in the ratio d:e. Consequently all six corresponding edges of each pair of triangular pyramids have that ratio; their corresponding triangular faces are similar, and the triangular pyramids are similar solids. [6.6, 6.4, 6.5, D11.9]

**Step 3.** Each pair of corresponding triangular pyramids is therefore in the triplicate ratio of d:e, namely R. Adding the antecedents and consequents gives
P_j:Q_j = R
at every stage. This is the direct reason for using triangular pyramids as the approximating solids. [12.8, 5.12]

**Step 4.** We show that each refinement removes more than half the solid still omitted from either cone. Consider consecutive vertices A,B of one polygon, and let M be the new vertex obtained by bisecting the central angle AOB. The bisecting radius OM is perpendicular to AB: the triangles on either side of it, formed with its intersection with AB, are equiangular and have equal corresponding sides. The line through M parallel to AB is consequently tangent to the circle. [6.6, 6.4, 3.16]

The minor circular segment bounded by AB and its arc lies strictly inside the rectangle having AB as one side and its opposite side on this tangent. The triangle AMB is half that rectangle. Join the rectangle, the triangle, and the circular segment to the cone's vertex. The rectangular pyramid contains the entire omitted solid over that segment, while the triangular pyramid over AMB is half the rectangular pyramid, since their heights are equal and their bases are in the ratio two to one. Thus this newly added triangular pyramid is greater than half the omitted solid over the segment. [1.41, 12.6, D11.18, CN5]

The omitted solids over the several circular segments partition the remainder of the cone. Adding the preceding inequalities shows that each refinement removes more than half that remainder. The same argument applies to the other cone. [CN5]

**Step 5.** Hence, by exhaustion, C−P_j and D−Q_j can each be made smaller than any assigned positive solid magnitude. The same holds for any fixed positive integral multiple of either remainder, since those multiples likewise decrease by more than half at each refinement. [10.1]

**Step 6.** We now justify the passage from the approximating ratios to the cone ratio by the definition of equal ratios. Fix P_0,Q_0. Since
P_j:Q_j = P_0:Q_0,
subtracting these corresponding parts gives, for j>0,
(P_j−P_0):(Q_j−Q_0) = P_0:Q_0. [5.19]

Let m,n be arbitrary positive integers. Suppose first that mP_0>nQ_0, and put δ=mP_0−nQ_0. The equality of the preceding ratios implies
m(P_j−P_0)>n(Q_j−Q_0),
and therefore mP_j>nQ_j+δ. Choose j so that n(D−Q_j)<δ. Then
mC>mP_j>nQ_j+δ>nD.
Thus mP_0>nQ_0 implies mC>nD. Interchanging the two cones proves likewise that mP_0<nQ_0 implies mC<nD. [D5.5, 10.1, CN5]

**Step 7.** If instead mP_0=nQ_0, the equality P_j:Q_j=P_0:Q_0 gives mP_j=nQ_j at every stage. Were mC>nD, choose j such that
m(C−P_j)<mC−nD.
Then mP_j>nD>nQ_j, a contradiction. The opposite inequality mC<nD is excluded in the same way by exhausting D. Therefore mC=nD. [D5.5, 10.1, CN5]

All equimultiples of C,D consequently compare exactly as the corresponding equimultiples of P_0,Q_0. By the definition of equal ratios,
C:D = P_0:Q_0 = R.
Thus similar cones are in the triplicate ratio of their base diameters. [D5.5, 12.8, 5.12]

**Step 8.** Finally, let two similar cylinders be given, and take the cones having their respective bases and equal heights. These cones are similar, because their axes and base diameters have the same proportionality as those of the cylinders. Each cylinder is three times its corresponding cone, and equal multiples preserve a ratio. The cylinders therefore have the same ratio as the cones, namely the triplicate ratio of their base diameters. Hence similar cones and cylinders are to one another in the triplicate ratio of the diameters in their bases. [D11.24, 12.10, 5.15]

## Proposition 12.13
**Statement:** If a cylinder be cut by a plane which is parallel to its opposite planes, then, as the cylinder is to the cylinder, so will the axis be to the axis.

**Step 1.** Let the cylinder have axis AB, and let the cutting plane, parallel to its two bases, meet AB at C. Denote the parts on AC and CB by K and L. In any axial plane, the cutting plane meets the generating rectangle in a line parallel to its end sides [11.16]. This divides the generating rectangle into two rectangles [1.29], with equal radial widths [1.34]. Rotating these rectangles about AC and CB gives precisely K and L. Thus the two parts are cylinders with the same radius and with axes AC and CB [D11.21, D11.22, D11.23].

**Step 2.** We use the equimultiple criterion directly, since cylinders of this fixed radius can be compared by placing them on one base [D5.5]. Let m and n be arbitrary positive integers. Place m copies of K end to end on a straight axis, obtaining a cylinder U; similarly place n copies of L end to end, obtaining a cylinder V. The generating rectangles join to form single rectangles of the original radial width, so U and V are cylinders whose axes have lengths m·AC and n·CB [D11.21, D11.22]. Each constituent copy equals its original by coincidence, and adding these equal copies gives U = mK and V = nL [CN4, CN2].

**Step 3.** Place U and V with their initial circular bases coincident and their axes extending along the same ray. If m·AC = n·CB, their generating rectangles, and hence their cylinders, coincide; therefore mK = nL [D11.21, CN4]. If m·AC > n·CB, V is a proper part of U: its generating rectangle is the initial portion of the generating rectangle of U. Hence mK > nL [D11.21, CN5]. Likewise, if m·AC < n·CB, then mK < nL [D11.21, CN5]. Coincidence is the direct justification in the equality case; no cylinder-ratio theorem is needed.

**Step 4.** Consequently, for every m and n, the multiples mK and nL alike exceed, are equal to, or fall short of one another exactly as m·AC and n·CB do. By the definition of equal ratios,
K : L = AC : CB [D5.5].
Thus, as the cylinder is to the cylinder, so is the axis to the axis, as required.

## Proposition 12.14
**Statement:** Cones and cylinders which are on equal bases are to one another as their heights.

**Step 1.** Let X and Y be cylinders on equal bases B and B′, with heights h and k respectively. Choose the parallel-cut route, since it exhibits both prescribed heights directly without a comparison of their sizes. Continue X coaxially beyond its upper base through the additional height k, obtaining one cylinder T. The plane of the former upper base divides T into X and an additional cylinder Z. By the rectangular generation of a cylinder, Z has a base equal to B, and the axes of X and Z have lengths h and k respectively. [D11.21, D11.22, D11.23]

**Step 2.** The cylinders Z and Y have the same height k. Therefore, by the equal-height theorem,
Z:Y = B:B′.
But B = B′. In the definition of equal ratios, take each multiplier to be one: since the third and fourth magnitudes are equal, the first and second must also be equal. Hence Z = Y. [12.11, D5.5]

**Step 3.** The plane dividing T into X and Z is parallel to its opposite base planes. Thus the parallel-cut theorem gives
X:Z = h:k.
Since Z = Y, equal magnitudes have the same ratio to them from X; consequently
X:Y = X:Z = h:k.
The proposition is therefore established for cylinders. [12.13, 5.7, 5.11]

**Step 4.** Now let K and L be cones on equal bases, with heights h and k. Take cylinders X and Y having respectively the same bases and heights as these cones. Each cone is a third part of its corresponding cylinder, so X and Y are respectively the triple multiples of K and L. Parts have the same ratio as their corresponding equal multiples; hence
K:L = X:Y.
By Step 3, X:Y = h:k, and therefore K:L = h:k. Thus cones to cones, and cylinders to cylinders, on equal bases are to one another as their heights. [12.10, 5.15, 5.11]

## Proposition 12.15
**Statement:** In equal cones and cylinders the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; and those cones and cylinders in which the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights are equal.

**Step 1.** Let X and Y be two cones, or two cylinders. Denote their base areas by B_X and B_Y and their heights by h_X and h_Y. Construct an auxiliary solid Z of the same kind, with base equal to that of Y and height equal to that of X. We use the equal-height comparison first, followed by the equal-base comparison; this route applies directly to both cones and cylinders. Since X and Z have equal heights,
X : Z = B_X : B_Y. [12.11]

**Step 2.** Since Y and Z have equal bases, and Z has height h_X,
Y : Z = h_Y : h_X. [12.14]

**Step 3.** Suppose X and Y are equal. Equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude, so X : Z = Y : Z. [5.7] Combining this with Steps 1 and 2 gives
B_X : B_Y = h_Y : h_X. [5.11]
Thus their bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights.

**Step 4.** Conversely, suppose their bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights, so that
B_X : B_Y = h_Y : h_X.
By Steps 1 and 2 and equality of ratios, X : Z = Y : Z. [5.11] Magnitudes having the same ratio to the same magnitude are equal; hence X = Y. [5.9]

Therefore, in equal cones and likewise in equal cylinders, the bases are reciprocally proportional to the heights; conversely, cones, and likewise cylinders, whose bases are reciprocally proportional to their heights are equal.

## Proposition 12.16
**Statement:** Given two circles about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater circle an equilateral polygon with an even number of sides which does not touch the lesser circle.

**Step 1.** Let O be the common centre. We use subdivision of equal arcs, followed by equality of the corresponding chord-distances. Inscribe a square ABCD in the greater circle. Its sides are equal, so its four successive minor arcs are equal. [4.6, D1.22, 3.28]

**Step 2.** Let H be the intersection of OA with the lesser circle. Through H draw the straight line ℓ perpendicular to OA; since H is inside the greater circle, ℓ cuts its circumference at two points T and U. Choose the naming so that the short arc from A to T proceeds from A in the direction of B. This arc, except for T, lies in the open half-plane bounded by ℓ which contains A, whereas O lies in the other half-plane. [1.11]

**Step 3.** Bisect each of the four equal arcs, and then bisect each resulting arc again. Repeat this double subdivision as necessary. All arcs remain equal, and each round replaces the first arc starting at A by its first quarter. Thus each round removes more than half of that arc. By 10.1, after finitely many rounds the first arc AP is less than the fixed arc AT; if equality occurs, one further round makes the inequality strict. If the initial arc is already smaller, no subdivision is needed. After n rounds there are 4·4ⁿ equal arcs. [3.30, 10.1]

**Step 4.** Join the successive division points. Equal arcs are subtended by equal chords, so these chords form an equilateral polygon inscribed in the greater circle, with the even number 4·4ⁿ of sides. Since arc AP is less than arc AT and starts in the same direction from A, P lies strictly between A and T on that arc. Consequently the entire side AP lies in the open half-plane bounded by ℓ which contains A. [3.29]

**Step 5.** Bisect AP at M. The straight line OM is perpendicular to AP. Since M and O are on opposite sides of ℓ, OM meets ℓ at a point K between O and M. If K=H, then OK=OH. Otherwise triangle OHK is right-angled at H; its other angles are acute, and therefore its hypotenuse OK is greater than OH. In either case, OM>OK≥OH, so OM>OH. [1.10, 3.3, 1.17, 1.19, CN5]

**Step 6.** Let XY be any side of the polygon, and N its midpoint. Then ON is perpendicular to XY. Apply 3.14 directly, since the polygon’s sides have already been proved equal: their perpendicular distances from O are equal, and hence ON=OM>OH. For any point Z on XY, either Z=N, or the right triangle ONZ gives OZ>ON. Thus every point of every side has distance from O strictly greater than OH, the radius of the lesser circle. No side can therefore meet or touch that circle. The constructed polygon is equilateral, has an even number of sides, is inscribed in the greater circle, and does not touch the lesser circle, as required. [1.10, 3.3, 3.14, D3.4, 1.17, 1.19, D1.15]

## Proposition 12.17
**Statement:** Given two spheres about the same centre, to inscribe in the greater sphere a polyhedral solid which does not touch the lesser sphere at its surface.

**Step 1.** Let O be the common centre, and let R and r be the greater and lesser radii, with R>r. Choose a plane E through O and an axis through O perpendicular to E. A plane containing this axis will be called a meridian plane. The definition of a sphere, together with the right-triangle theorem, shows that its central sections are circles and that its surface consists of points at its radius from O. Construct s=(R+r)/2. Applying II.5 to a segment divided into lengths R and r gives
s²=Rr+((R−r)/2)²>Rr.
Thus r<s<R. [11.12, D11.14, 1.47, 1.10, 2.5]

**Step 2.** In a meridian plane apply XII.16 to the concentric circles of radii R and s. Obtain an equilateral inscribed polygon P with an even number n of sides, enclosing and not touching the circle of radius s. This is the direct finite-polygon route: XII.16 supplies the approximation needed for the construction. The triangles joining O to successive vertices have equal corresponding sides, so their central angles are equal. Hence P is regular. Perpendiculars from O bisect its equal sides and have a common length a. Since the circle of radius s is strictly inside P, a>s. Put k=a/R. Then 0<k<1 and
ka=a²/R>s²/R>r.
[12.16, 1.8, 3.3, 1.47]

**Step 3.** Orient P so that two opposite vertices N and S lie on the axis. In E construct a congruent regular n-gon Q, centred at O, with circumradius R and apothem a. Its successive radii determine n equally spaced meridian half-planes. Take the half of the boundary of P running from N to S on one side of the axis, and copy it into each of these half-planes by turning it about the axis. Every copied vertex lies on the greater sphere. At each intermediate height, join the n corresponding vertices in their cyclic order; they form a regular horizontal polygon. At N and S the corresponding vertices coincide. [1.23, D11.14]

**Step 4.** Join corresponding vertices on consecutive horizontal polygons. Corresponding horizontal sides are parallel, since all these polygons have the same orientation and differ only in size and height. Thus each pair of corresponding sides bounds a plane trapezium; the faces adjoining N and S are triangles. These finitely many faces form a closed polyhedral solid K, with O in its interior.

More precisely, let H be any point on the axis between N and S, and let Y be the point at the height of H on the chosen half-boundary of P. Write t=HY. The section of K through H parallel to E is the copy of Q centred at H and reduced in the ratio t:R. Indeed, a section parallel to the bases of each trapezium divides its two meridian sides in the same proportion, so its endpoints have exactly the distances from the axis prescribed by Y. This also describes the whole solid without overlap or gaps. [11.7, 6.2]

**Step 5.** The solid K is inscribed in the greater sphere. Its vertices already lie on that sphere. To verify that its remaining points lie inside, take any point X of K and use the horizontal section just described. Put z=OH. That section is contained in the circle with centre H and radius t, so HX≤t. Also, Y lies on an inscribed polygon side, whence OY≤R. Therefore
OX²=z²+HX²≤z²+t²=OY²≤R².
Here the two decompositions are right-triangle decompositions because the axis is perpendicular to the horizontal section. [3.2, D11.3, 1.47]

**Step 6.** Now let X be any boundary point of K other than a pole, and retain H, Y, t and z from its horizontal section. The point X lies on a side of that section polygon. By similarity with Q, the perpendicular distance from H to the line of this side is kt. Consequently HX≥kt. Likewise, Y lies on a side of P whose line is at perpendicular distance a from O, so OY≥a. Thus
HX²≥k²t²,
and
z²+t²=OY²≥a².
These inequalities follow by dropping the perpendiculars and applying the right-triangle theorem. [3.3, 6.4, 1.47]

**Step 7.** Since 0<k<1, the preceding inequalities give
OX²=z²+HX²
≥z²+k²t²
≥k²(z²+t²)
≥k²a²
>r²,
the last inequality following from ka>r in Step 2. Hence OX>r. The poles also satisfy this inequality, since ON=OS=R>r. Every point of the polyhedral surface is therefore strictly outside the lesser sphere. [1.47]

**Step 8.** Since O is inside K, the lesser sphere is wholly inside K: otherwise a segment from O to a point of that sphere lying outside K would meet the polyhedral boundary at distance at most r, contradicting Step 7. Thus K is a polyhedral solid inscribed in the greater sphere whose surface does not touch the lesser sphere, as required. [D11.14]

## Proposition 12.18
**Statement:** Spheres are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their respective diameters.

**Step 1.** Let the two spheres have solid magnitudes S and T and diameters d and e. Write R for the triplicate ratio of d to e. We use the polyhedral route: 12.17 supplies inscribed polyhedra, and 12.8 applies directly to the triangular pyramids obtained by joining their triangulated faces to the centre. No formula for the magnitude of a sphere is assumed. [D11.14, D11.17, D5.10]

**Step 2.** Consider a convex polyhedron containing the centre O, and another obtained by multiplying every distance from O in the same ratio. Such corresponding distances can be constructed by 6.12. For any two vertices, the triangles formed with O have proportional sides about their common angle; hence their corresponding edges are proportional. Consequently corresponding triangular faces are similar, as are the triangular pyramids having vertex O and those faces as bases. [6.12, 6.6, 6.4, 6.5, D11.9]

By 12.8, every pair of corresponding triangular pyramids has the triplicate ratio of the corresponding radial distances. By 5.12, their sums—the two polyhedra—have that same ratio. In particular, corresponding polyhedra inscribed in our two spheres have ratio R, since their radii have ratio d:e. Also, enlarging a polyhedron by a rational linear factor a multiplies its solid magnitude by a³; this is merely numerical notation for the triplicate ratio. [12.8, 5.12, D11.17, D5.10]

**Step 3.** We show that an inscribed polyhedron can leave less than any assigned positive solid magnitude E outside it. Let the sphere in question have magnitude W and radius r. Choose a positive integer N such that NE > 7W. This is possible by D5.4. Within the sphere draw the concentric sphere of radius Nr/(N+1). By 12.17, inscribe a polyhedron P in the original sphere which surrounds the smaller sphere without touching its surface. Enlarge P about the centre by the factor (N+1)/N, obtaining P⁺. Since the smaller sphere is thereby carried onto the original sphere, P⁺ surrounds the original sphere. [D5.4, D11.14, 6.12, 12.17]

Thus P < W < P⁺. By Step 2,
P⁺ − P = (3/N + 3/N² + 1/N³)P ≤ 7P/N < 7W/N < E.
Therefore W − P < E. Here rational coefficients denote parts and multiples of magnitudes; no scaling assertion about sphere magnitudes has been used. [12.8, 5.12, D5.10, CN5, CN3]

**Step 4.** Fix an inscribed polyhedron U in the first sphere that surrounds its centre, and let V be its corresponding radial copy in the second sphere. By Step 2, U:V = R. We shall verify the definition of equality of ratios for S:T and U:V. [12.17, 6.12, 12.8, 5.12, D5.5]

Let m and n be any positive integers, and suppose mS > nT. By Step 3, choose an inscribed polyhedron P in the first sphere with
S − P < (mS − nT)/m.
Then mP > nT. Its corresponding copy Q in the second sphere satisfies Q < T, so mP > nQ. Step 2 gives P:Q = R = U:V; hence, by equality of ratios, mU > nV. [CN2, CN3, CN5, 5.11, D5.5]

**Step 5.** If instead mS < nT, apply Step 4 with the spheres interchanged and with n and m in place of m and n. It follows that nV > mU, or mU < nV. Thus both strict comparisons between arbitrary multiples of the spheres are preserved for the corresponding multiples of U and V. [D5.5; Step 4]

**Step 6.** Suppose now that mS = nT. If mU > nV, choose a positive integer k such that k(mU − nV) > V. Then kmU > (kn+1)V. But kmS < (kn+1)T, so Step 5 gives the opposite inequality, a contradiction. [D5.4, CN2, CN5]

If mU < nV, choose k such that k(nV − mU) > U. Then (km+1)U < knV. But (km+1)S > knT, so Step 4 again gives the opposite inequality. Therefore mU = nV. [D5.4, CN2, CN5]

**Step 7.** For every pair of positive integers m,n, the comparison of mS with nT agrees exactly with that of mU with nV. Therefore S:T = U:V by D5.5. Since U:V is the triplicate ratio of d:e, the spheres are to one another in the triplicate ratio of their respective diameters. [D5.5, 5.11, D5.10]

## Proposition 13.1
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the greater segment added to the half of the whole is five times the square on the half.

**Step 1.** Let AB be cut at C in extreme and mean ratio, with AC the greater segment. Write w = AB, a = AC, and b = CB, so w = a + b. Bisect AB and denote its half by h; thus w = h + h. This bisection is supplied by 1.10. Write S(x) for the square on a length x, and R(x,y) for the rectangle contained by lengths x and y.

**Step 2.** By the definition of extreme and mean ratio, w : a = a : b (D6.3). Apply 6.17, which directly concerns these three proportional straight lines, to obtain
S(a) = R(w,b).

**Step 3.** We use 2.4 because the side of the required square is the sum a + h. It gives
S(a+h) = S(a) + S(h) + 2R(a,h).
Since w consists of two halves equal to h, 2.1 gives R(w,a) = 2R(a,h). Therefore
S(a+h) = S(a) + R(w,a) + S(h).
[2.4, 2.1, CN1]

**Step 4.** Substitute the equality from Step 2. Since w is cut into a and b, 2.2 gives R(w,a) + R(w,b) = S(w). Consequently,
S(a+h) = R(w,b) + R(w,a) + S(h) = S(w) + S(h).
[2.2, CN2, CN1]

**Step 5.** Apply 2.4 to the whole w cut into its two equal halves h. The rectangle contained by h and h is the square on h, so
S(w) = S(h) + S(h) + 2S(h) = 4S(h).
[2.4]

**Step 6.** Adding S(h) to this equality and using Step 4 gives
S(a+h) = 4S(h) + S(h) = 5S(h).
Thus the square on the greater segment added to half the whole is five times the square on half the whole, as required. [CN2, CN1]

## Proposition 13.2
**Statement:** If the square on a straight line be five times the square on a segment of it, then, when the double of the said segment is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the greater segment is the remaining part of the original straight line.

**Step 1.** Let the original straight line have length a, the specified segment length b, and the remaining part length r. Thus a=b+r, and by hypothesis a²=5b². Consider the prescribed division of a line of length 2b in extreme and mean ratio, and let its greater segment have length x. Its half has length b, so XIII.1 gives (x+b)²=5b². This is the direct route: XIII.1 supplies exactly the fivefold square appearing in the hypothesis. [13.1]

**Step 2.** Since a² and (x+b)² are both equal to 5b², they are equal to one another. [CN1]

**Step 3.** Therefore a=x+b. For if either of these two lengths exceeded the other by a positive length d, II.4 would make the square on the longer equal to the square on the shorter together with the square on d and twice the rectangle contained by the shorter and d. The square on the longer would consequently be greater, contrary to Step 2. [2.4, CN5]

**Step 4.** Subtract b from the equal lengths a and x+b. The remainders are equal; since a−b=r, we obtain r=x. Thus the greater segment of the double of the specified segment, when cut in extreme and mean ratio, is the remaining part of the original straight line, as required. [CN3]

## Proposition 13.3
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the lesser segment added to the half of the greater segment is five times the square on the half of the greater segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio at C, with AC the greater segment and CB the lesser. Bisect AC at D, so that AD = DC and the points occur in the order A, D, C, B. Thus DB is the lesser segment CB added to half the greater segment. Write S(XY) for the square on XY and R(XY, ZW) for the rectangle contained by XY and ZW. [1.10]

**Step 2.** By the definition of extreme and mean ratio, AB : AC = AC : CB. Hence the rectangle contained by the extremes equals the square on the mean:
R(AB, CB) = S(AC).
The three-proportional-lines theorem applies directly to the defining proportion. [D6.3, 6.17]

**Step 3.** Use the bisected-line identity directly, since its half-plus-added segment is precisely DB. The line AC is bisected at D and CB is added to it in a straight line; therefore
R(AB, CB) + S(DC) = S(DB). [2.6]

**Step 4.** Applying the square-of-a-divided-line identity to AC gives
S(AC) = S(AD) + S(DC) + 2R(AD, DC).
Since AD = DC, each square on the right equals S(DC), and R(AD, DC) is also the square on a length equal to DC. Consequently,
S(AC) = 4S(DC). [2.4]

**Step 5.** Adding S(DC) to the equality in Step 2 and using Steps 3 and 4 yields
S(DB) = S(AC) + S(DC) = 4S(DC) + S(DC) = 5S(DC).
Since DB is CB added to half of AC, the square on the lesser segment added to half the greater segment is five times the square on half the greater segment, as required. [CN2, CN1]

## Proposition 13.4
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the whole and the square on the lesser segment together are triple of the square on the greater segment.

**Step 3.** Apply the whole-and-segment identity to AB, choosing the lesser segment CB because this gives exactly the sum required in the proposition. Thus
S(AB) + S(CB) = 2R(AB, CB) + S(AC). [2.7]

## Proposition 13.5
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, and there be added to it a straight line equal to the greater segment, the whole straight line has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the original straight line is the greater segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be cut at C in extreme and mean ratio, with AC the greater segment. Let the added straight line BD lie beyond B and equal AC, so that AD is the augmented line. By the definition of extreme and mean ratio,
AB : AC = AC : CB. [D6.3]

**Step 2.** Use the rule for summing antecedents and consequents directly, since these sums give the augmented line and the original line. Applied to the proportion in Step 1, it gives
(AB + AC) : (AC + CB) = AB : AC. [5.12]

**Step 3.** Since AC = BD, adding AB gives AB + AC = AB + BD = AD. Also AC + CB = AB. Substituting these equal lengths into the preceding proportion, and replacing AC by BD, yields
AD : AB = AB : BD. [CN2]

**Step 4.** The whole AB is greater than its part AC; since AC = BD, we have AB > BD. Thus the proportion in Step 3 says that the whole AD is to its greater segment AB as AB is to its lesser segment BD. Therefore AD is cut at B in extreme and mean ratio, and the original straight line AB is the greater segment. [CN5, D6.3]

## Proposition 13.6
**Statement:** If a rational straight line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, each of the segments is the irrational straight line called apotome.

**Step 1.** Let the rational straight line have length L, and let its greater and lesser segments in extreme and mean ratio have lengths a and b. Thus L = a + b. Bisect L, and write h = L/2. Set s = a + h and t = 3h. Here sums denote concatenated lengths, and x² denotes the square on length x. [1.10]

**Step 2.** The direct choice is XIII.1, because it uses half the given rational whole rather than half an as-yet-unclassified segment. It gives
s² = 5h².
Also, since squares have the duplicate ratio of their corresponding sides,
L² = 4h² and t² = 9h². [13.1; 6.20]

**Step 3.** The area h² therefore measures each of L², s², and t². Consequently h, s, and t are all commensurable in square with L, and s is commensurable in square with both h and t. Since L is rational, its square is commensurable with the square on the assigned rational straight line. Transitivity of commensurability shows that the same holds for the squares on h, s, and t; hence all three straight lines are rational. [D10.1.2; 10.12; D10.1.3]

**Step 4.** The ratio s²:h² is 5:1, which is not a ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore s and h are incommensurable in length. But h measures t three times, so h and t are commensurable in length. It follows that s and t are likewise incommensurable in length. Together with Step 3, this proves that s and h, and also t and s, are commensurable in square only. [10.9; D10.1.1; 10.13]

**Step 5.** Since s = a + h, the greater segment is a = s − h. Thus it is the remainder when the rational straight line h is subtracted from the rational straight line s, the two being commensurable in square only. Therefore a is irrational and is an apotome. [10.73]

**Step 6.** Likewise,
t − s = 3h − (a + h) = 2h − a = L − a = b.
Since b is positive, this subtracts the lesser rational straight line s from the greater rational straight line t. These are commensurable in square only, so b too is irrational and is an apotome. Hence each segment of the rational straight line cut in extreme and mean ratio is the irrational straight line called apotome. [10.73]

## Proposition 13.7
**Statement:** If three angles of an equilateral pentagon, taken either in order or not in order, be equal, the pentagon will be equiangular.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the given equilateral pentagon, with vertices in boundary order, and write AB = BC = CD = DE = EA = s. Up to cyclic relabelling and reversal, the three selected equal angles occur either at A, B, C or at A, C, D. We treat these two arrangements separately. Side-angle-side is the natural first comparison, since equal adjacent sides and their included angles are given. All diagonals used below are joined by [P1].

**Step 2.** First suppose the angles at A, B, C are equal, each being α. The triangles EAB, ABC, BCD have their two sides of length s and their included angles equal. Hence their bases are equal:
BE = AC = BD = d.
Their base angles are also all equal; denote each by β. In particular,
∠AEB = ∠CDB = ∠BCA = β. [1.4, 1.5, CN1]

**Step 3.** Since BE = BD, the base angles ∠BED and ∠BDE are equal. Adding the equal angles ∠AEB and ∠CDB shows that the pentagon’s angles at E and D are equal; denote each by δ. Put u = ∠ACD and v = ∠BDE. The diagonals divide the angles at C and D so that
α = β + u,   δ = β + v. [1.5, CN2]

**Step 4.** We now compare α and δ by [1.24], since each required triangle comparison already has two corresponding sides equal.

If α > δ, then u > v. In triangles ACD and BDE, AC = BD and CD = DE; therefore u > v gives AD > BE = d. But in triangles ABC and AED, AB = AE and BC = ED, while their included angles are α and δ. Thus α > δ gives AC > AD, or d > AD—a contradiction.

If α < δ, the same two comparisons give respectively AD < BE = d and AC < AD, or d < AD—again a contradiction.

Consequently α = δ. Thus all five angles are equal in the consecutive arrangement. [1.24, CN1]

**Step 5.** Now suppose the three equal angles are at A, C, D, each being α. The triangles EAB, BCD, CDE have two corresponding sides of length s and equal included angles. Therefore
BE = BD = CE,
and all their base angles are equal; call each β. In particular,
∠AEB = ∠CDB = ∠ABE = ∠ECD = β. [1.4, 1.5, CN1]

**Step 6.** In triangle BDE, BE = BD, so ∠BED = ∠BDE. Consequently
∠DEA = ∠BED + ∠BEA
= ∠BDE + ∠CDB
= ∠CDE = α.
Thus the angle at E equals the given angle at D. [1.5, CN2, CN1]

**Step 7.** In triangle BEC, BE = CE, so ∠EBC = ∠BCE. Hence
∠ABC = ∠ABE + ∠EBC
= ∠ECD + ∠BCE
= ∠BCD = α.
Thus the angle at B also equals α. Together with Step 6 and the three given equal angles, this proves that all five angles are equal in the nonconsecutive arrangement as well. The two possible arrangements are exhausted; therefore the equilateral pentagon is equiangular. [1.5, CN2, CN1]

## Proposition 13.8
**Statement:** If in an equilateral and equiangular pentagon straight lines subtend two angles taken in order, they cut one another in extreme and mean ratio, and their greater segments are equal to the side of the pentagon.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the equilateral and equiangular pentagon, with its vertices in order. The straight lines subtending two consecutive angles may be named AC and BD; let their interior intersection be F. We use the direct angle-and-similarity route. Join AD. The triangles ABC, ACD, and ADE divide the pentagon, so its interior angles together equal six right angles. Let u be one fifth of two right angles. Each interior angle of the pentagon is therefore 3u, while the angles of any triangle sum to 5u. [P1, 1.32]

**Step 2.** Since AB = BC and BC = CD, the triangles ABC and BCD are isosceles. Their vertex angles at B and C respectively are 3u, so their base angles are u:
∠BAC = ∠BCA = ∠CBD = ∠BDC = u.
Consequently,
∠ABF = ∠ABC − ∠CBD = 2u,
and
∠FCD = ∠BCD − ∠BCA = 2u. [1.5, 1.32]

**Step 3.** In triangle ABF, the angles at A and B are u and 2u, so the angle at F is 2u. The equal angles at B and F therefore give AF = AB. Similarly, in triangle CDF, the angles at C and D are 2u and u, so its angle at F is 2u; hence DF = CD. Thus AF and DF both equal the side of the pentagon. [1.32, 1.6]

**Step 4.** In triangle BCF, the angles at B and C are both u, so BF = CF. Moreover, in triangle ABF, the angle at B is 2u and exceeds the angle u at A; therefore AF > BF. It follows that AF > CF and, since DF = AF, that DF > BF. Thus AF and DF are indeed the greater segments of AC and BD respectively. [1.6, 1.19]

**Step 5.** The angles of triangle BFC, at B, F, C respectively, are u, 3u, u. Thus triangles ABC and BFC are equiangular in the indicated order. Applying the proportionality theorem for equiangular triangles—the direct theorem for the angle equalities just established—gives
AC : BC = BC : FC.
Likewise, triangles BCD and CFB are equiangular in the indicated order, giving
BD : CD = CB : FB.
Since AF = BC = CD = DF, these proportions become
AC : AF = AF : FC,
and
BD : DF = DF : FB. [1.32, 6.4]

**Step 6.** Each whole diagonal is therefore to its greater segment as that greater segment is to its lesser segment. By the definition of extreme and mean ratio, AC and BD cut one another in extreme and mean ratio; and their greater segments AF and DF are each equal to the side of the pentagon, as required. [D6.3]

## Proposition 13.9
**Statement:** If the side of the hexagon and that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle be added together, the whole straight line has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and its greater segment is the side of the hexagon.

**Step 1.** Let O be the centre of the common circle, and let h and d denote the sides of its inscribed regular hexagon and decagon respectively. Write R for a right angle. Join O to the vertices of each polygon. All these radii are equal (D1.15). Within each polygon, the triangles formed by consecutive radii have their three sides respectively equal, so their angles at O are equal (1.8). These angles together make four right angles (1.13). Hence each central angle of the hexagon is 2R/3, and each central angle of the decagon is 2R/5.

**Step 2.** Let HK be a side of the hexagon. Since OH = OK, the base angles of triangle OHK are equal (1.5); their sum is 2R − 2R/3, so each is 2R/3 (1.32). Thus the triangle is equiangular, and HK = OH (1.6). Consequently the radius equals h. Now let AB be a side of the decagon. In triangle OAB, OA = OB = h and AB = d. Its angle at O is 2R/5, so each base angle is 4R/5 (1.5, 1.32).

**Step 3.** Bisect angle OAB by AC, meeting OB at C (1.9). Then ∠OAC = ∠CAB = 2R/5. Since ∠AOC also equals 2R/5, triangle AOC gives AC = OC (1.6). In triangle ABC, the angles at A and B are respectively 2R/5 and 4R/5; therefore the angle at C is 4R/5 (1.32). Hence AC = AB (1.6). Thus OC = AC = AB = d.

**Step 4.** In triangle ABC, the angle at B is greater than the angle at A. Therefore AC > BC (1.19). Since AC = OC, it follows that OC > CB.

**Step 5.** Because AC bisects angle OAB, the angle-bisector theorem gives OC : CB = OA : AB (6.3). Substituting OA = OB and AB = OC yields OB : OC = OC : CB. Together with OC > CB, this says that OB has been cut at C in extreme and mean ratio, with OC its greater segment (D6.3).

**Step 6.** We now use 13.5 directly, since its hypothesis is exactly the subdivision just obtained: add to OB a straight line equal to its greater segment OC. The resulting whole is cut in extreme and mean ratio, and its greater segment is the original line OB (13.5). Since OB = h and OC = d, this whole is h + d, and (h + d) : h = h : d. Therefore the sum of the hexagon side and the decagon side is cut in extreme and mean ratio, with the hexagon side as its greater segment, as required.

## Proposition 13.10
**Statement:** If an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the given equilateral pentagon, O the centre of its circle, r the radius, and p = AB. Equal chords cut off equal arcs, so the five consecutive arcs are equal. Bisect arc AB at F. Bisecting all five arcs gives ten equal arcs and therefore equal chords; thus d = AF is the side of the inscribed decagon. The central angles AOF and FOB are each 36°. All radii are equal. [D1.15, 3.28, 3.30, 3.29, 3.27]

**Step 2.** The side of the inscribed equilateral hexagon equals r. Indeed, its six equal arcs give central angles of 60°. Each triangle formed by a hexagon side and the two radii to its endpoints is isosceles; its remaining angles are consequently also 60°, and its three sides are equal. It therefore suffices to prove p² = r² + d². [3.28, 3.27, 1.5, 1.32, 1.6]

**Step 3.** Let OF meet AB at H. Triangles OAH and OBH have OA = OB, OH common, and equal included angles. Hence AH = HB and their adjacent angles at H are equal, so both are right angles. Thus AB = 2AH and AH is perpendicular to OF. [1.4, D1.10]

**Step 4.** In the isosceles triangle OAF, the angle at O is 36°, so the angles OAF and AFO are each 72°. Bisect angle OAF by AP, meeting OF at P. Then angle OAP = angle AOP = 36°, whence OP = AP. Also angle PAF = 36° and angle AFP = 72°, so angle APF = 72° and AP = AF. Consequently OP = AP = AF = d. [1.5, 1.32, 1.9, 1.6]

**Step 5.** Apply the right-triangle square theorem to AHP and AHF. Since AP = AF and AH is common, subtraction gives HP² = HF², hence HP = HF. As P and F are distinct points on the line through H, H is the midpoint of PF. Therefore
2OH = 2OP + PF = OP + OF = d + r.
Thus the two legs of the right triangle OHA satisfy 2AH = p and 2OH = r + d. [1.47, CN3, CN2]

**Step 6.** By XIII.9, the sum r + d of the hexagon and decagon sides is cut in extreme and mean ratio, with greater segment r and lesser segment d. We use XIII.4 directly here because its square identity concerns exactly this whole and these two segments. It gives
(r + d)² + d² = 3r². [13.9, 13.4]

**Step 7.** In the right triangle OHA,
AH² + OH² = OA² = r².
The square on twice a segment is four times the square on that segment. Multiplying the preceding equality by four and using Step 5 therefore gives
p² + (r + d)² = 4r². [1.47, 2.4, CN2]

**Step 8.** Add d² to the equality in Step 7 and substitute the equality from Step 6:
p² + 3r² = 4r² + d².
Subtracting 3r² yields p² = r² + d². Since p, r, and d are respectively the pentagon, hexagon, and decagon sides in the same circle, the square on the pentagon side equals the squares on the hexagon and decagon sides together. [CN2, CN3]

## Proposition 13.11
**Statement:** If in a circle which has its diameter rational an equilateral pentagon be inscribed, the side of the pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor.

**Step 1.** Let D be the rational diameter of the given circle, and p the side of its inscribed equilateral pentagon. Inscribe a regular hexagon and denote its side by r [4.15]. Its six central angles are equal, since the radii are equal and the six corresponding chords are equal [D1.15, 1.8]. These angles together make four right angles [1.13]. Thus each central angle is one-third of two right angles. Each corresponding isosceles triangle consequently has all three angles equal [1.5, 1.32], and therefore all three sides equal [1.6]. Hence r is the radius, so r = D/2 and is rational [D10.1.3].

**Step 2.** Let d be the side of the regular decagon inscribed in the same circle. The line r + d is cut in extreme and mean ratio, with r its greater segment [13.9]. Put h = r/2 and t = d + h. Proposition 13.3 applies directly to the lesser segment together with half the greater segment, and gives
 t² = 5h².
This is the direct route we use: express p² as the rectangle contained by a rational line and a fourth apotome.

**Step 3.** Expanding the square on t = d + h gives
 d² + 2dh + h² = 5h²,
so, since r = 2h,
 d² + rd = r²
[2.4]. Also, the square on the pentagon side equals the squares on the hexagon and decagon sides together [13.10]. Consequently,
 p² = r² + d² = 2r² − rd = r(2r − d),
where the last equality is the distributive relation for rectangles [2.1].

**Step 4.** Set a = 5h and q = a − t. Because r is the greater segment in Step 2, d < r; therefore
 q = 5h − (d + h) = 2r − d > 0.
Moreover,
 a² = 25h²,   t² = 5h²,   r² = 4h².
Thus a and t are rational straight lines and are commensurable in square: their squares and the square on the rational line r are measured by h² [D10.1.2, D10.1.3].

**Step 5.** The ratio a²:t² is 25:5. This cannot be the ratio of a square number to a square number: otherwise, since 25 is square, 5 would also be square [8.24]. Hence a and t are incommensurable in length [10.9]. They are therefore rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and their difference q = a − t is an apotome [10.73].

**Step 6.** The difference between the squares on the whole a and its annex t is
 a² − t² = 20h² = (2t)².
Now a²:(2t)² = 25:20. Since 25 is square and 20 is not, this is not a ratio of square numbers [8.24]; therefore a and 2t are incommensurable in length [10.9]. On the other hand, a:r = 5:2, so the whole a is commensurable in length with the rational line r. Accordingly, taking r as the rational straight line set out, q is a fourth apotome [D10.3.4].

**Step 7.** Steps 3 and 4 give p² = rq. Thus the square on p is the rectangle contained by the rational straight line r and the fourth apotome q. The side of such an area is minor [10.94]. Therefore the side of the inscribed equilateral pentagon is the irrational straight line called minor, as required.

## Proposition 13.12
**Statement:** If an equilateral triangle be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the triangle is triple of the square on the radius of the circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be an equilateral triangle inscribed in the given circle, and let q denote a right angle. Since AB = BC = CA, the angles of ABC are equal; their sum is 2q, so each is 2q/3. [D1.20, 1.5, 1.32]

**Step 2.** Find the centre O. Draw AO and produce it through O to meet the circle again at D; join BD and BO. We choose this diameter route because it directly supplies a right triangle for the square calculation. Write r for the radius. Then AO = BO = OD = r, and AD = 2r. [3.1, P1, P2, D1.15, D1.17]

**Step 3.** D is neither B nor C: otherwise the angle at the third vertex of ABC would be an angle in a semicircle and therefore right, contrary to Step 1. Since AD is a diameter, ∠ABD = q, and consequently ∠ADB is acute. The angle ∠ACB is also acute. Thus C and D both lie in the greater segment bounded by chord AB. Use the same-segment theorem here, since it directly compares the two angles subtending AB: ∠ADB = ∠ACB = 2q/3. The angle sum in triangle ABD therefore gives ∠BAD = q/3. [3.31, 3.21, 1.32]

**Step 4.** Because OA = OB, triangle AOB has ∠ABO = ∠BAO. Since O lies on AD, ∠BAO = ∠BAD = q/3. Moreover, O lies between A and D, so BO lies inside ∠ABD. Hence ∠OBD = q − q/3 = 2q/3. But ∠BDO = ∠BDA = 2q/3. The equal angles in triangle BOD therefore give BD = BO = r. [D1.15, 1.5, 1.6]

**Step 5.** In the right-angled triangle ABD, the square on AD equals the squares on AB and BD:
AD² = AB² + BD². [1.47]
Since AD is divided at O into two equal radii, the square-on-a-divided-line identity gives
AD² = AO² + OD² + 2(AO·OD) = 4r². [2.4]
Substituting BD² = r² and subtracting that square yields AB² = 3r². Thus the square on the side of the inscribed equilateral triangle is triple the square on the radius of the circle. [CN3]

## Proposition 13.13
**Statement:** To construct a pyramid, to comprehend it in a given sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid.

**Step 1.** Let the given sphere be generated by a semicircle with diameter AB and centre O. Thus A and B are on the sphere, O is its centre, and OA = OB. Cut off HB equal to one third of AB, so that AH = 2HB. Then H lies between O and B. Writing t = OH, we have HB = 2t, OA = OB = 3t, AH = 4t, and AB = 6t. [D11.14, D11.16, D11.17, D1.15, 6.9]

**Step 2.** In the plane of the generating semicircle, draw HC perpendicular to AB, meeting the semicircular circumference at C. At H erect HK perpendicular to that plane. Consequently HK is perpendicular to AB. Since AB is perpendicular to both HC and HK at their intersection H, it is perpendicular to the plane Π through those two lines. [1.11, 11.12, D11.3, 11.4]

**Step 3.** In Π describe the circle Γ with centre H and radius HC. As the generating semicircle turns about AB, C describes precisely this circle: its distance from H remains HC, and HC turns in the plane perpendicular to AB at H. Therefore every point of Γ lies on the given sphere. This perpendicular circular section will provide the base of the pyramid. [P3, D11.14]

**Step 4.** Write XY² for the area of the square on XY. Squares have the duplicate ratio of their sides, so the square on a length nt is n² times the square on t. Join OC. Since OC is a radius of the generating circle, OC = OA = 3t. The triangle OHC is right-angled at H; hence
OC² = OH² + HC²,
and therefore
HC² = 9t² − t² = 8t². [6.20, P1, D1.15, 1.47, CN3]

**Step 5.** Construct an equilateral triangle as a model; its angles are equal. In Γ inscribe a triangle EFG equiangular with that model. Its equal angles give equal sides, so EFG is equilateral. For its side–radius relation, use XIII.12 directly, since it supplies exactly the required equality without an auxiliary chord construction:
EF² = FG² = GE² = 3HC² = 24t². [1.1, 1.5, 4.2, 1.6, 13.12]

**Step 6.** Join A to E, F, and G, and join H to those three points. Since AB is perpendicular to Π, each of AHE, AHF, and AHG is right-angled at H. Also HE = HF = HG = HC, since these are radii of Γ. Consequently
AE² = AH² + HE² = 16t² + 8t² = 24t²,
and likewise AF² = AG² = 24t². Comparing with Step 5, and using the duplicate-ratio property of squares, all six edges AE, AF, AG, EF, FG, and GE are equal. [P1, D11.3, D1.15, 1.47, 6.20, CN2]

**Step 7.** The triangle EFG and the three triangles AEF, AFG, and AGE therefore bound a pyramid with four equilateral faces. Its vertex A lies outside the base plane, and all four vertices lie on the given sphere; thus the pyramid is comprehended in that sphere. If s denotes its common edge, then s² = 24t², whereas the square on the sphere’s diameter is
AB² = (6t)² = 36t² = (3/2)·24t² = (3/2)s².
Hence the required pyramid has been constructed in the given sphere, and the square on the sphere’s diameter is one and a half times the square on the side of the pyramid. [D11.12, D11.14, 6.20]

## Proposition 13.14
**Statement:** To construct an octahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, as in the preceding case; and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is double of the square on the side of the octahedron.

**Step 1.** Let AC be the prescribed diameter of the sphere. Bisect AC at O. In a plane π containing AC, describe the circle Γ with centre O and radius OA. Through O draw a straight line perpendicular to AC, meeting Γ at B and D, so that A, B, C, D occur successively around Γ. Thus AC and BD are diameters, and OA = OB = OC = OD. [1.10, 1.11, P2, P3, D1.15, D1.17]

**Step 2.** At O set up a straight line perpendicular to π, and produce it in both directions. This line and AC lie in one plane. In that plane describe another circle with centre O and radius OA, meeting the perpendicular at E and F on opposite sides of π. Consequently OE = OF = OA, and all six segments OA, OB, OC, OD, OE, OF are equal. [11.12, P2, 11.2, P3, D1.15]

**Step 3.** Join AB, BC, CD, DA, and join each of E and F to each of A, B, C, D. We compare these edges directly by side–angle–side, since the construction supplies equal radii and included right angles. Indeed, the four triangles OAB, OBC, OCD, ODA and the eight triangles OEA, OEB, OEC, OED, OFA, OFB, OFC, OFD each have two sides equal to OA and their included angle right. They are therefore equal by I.4, and their bases—the twelve proposed edges of the octahedron—are all equal. [P1, D11.3, P4, 1.4, CN1]

**Step 4.** Each angle of ABCD stands in a semicircle of Γ: the angles at B and D subtend diameter AC, and those at A and C subtend diameter BD. Hence all four angles are right. Together with the equalities established in Step 3, this makes ABCD a square, with O inside it. Form the pyramids with common base ABCD and vertices E and F. They lie on opposite sides of π; their common base is internal to their union. Their union is therefore bounded by precisely the eight triangles EAB, EBC, ECD, EDA, FAB, FBC, FCD, FDA. [3.31, D1.22, D11.12]

**Step 5.** Each of these eight triangles is equilateral, since its three sides are among the equal edges of Step 3. Moreover, any two have their three corresponding sides equal: I.8 gives equal corresponding included angles, and I.4 then gives equality of the triangles themselves. Thus the solid is contained by eight equal and equilateral triangles, and is an octahedron. [D1.20, 1.8, 1.4, D11.26]

**Step 6.** In the circle constructed in Step 2, take the semicircle with diameter EF passing through A, and revolve it about EF. It generates a sphere with centre O. Because OA is perpendicular to EF, the point A describes exactly Γ during the revolution. Thus A, B, C, D lie on the generated spherical surface, while E and F remain on that surface as the fixed endpoints of the diameter. The sphere therefore comprehends the constructed octahedron. Since AC passes through O and has both endpoints on its surface, AC is a diameter of this sphere, as prescribed. [D11.14, D11.16, D11.17]

**Step 7.** The angle ABC is right, so the square on AC equals the sum of the squares on AB and BC. Since AB = BC, this sum is twice the square on AB. But AC is the diameter of the sphere and AB is a side of the octahedron. Therefore the square on the diameter of the sphere is double the square on the side of the octahedron. The required construction and proof are complete. [3.31, 1.47, CN2]
